title: Verbs that need an object, and verbs that link

article_json.also_called: Transitivity, copular verbs and the dative alternation
article_json.one_line: This tells you whether a verb takes an object at all, and which verbs take a describing word instead.
article_json.short_answer: Ask *what?* after the verb. If there is an answer, the verb takes an object. After a linking verb, use a plain describing word.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Does this verb need something after it, and what kind of something?

body.text: Three kinds of verb, and they behave differently
Some verbs act on something. Some never do. A third group does neither: it holds a subject and a description together, and it is the group that causes the most trouble.

body.gloss: a verb that takes an object / one that does not

show_first.text: The storm damaged four roofs.
The old warehouse collapsed overnight.
The committee approved the budget.

body.name_line: The first and third are **transitive** and the second is **intransitive**.
body.anchor_line: Ask *what?* after each verb. Two of them have an answer, and one of them does not.

body.text: The linking verbs, in full
This list is closed. Fourteen verbs can hold a subject and a description together, and no others do it.

body.lead_in: These fourteen verbs take a describing word, not an *-ly* word:
items: *be*, *seem*, *appear*
*become*, *get*, *turn*, *grow*, *go*
*remain*, *stay*, *keep*
*look*, *sound*, *feel*, *taste*, *smell*

body.text: Several of them also work as ordinary action verbs. When they do, the *-ly* word is correct again, and the meaning is different.

body.question: Is the verb describing the subject, or saying how something was done?

options.label: linking, so a plain describing word
options.use_it_when: The word after the verb tells you what the subject is or is like.
options.example: The corridor grew dark.

options.label: acting, so an *-ly* word
options.use_it_when: The word after the verb tells you how the action was carried out.
options.example: The queue grew slowly.

a.text: The queue grew long.
a.means: By the end there were a lot of people in it.

b.text: The queue grew slowly.
b.means: People joined it a few at a time.

a.text: The leaves turned brown.
a.means: They changed colour.

b.text: The leaves turned slowly.
b.means: They were moving round in the wind.

a.text: The fault appeared serious.
a.means: It looked like a bad problem.

b.text: The fault appeared suddenly.
b.means: It came out of nowhere.

a.text: The kitchen smells damp.
a.means: There is a damp smell in there.

b.text: The kitchen smells strongly of paint.
b.means: The paint smell in there is powerful.

body.deciding_factor: Ask whether the word after the verb describes the subject. If it does, the *-ly* ending has to go.
body.trap: You were taught that describing words go with nouns and *-ly* words go with verbs. That splits the world in the wrong place, because a linking verb is followed by a description of the subject.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The choice shows up most in Speaking Part 2, where *it looked amazing* and *it sounded strange* are constant.

body.text: The rule for what follows a linking verb
After one of the fourteen linking verbs, use a plain describing word. The *-ly* form belongs after an action verb.

body.lead_in: Four linking verbs, each followed by a plain describing word.

items.text: The rules remain unclear for part-time students.
items.gloss: Nobody has explained them properly.

items.text: The milk in the fridge has gone sour.
items.gloss: It is no longer safe to drink.

items.text: The applicants stayed calm during the delay.
items.gloss: Nobody got upset while they waited.

items.text: The estimate seems low for a job this size.
items.gloss: It looks as though it will cost more.

body.so_what: Not one of them takes an *-ly* ending, and every one describes the subject.

body.text: Two orders for a verb with two things after it
*Give*, *send*, *show*, *offer* and *lend* allow both orders. *Explain*, *describe*, *suggest*, *mention* and *report* allow only one. This is fixed for each verb.

body.caption: Some verbs give you a choice of order; some give you one.
rows: gave the form to the office
sent a notice to the tenants
explained the change to the staff
described the route to the group
suggested a date to the panel
footnotes: The dashes are not gaps in the language. Those three verbs have no person-first order at all.

body.text: Three errors from getting the class wrong

body.wrong: Traffic on the bypass has become seriously.
body.right: Traffic on the bypass has become serious.
body.why_it_happens: *Become* is a verb, and *-ly* words are taught as the ones that follow verbs. *Become* links the subject to a description, so the description has no ending.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-ly* off anything following *be*, *become*, *seem*, *look*, *feel*, *stay* or *remain*.

body.wrong: The accident was happened at the junction.
body.right: The accident happened at the junction.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence describes something the subject did not choose, and that feels like something being done to it. Only a verb that takes an object can be turned round this way.
body.smallest_fix: Ask *what?* after the verb. No answer means no *was* form: *happened*, *occurred*, *arrived*.

body.wrong: I really enjoyed during the placement.
body.right: I really enjoyed the placement.
body.why_it_happens: *Enjoy* feels like *relax*, which needs nothing after it. *Enjoy* always takes an object, even when it is only *it* or *myself*.
body.smallest_fix: Add the thing that was enjoyed straight after the verb.

body.heard: An adverb describes a verb, so after a verb you use the *-ly* word.
also_known_as: *-ly* words go with verbs
body.truth: That holds for action verbs and fails for the fourteen linking verbs. In *the results look bad*, the word describes the results, not the looking, so it takes no ending.
body.what_to_do: Learn the fourteen. After any of them, ask what is being described, and use the plain word when the answer is the subject.

body.mechanism: Arabic builds a passive shape from most verbs regularly, so the pattern is easy to extend to English verbs that take no object.
body.wrong: Three deliveries were arrived this morning.
body.right: Three deliveries arrived this morning.
body.fix: Only verbs that can take an object have this form. *Arrive*, *happen* and *sleep* do not.

body.headline: Ask *what?* after the verb. No answer means no object.

table.caption: Three kinds of verb, and what each one takes.

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Which is right? *The soup tastes salty.* / *The soup tastes saltily.*
items.answer: *The soup tastes salty.*
items.why: *Taste* is on the list of fourteen, so the word describes the soup.

items.prompt: Why is *The meeting was occurred on Tuesday* wrong?
items.answer: *Occur* takes no object, so it has no turned-round form. Write *The meeting occurred on Tuesday.*
items.why: Only a verb that can take an object can be rewritten that way.

terms_introduced.gloss: a verb that takes an object / one that does not

related_articles.reason: the describing part itself, and what it attaches to
the closed list of verbs that cannot be turned round
the seven shapes these verb classes produce
every verb with the patterns it allows, in one table

intents: work out whether a verb needs an object
choose the right word after look, feel or seem

title: The order English puts things in

article_json.also_called: Canonical word order, adverbial position, verb–object adjacency and inversion
article_json.one_line: This explains why English order is fixed where other languages are free, and names the four places it flips.
article_json.short_answer: Subject, verb, object, and nothing between the verb and the object. Extra parts go after the object or at the front.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Why can't I move the words around?

body.text: Order is what English uses instead of endings
Many languages put an ending on each word to show its job. Once the endings are there, the words can move about and the meaning holds.
English dropped almost all of those endings. Position took over the job, so the order is not a style preference. It is what tells your reader who did what.

body.lead_in: The same three words, in two orders. Nothing else changes.

items.text: The inspector questioned the driver.
items.gloss: The driver was the one answering questions.

items.text: The driver questioned the inspector.
items.gloss: Now the inspector is the one answering.

items.text: The storm damaged the sea wall.
items.gloss: The wall is broken and the storm did it.

items.text: It's the wall that's damaged, not the road.
items.gloss: The road is fine. The wall is the problem.

body.so_what: Swapping the two names swapped who did it. No word changed shape.

body.text: Nothing comes between a verb and its object
The object sits against its verb. Every extra part waits until after the object.
One rule covers a whole family of errors that other books treat one at a time. If the object is there, nothing gets in front of it.

body.lead_in: Three kinds of extra part, all pushed out to the far side of the object.

items.text: She speaks Portuguese very well.
items.gloss: Her Portuguese is strong.

items.text: We reviewed the applications carefully.
items.gloss: Nobody rushed through them.

items.text: The team finished the survey on Thursday.
items.gloss: Thursday was the last day of the work.

body.so_what: In each one the object touches the verb, and the extra part sits behind it.

body.text: The order two or three extra parts take

body.caption: How, then where, then when. That is the usual order.
footnotes: Full sentence: *They worked quietly in the back office all morning.*
Any of the three can move to the front instead, and then it comes first.

body.lead_in: Two extra parts at a time, in the order the table gives.
body.dimension: the order of two extra parts

items.text: The results were published online last Friday.
items.gloss: You could see them on a website from Friday.

items.text: We met at the depot on Tuesday.
items.gloss: Tuesday was the day, and the depot was the place.

items.text: They cycle to the campus every day.
items.gloss: It is how they get in each morning.

body.so_what: Where comes before when in all three. Reversing it sounds wrong to a reader.

body.text: Four places where the order flips

body.gloss: putting the helping verb in front of the subject

show_first.text: Has the committee published the figures?
Never before had the service been so unreliable.
Had the funding arrived earlier, the work would be finished.

body.name_line: That flip is called **inversion**.
body.anchor_line: One mechanism, three uses. The helping verb steps in front of the subject and nothing else moves.

body.lead_in: The order flips in four places and nowhere else:
items: in a question: *Have the trains started running?*
after a negative word at the front: *Never had the queue been so long.*
in a formal *if*-sentence with *if* removed: *Had we known, we would have waited.*
after *so* and *neither* in a short reply: *So did we.*

body.text: The second and third are formal and risky, and they are covered where they belong. The point here is that all four are one mechanism, not four rules.
Three errors that come from moving words

body.wrong: She speaks very well Portuguese.
body.right: She speaks Portuguese very well.
body.why_it_happens: The describing part belongs to the verb, so it feels natural to keep it next to the verb. English keeps the object next to the verb instead.
body.smallest_fix: Move the describing part to the end, behind the object.

body.wrong: We met on Tuesday at the depot.
body.right: We met at the depot on Tuesday.
body.why_it_happens: Several languages put the time first because it sets the scene. English works outwards from the action, so the place comes before the time.
body.smallest_fix: Put where before when, or move the time part to the front of the sentence.

body.wrong: Could you tell me where is the registration office?
body.right: Could you tell me where the registration office is?
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is a question overall, so the flipped order feels required all the way through. Only the outer question flips; the part inside goes back to normal order.
body.smallest_fix: Put the subject back in front of the verb after *where*, *what*, *how* or *why*.

body.heard: English word order is subject, verb, object, and it never changes.
also_known_as: English order is completely fixed
body.truth: It holds for ordinary statements, and it flips in four named places: questions, after a negative word at the front, in a formal *if*-sentence, and after *so* or *neither*. Everywhere else it holds.
body.what_to_do: Use the normal order unless you are doing one of those four things. The flip is a device, not a free choice.

body.mechanism: Tamil puts the verb at the end of the sentence, and endings on the words show which one is the doer.
body.wrong: The council the parking charges last month increased.
body.right: The council increased the parking charges last month.
body.fix: Put the verb straight after the subject, then the object, then the time.

body.mechanism: Chinese puts the time and place in front of the verb, so those parts naturally land between the subject and the verb.
body.wrong: The engineers at the depot on Monday checked the pumps.
body.right: The engineers checked the pumps at the depot on Monday.
body.fix: Keep the subject, verb and object together. Send time and place to the end.

body.headline: Subject, verb, object, then how, where, when.

table.caption: The default order, and the one place it flips in everyday use.
rows: worked quietly at the depot all day
I asked when the wall would be repaired.

terms_introduced.gloss: putting the helping verb in front of the subject

related_articles.reason: what the extra parts are, before you order them
the three positions an *-ly* word takes, stated exactly
why the flip is dropped inside a longer sentence
the formal flip after a negative word, with its risk warning

intents: put the words of a sentence in the right order

title: Ordinary names, specific names, and two nouns together

article_json.also_called: Common nouns, proper nouns and compound nouns
article_json.one_line: This lets you tell an ordinary naming word from the name of one particular thing, and write a two-word name correctly.
article_json.short_answer: Ordinary names stay lower case: *a city*. The name of one particular thing takes a capital: *Norland*. In a two-noun name the first noun stays singular.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Which naming words take a capital letter, and can I put two of them together?

body.text: Two sorts of naming word, written two different ways
A noun names something. Most nouns name a kind of thing, so they fit any member of that kind: *a river*, *a college*, *a delay*. These stay lower case wherever they sit in a sentence.

A smaller group names one particular thing and nothing else: *Norland*, *Tuesday*, *March*. These take a capital letter every time, because the capital is what marks them out as the name of one thing.

body.caption: A capital letter marks the name of one particular thing.
rows: a river runs through the town
the Ashfield runs through the town
the new college opened in May
footnotes: Languages, nationalities and the names of subjects taught as courses also take a capital: *Arabic*, *Norwegian*, *Environmental Science*.

body.lead_in: Only the naming word changes here. Watch the capital letter follow it.

items.text: A new footbridge opened last spring.
items.gloss: Some footbridge somewhere opened. You are not saying which.

items.text: The Marlow footbridge opened last spring.
items.gloss: One particular footbridge opened, and you have named it.

items.text: Two of the volunteers study engineering.
items.gloss: They are engineering students.

items.text: Two of the volunteers study at Brackenfield.
items.gloss: They study at one particular place, and you have named it.

body.so_what: The capital letter is not decoration. It tells the reader you mean one particular thing, not a kind of thing.

body.text: Two nouns together, where the first one describes the second

English packs meaning by putting one noun in front of another. The second noun is the thing you are talking about. The first one narrows it down, so *traffic congestion* is congestion, and *energy policy* is policy.
When one noun describes another, put it in front, and leave it singular. Any plural ending goes on the second noun.

body.lead_in: Only the number of things changes here. Watch which noun takes the *-s*.

items.text: The council published its energy policy in June.
items.gloss: One policy about energy is now public.

items.text: Three councils published their energy policies in June.
items.gloss: Three separate policies about energy are now public.

items.text: Traffic congestion is worst on the ring road.
items.gloss: The traffic backs up there more than anywhere else.

items.text: We need a bicycle rack outside every station entrance.
items.gloss: There should be somewhere to leave bicycles at each station.

body.so_what: The first noun never takes *-s*, however many things there are. The count lives on the second noun.

body.text: What goes wrong with names and two-noun groups

body.wrong: The report compares three energies sources across the county.
body.right: The report compares three energy sources across the county.
body.why_it_happens: There are three of them, so the plural ending feels as though it should go on both words. In English the first noun is doing the work of a describing word, and describing words never take *-s*.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-s* off the first noun. Leave it on the second.

body.wrong: The Norland is the fastest growing town in the county.
body.right: Norland is the fastest growing town in the county.
body.why_it_happens: *The* points at one particular thing, and a place name already does that on its own. Adding *the* is saying the same thing twice, so English leaves it out.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *the* in front of the name of a town, a city or a person.

body.label: Three place names that keep *the*, and they are a closed set

items.text: Country names that are plural or that contain an ordinary noun keep *the*.
items.example: The Netherlands sent two observers to the conference.

items.text: Rivers, seas, oceans, deserts and mountain ranges keep *the*.
items.example: The delta has widened by half a kilometre since 2015.

items.text: Buildings and organisations named with *of* keep *the*.
items.example: The University of Sandmouth runs the survey every autumn.

body.heard: A noun is the name of a person, a place or a thing.
also_known_as: nouns are naming words for things you can touch
body.truth: That misses most of the nouns in an essay. *Progress*, *a decision*, *the meeting* and *unemployment* are all nouns, and none of them is a person, a place or a thing you can touch.
body.what_to_do: Use a test instead of a meaning. If you can put *the* or *a* in front of the word, or add *-s* to it, it is a noun.

body.headline: Capital for one particular thing. First noun singular.

table.caption: One row per decision.

article_json.no_practice_reason: No practice point covers ordinary and specific names or two-noun compounds. They are written conventions the reference alone carries.

related_articles.reason: whether a noun can be counted at all, which decides everything in front of it
how the *-s* is spelt, and the nouns that do not take one
why most place names take no word in front of them

intents: write the name of a place or an organisation correctly

title: Time in the world, and the shape of the verb

article_json.also_called: Tense and aspect: where the twelve tenses come from
article_json.one_line: This shows you how the whole verb system fits together, so twelve tenses turn into three times and two switches.
article_json.short_answer: English changes the verb itself for two times only: now and before now. Everything else adds a helping verb. *writes*, *has written*, *will write*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How many tenses does English have, and how do they fit together?

body.text: Time is one thing. The shape of the verb is another
Ask when something happens and you get an answer about the world. Ask what shape the verb takes and you get an answer about English. The two do not always match.
*The ferry leaves at six tomorrow.* The verb sits in its present shape and the event sits in the future. So the shape of the verb is a choice you make, not a clock you read.

body.gloss: the form of a verb that shows when

show_first.text: The Ashfield clinic opens at eight.
The Ashfield clinic opened late yesterday.
Two nurses write the notes each evening.

body.name_line: The shape the verb takes there is its **tense**.
body.anchor_line: English changes the verb itself for two of these only: now and before now. Everything further needs a helping verb in front of it.

body.gloss: how the action is spread out in time

show_first.text: The crew paints the railings each spring.
The crew is painting the railings today.
The crew has painted the railings already.

body.name_line: What changes across those three is the **aspect**.
body.anchor_line: The time is the same in all three. What moves is how much of the event you are showing the reader.

body.text: Two switches sit on top of the time you pick

body.lead_in: Whatever time you are talking about, two switches are available:
items: *have* plus the third form links the event back from a later point
*be* plus the *-ing* form shows the event in the middle of happening

body.gloss: the plain form: no *be + -ing*, no *have* + third form

show_first.text: The council funds two youth centres.
The council funded two youth centres.
The council will fund two youth centres.

body.name_line: With both switches off, the form is called **simple**.
body.anchor_line: That is the plainest thing you can say about an event. It is a choice you make, not something missing.

body.gloss: the *-ing* form, used for something in the middle of happening

show_first.text: The team is writing the safety report.
The team was writing it all Friday.
The team will be writing it next week.

body.name_line: A form built from *be* and *-ing* is called **continuous**.
body.anchor_line: Nothing in any of those says the job is finished. That is what the *-ing* is doing.

body.gloss: a form that links an earlier time to a later time

show_first.text: The trust has painted every bridge on the line.
The trust had painted it before the inspection.
The trust will have painted it by June.

body.name_line: A form built from *have* and the third form is called **perfect**.
body.anchor_line: Each one stands at a later point and looks back at an earlier one. The two points are what the form is for.

body.text: Why books say English has twelve tenses

Three times, two switches, and every combination gets a name. Three multiplied by four is twelve. The number comes from the layout, so it is a way of showing the system rather than twelve separate things to learn.

body.caption: Three times down the side, two switches across the top.
footnotes: Only two cells change the verb itself: *writes* and *wrote*. Every other cell adds a helping verb.
The same twelve, with how often each one is used, are in [th_tense_grid].

body.lead_in: Only the switches move here. The time stays at now in all four.

items.text: The centre runs a free class on Saturdays.
items.gloss: That is what happens week after week.

items.text: The centre is running a free class this month.
items.gloss: It is on at the moment and it will stop.

items.text: The centre has run the class since March.
items.gloss: It started in March and it is still going.

items.text: The centre has been running the class since March.
items.gloss: The same thing, with the length of time in view.

body.so_what: The time never moved. What moved is how much of the event the reader can see.

body.heard: English has twelve tenses, and you have to learn all twelve before you can write anything.
also_known_as: the twelve tenses
the tense table
body.truth: Twelve is the size of the layout, not the size of the job. English changes the verb itself in two places only, now and before now. The other ten forms are those two with a helping verb added.
body.what_to_do: Learn the two switches instead of twelve names. Six of the twelve carry almost all of everyday English, and [th_tense_grid] marks which six.

body.headline: Three times, two switches. That is the whole system.

table.caption: One row per switch setting, at any of the three times.
rows: looking back from a later point
how long it has been going on

terms_introduced.gloss: the form of a verb that shows when
how the action is spread out in time
the plain form: no *be + -ing*, no *have* + third form
the *-ing* form, used for something in the middle of happening
a form that links an earlier time to a later time

article_json.no_practice_reason: This is the map of the whole system. The practice ladder drills one tense at a time and never the grid.

related_articles.reason: all twelve forms in one table, with how often each is used
the single idea behind every *have* + third form

title: Things you can count, and things you cannot

article_json.also_called: Countable and uncountable nouns, and the nouns that are both
article_json.one_line: This decides whether a noun can take *-s*, whether it can take *a*, and which word for amount goes in front of it.
article_json.short_answer: Ask whether you can say *two* of it. *Two reports*, yes, so it takes *a* and *-s*. *Two informations*, no, so write *information* alone or *a piece of information*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I know whether a word can take *-s* and *a*?

body.text: One question decides three things about a noun

Put *two* in front of the noun and say it out loud. *Two reports* works. *Two equipments* does not. That single test tells you whether the noun can take *-s*, whether it can take *a*, and which word for amount goes with it.

body.gloss: things you can count one by one / stuff you measure

show_first.text: The panel received four reports and one letter.
The site needs new equipment before the winter.
Two of the applications arrived after the deadline.

body.name_line: A noun you can count is **countable**. A noun you measure instead is **uncountable**.
body.anchor_line: *Reports* and *applications* come in ones you can point at. *Equipment* comes in an amount, so English never counts it directly.

body.caption: The answer to *can I say two of it?* settles the rest.
footnotes: *Some*, *any*, *a lot of*, *plenty of* and *no* go with both, which is why they are the safe choice when you are unsure.

body.lead_in: Only the noun changes here. Watch what has to change around it.

items.text: The tutor gave me three suggestions about the draft.
items.gloss: She made three separate points about my writing.

items.text: The tutor gave me some advice about the draft.
items.gloss: She told me what to do about my writing.

items.text: Many households now heat their water with a heat pump.
items.gloss: Heat pumps are common in homes now.

items.text: There isn't much evidence that the scheme reduced traffic.
items.gloss: Almost nothing shows that the scheme worked.

body.so_what: Nothing moved except the noun, and the noun dragged the word for amount and the verb ending with it.

body.text: The ten nouns that look countable and are not

Some nouns name something that arrives in separate pieces, so they feel countable. English still treats them as an amount. The list below is short and it is worth learning as a list, because each one is highly visible when it goes wrong.

body.caption: None of these ever takes *-s* or *a*. All of them take *is*.
footnotes: *Furniture*, *luggage*, *homework*, *traffic*, *transport* and *weather* behave the same way.
*Researches* and *trainings* do occur in some technical and institutional writing. Treat all ten as uncountable and nobody will mark you down.

body.text: To count an uncountable noun, count the container instead: *a piece of*, *an item of*, *a body of*, *two pieces of*.

body.lead_in: Same noun each time. Only the counting phrase in front of it changes.

items.text: The tutor left one piece of feedback on each section.
items.gloss: She wrote one comment per section.

items.text: The depot ordered six items of safety equipment.
items.gloss: Six separate pieces of kit are on the way.

items.text: A growing body of research links air quality to absence rates.
items.gloss: More and more studies show the same link.

items.text: Can you send me a bit of information about the deadline?
items.gloss: You want to know when the deadline is.

body.so_what: The noun never changes. The phrase in front of it does the counting.

body.text: Nouns that are both, and the meaning moves when they switch
A group of nouns sits on both sides. The two versions are not the same word used loosely. They mean different things, and the *a* or the *-s* is what tells the reader which one you mean.

body.caption: Adding *a* or *-s* changes what the word refers to.
rows: what you have learnt by doing
*a paper* = an article, or a newspaper
*works* = a factory, or an artist's output
footnotes: *Chicken*, *iron* and *coffee* work the same way: the material against one object or one serving.

body.lead_in: The same noun twice. Only *a* or *-s* changes, and the meaning moves with it.

items.text: She has ten years of experience in transport planning.
items.gloss: She has been doing this work for ten years.

items.text: Cycling to the depot in February was an experience.
items.gloss: It was one memorable occasion, and not a comfortable one.

items.text: The engineer published a paper on flood defences.
items.gloss: She wrote one article and it came out.

items.text: The wrapping is made from recycled paper.
items.gloss: The material it is made of has been used before.

body.so_what: One small word decides whether you mean the stuff or one particular item of it.

body.text: What goes wrong when the test is skipped

body.wrong: The team collected many evidences from three different sites.
body.right: The team collected a great deal of evidence from three different sites.
body.why_it_happens: The evidence arrived in separate pieces, so it feels countable, and *many* asks for a plural. English stores *evidence* as an amount, so the counting has to move to a phrase in front of it.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the *-s* and change *many* to *a great deal of* or *a lot of*.

body.wrong: My supervisor gave me an advice about the second draft.
body.right: My supervisor gave me some advice about the second draft.
body.why_it_happens: It was one thing she said, so *an* feels right. *An* means one countable item, and *advice* is not counted in ones, so English uses *some* or *a piece of* instead.
body.smallest_fix: Replace *an* with *some*, or write *a piece of advice*.

body.wrong: The amount of students applying has risen sharply since 2019.
body.right: The number of students applying has risen sharply since 2019.
body.why_it_happens: *Amount* and *number* both mean how much there is, so they feel like the same word. *Amount* goes with things you measure and *number* goes with things you count.
body.smallest_fix: Count the noun. If you can say *two* of it, use *the number of*.

body.mechanism: Russian marks how many by changing the ending of the noun and the words around it, and there is no separate word for *a*.
body.wrong: Council published informations about the closure.
body.right: The council published information about the closure.
body.fix: Choose the word in front of the noun first, then leave the noun alone.

body.heard: Uncountable nouns are things you cannot see or touch.
also_known_as: abstract nouns are uncountable
body.truth: Meaning does not decide it. *Furniture* and *luggage* are things you can carry, and both are uncountable. *An idea* and *a decision* are things you cannot touch, and both are countable.
body.what_to_do: Ignore what the thing is like. Say *two* in front of the noun. If that sounds wrong, treat the noun as uncountable, whatever it names.

body.headline: Say *two* in front of it. That answer decides everything else.

table.caption: One row per outcome of the test.

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Fix this: *We need more furnitures for the reading room.*
items.answer: *We need more furniture for the reading room.*
items.why: *Furniture* is measured, not counted, so it never takes *-s* even though chairs can be counted.

items.prompt: Which is right? *a large number of complaints* or *a large amount of complaints*?
items.answer: *a large number of complaints*
items.why: You can say *two complaints*, so the noun is counted, and counted nouns take *number*.

title: States, actions, and what a verb needs around it

article_json.also_called: State verbs, transitivity, and verbs that work both ways
article_json.one_line: This tells you why some verbs refuse the *-ing* form, and why some verbs need something after them.
article_json.short_answer: A verb that describes a state, not an action, stays in the plain form. *I know the answer*, never *I am knowing the answer*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Why can I say *I am reading* but not *I am knowing*?

body.text: Some verbs describe a state, and a state has no middle
You can be in the middle of reading, so *I am reading* works. You cannot be in the middle of knowing. You either know a thing or you do not, so English keeps the verb plain.

body.gloss: a verb that describes a state, not an action

show_first.text: The report contains three recommendations.
Most residents prefer the earlier bus.
The site belongs to the water company.

body.name_line: A verb like that is called a **state verb**.
body.anchor_line: None of those three is something you do. Each one is something that is simply the case, so the continuous form has nothing to show.

body.text: The five families of state verb

body.caption: Five meanings, and the verbs that carry them stay plain.
rows: *like, love, hate, prefer, want, need, wish*
*have, own, belong, contain, include, consist of*
footnotes: This is a list of meanings, not a fixed list of words. The next section shows why.

body.lead_in: Every one of these is about a state, so every verb stays plain.

items.text: The building belongs to the university now.
items.gloss: That is who owns it.

items.text: I need the figures before Thursday.
items.gloss: Without them the work stops.

items.text: The scheme costs the council very little.
items.gloss: It is cheap to run.

items.text: Most drivers know the new route already.
items.gloss: They have learned it and they use it.

body.so_what: Not one of them is an activity you could stop halfway through.

body.text: The same word can name a state or an action
Several of these verbs have two meanings. One is a state and stays plain. The other is something you actually do, and then the continuous is right, because there is a middle to be in.

body.question: Is this something I am doing, or something that is simply the case?

options.label: the state meaning, plain form
options.use_it_when: The verb reports how things are: what you own, what you think, how something strikes you.
options.example: I think the second design is cheaper.

options.label: the action meaning, *-ing* form
options.use_it_when: The verb reports an activity you could stop and start: considering, meeting, tasting, behaving.
options.example: I am thinking about the second design.

a.text: They have two offices in the city.
a.means: Those are the offices the firm owns.

b.text: They are having a meeting in the city.
b.means: The meeting is going on right now.

a.text: The supervisor sees the problem.
a.means: She understands what has gone wrong.

b.text: The supervisor is seeing the contractor.
b.means: They have an appointment together.

a.text: The water tastes strange today.
a.means: That is what it is like when you drink it.

b.text: The inspector is tasting the water today.
b.means: She is carrying out a test on it.

a.text: He is careful with the equipment.
a.means: That is what he is like as a worker.

b.text: He is being careful with the equipment.
b.means: He is behaving that way today, and normally he does not.

body.deciding_factor: If you could stop halfway through it, the *-ing* form is available. If you could not, the verb stays plain.
body.trap: You reason that the state is true right now, so the form for right now must be correct. Being true now is not the same as being under way now.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The pair matters most in Speaking Part 1, where *I am wanting* and *I am knowing* are heard in the first minute.

body.text: A state verb takes the plain form. Put it in the *-ing* form only when you have switched to a meaning that names something you do.

body.lead_in: The verb is the same word each time. Only the meaning has switched.

items.text: The panel appears satisfied with the figures.
items.gloss: That is how they come across.

items.text: The author is appearing at the Marlow book fair.
items.gloss: She is going there to speak.

items.text: I feel this is the wrong week for it.
items.gloss: That is my opinion about the timing.

items.text: She is feeling much better since Tuesday.
items.gloss: Her health is improving.

body.so_what: *Appear* and *feel* did not change. What changed is whether they name a state or an activity.

body.text: What a verb needs after it, and what it refuses
A second thing is decided by the verb rather than by you: whether an object can follow it. *Discuss* takes one straight away. *Arrive* takes none at all, so nothing you add can become its object.

body.caption: Three groups, and the third one is where errors come from.
rows: Sales rose. The firm raised prices.
footnotes: The third group is the one to watch. The same verb can name the thing that changes or the person who changes it.

body.lead_in: One verb from the third group, used both ways. Watch what sits in front of it.

items.text: Bus fares increased by a fifth last year.
items.gloss: The fares went up. Nobody is named.

items.text: The operator increased bus fares by a fifth.
items.gloss: The operator did it, and the sentence says so.

items.text: The side door closes at six.
items.gloss: That is what the door does at six.

items.text: The caretaker closes the side door at six.
items.gloss: The caretaker is the one who shuts it.

body.so_what: The verb did not change shape. What changed is whether the sentence names the person behind the change.

body.wrong: I am not understanding the second question.
body.right: I do not understand the second question.
body.why_it_happens: You want to say that the problem is happening right now, and the *-ing* form is the one that means right now. *Understand* names a state, and a state has no middle to be in.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the helping verb and the *-ing*: *I do not understand*.

body.wrong: The committee discussed about the parking plan.
body.right: The committee discussed the parking plan.
body.why_it_happens: *Talk* and *argue* both need *about*, so *discuss* looks as though it should too. *Discuss* takes its object straight, with nothing in between.
body.smallest_fix: Take *about* out. The same goes for *enter*, *answer* and *approach*.

body.wrong: Two serious delays were happened on the Norland line.
body.right: Two serious delays happened on the Norland line.
body.why_it_happens: *Was* plus the third form sounds formal, and formal feels safer in an essay. *Happen* cannot take an object, so there is nobody for that form to hide.
body.smallest_fix: Use the verb on its own: *happened*, *occurred*, *rose*, *fell*.

body.label: Two places where a state verb turns up in the *-ing* form anyway

items.text: *Love*, *like* and *hate* take the *-ing* form in relaxed speech and in advertising.
items.example: I am loving the new cycle lane.

items.text: *Be* takes the *-ing* form when it means behaving that way for the moment.
items.example: The landlord is being difficult about the deposit.

body.heard: *Know*, *want* and *like* can never be used in the *-ing* form.
also_known_as: the list of stative verbs
verbs that have no continuous
body.truth: It is not the word that blocks the *-ing* form, it is the meaning. *I am seeing the supervisor at four* is normal English, because *see* there means meet, and meeting is something you do.
body.what_to_do: Ask what the verb means in this sentence rather than checking it against a list. Keep the plain form for a state, and write *I do not understand*, never *I am not understanding*.

body.mechanism: Tamil marks an event as still going on with an ending on the verb, and that ending is available with verbs of knowing and wanting.
body.wrong: I am knowing the timetable.
body.right: I know the timetable.
body.fix: Use the plain form for knowing, wanting and owning, even when you mean right now.

body.headline: No middle, no *-ing*. No object, no doer in front.

table.caption: One row per question you ask about the verb.
rows: Could I stop halfway through it?
Can something come straight after it?
Does the sentence name who did it?

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Which one is right? *She is owning three flats.* / *She owns three flats.*
items.answer: *She owns three flats.*
items.why: Owning is a state. There is no middle of owning to be in.

items.prompt: Why is *The strike was occurred in April* wrong?
items.answer: *Occur* cannot take an object, so it cannot be turned round. Write *The strike occurred in April.*
items.why: Nothing is done to the strike. The strike is the whole event.

title: Making a noun mean more than one

article_json.also_called: Regular and irregular plural formation
article_json.one_line: This gives you every way English turns one thing into more than one, including the endings that change and the nouns that do not change at all.
article_json.short_answer: Add *-s*. After a hissing sound add *-es*: *watches*. After a consonant and *y*, write *-ies*: *studies*. The rest are a short list to learn.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I write the *more than one* form of this word?

body.text: The spelling rules, and the nouns that ignore them

Most nouns add *-s* and nothing else happens. Five spelling rules cover the rest, and two of them exist because of sound rather than spelling. Everything outside those five is a list, and the list is below.

body.caption: Five spelling rules cover every regular plural in English.
body.form_line: the singular noun + *-s*, with five spelling changes

cells: bus → buses; class → classes; branch → branches; box → boxes
study → studies; city → cities; policy → policies
survey → surveys; delay → delays; key → keys
leaf → leaves; knife → knives; half → halves; shelf → shelves
roof → roofs; belief → beliefs; chief → chiefs; cliff → cliffs
*-s* or *-es*, and it is not predictable
photos, pianos, kilos, studios; potatoes, tomatoes, heroes, echoes
both accepted: volcanoes / volcanos; mosquitoes / mosquitos

sub_tables.caption: These change shape instead of adding an ending. There are not many.
These look the same whether there is one or a hundred.
Academic writing runs on these, and the singular is the half people forget.
rows: a section heading in a report

gaps.note: There is no rule. Which nouns take *-es* has to be learnt, so the common ones are listed in the cell instead.

examples.text: Both cities cut their bus services in the same year.
examples.gloss: Two places reduced how often the buses run.

examples.text: The council reviewed its funding criteria in March.
examples.gloss: It looked again at the standards it uses to decide.

examples.text: Twelve species of bird now nest on the reserve.
examples.gloss: Twelve different sorts of bird breed there.

examples.text: Two of the knives were missing from the kitchen.
examples.gloss: Somebody had taken two knives.

examples.text: The team collected three analyses of the same water sample.
examples.gloss: The sample was tested three separate times.

examples.text: Most of the children walk to school along the towpath.
examples.gloss: They go on foot, next to the canal.

notes: *Criteria* and *phenomena* are the more-than-one forms. One of them is *a criterion* and *a phenomenon*.
*People* is the everyday plural of *person*. *Persons* survives only in legal and official notices.
*Fishes* exists and means different species of fish, not more fish.

body.text: Nouns that only ever come in the plural shape
A small group of nouns has no singular at all. They take *are* rather than *is*, and you cannot put *a* in front of them. To count them, English uses *a pair of* or *a set of*.

body.caption: No singular, always *are*, counted with *a pair of* or *a set of*.
rows: the scissors are in the drawer
her savings are in a fixed account
footnotes: *Goods*, *earnings*, *clothes* and *thanks* behave the same way.
A dash means the noun has no counting phrase in normal use.

body.lead_in: Only the noun changes. Watch the verb stay plural every time.

items.text: The premises are closed until the survey is complete.
items.gloss: Nobody can go into the building for now.

items.text: Her savings were wiped out by two years of repairs.
items.gloss: The repairs cost her everything she had put aside.

items.text: I've left the scissors on the shelf by the door.
items.gloss: You will find them on that shelf.

body.so_what: None of these has a singular form, so the verb after them is always plural.

body.headline: Add *-s*. Five spelling rules and three short lists cover the rest.

table.caption: One row per group.

related_articles.reason: which nouns can take a plural at all
where the apostrophe goes once a noun is plural
the words for amount that need a plural noun after them

article_json.false_rule_absent_reason: The false rules about plurals attach to countability, not to spelling. They are named and killed in th_countability, which owns that decision.

title: Saying what is generally true

article_json.also_called: The present simple
article_json.one_line: This is the form for what does not depend on today, so you can state a fact, a habit, a state or a timetable.
article_json.short_answer: Use the base form. Add *-s* for *he*, *she*, *it* or one thing. *The depot opens at seven.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say what is generally true?

body.text: This form says: that is how things are
Use it for anything that does not depend on today. Facts, habits, rules, states and timetables all sit here. Nothing in the form says the event is going on at this minute.
So it is the ordinary form for explaining how a system works, and the ordinary form for describing a chart or a process.
Build it from the base form, and add *-s* for one thing

body.caption: Only the *he* row changes. Every other row is the base form.
body.form_line: the base form, plus *-s* for *he*, *she*, *it* or one thing

rows.note: The only row that changes, and the *-s* moves onto *does*.

sub_tables.caption: A short answer repeats the helping verb and stops.
Add *do* to a positive sentence when you are contradicting somebody.
rows: somebody has just said it does not
to insist that it is true

examples.text: The Verdon depot paints the bridge railings every third summer.
examples.gloss: It happens on a three-year cycle.

examples.text: The surveyor writes a short note after each visit.
examples.gloss: That is part of the job every time.

examples.text: We don't paint over the numbers on the posts.
examples.gloss: The numbers have to stay readable.

examples.text: Does he write the summary himself?
examples.gloss: The question is who does that piece of work.

notes: The *-s* moves onto *does* in a negative or a question. Never *he doesn't paints*.
There is no positive short form here. *I'm paint* and *he's paint* are not English.
Spelling of the *-s* ending is set out in [th_spelling_and_sound_of_endings].

body.text: The five jobs this one form does

body.caption: Five different meanings, and one form covers all of them.
headers: Words that turn up with it
rows: a fact that does not change
Coastal towns flood more often than inland ones.
something you do again and again
She cycles to the depot twice a week.
a situation that is set to last
My brother works for a housing charity.
a state rather than an action
The trust owns four listed buildings.
The last ferry leaves at eleven.
footnotes: The last row is about tomorrow, not about every day. The form does not care.

body.lead_in: One example for each row above, in the same order.
body.dimension: the job the form is doing

items.text: Older buildings lose heat through the roof first.
items.gloss: That is true of older buildings in general.

items.text: I check the water meter on the first of the month.
items.gloss: It is a habit, once a month.

items.text: The charity runs three shops in the town.
items.gloss: That is the situation, and it is not about to change.

items.text: The new pass costs less than a weekly ticket.
items.gloss: That is the price.

items.text: The course starts on the second Monday in October.
items.gloss: That is the date in the timetable.

body.so_what: Five different meanings came out in the same shape, and no time word was needed for three of them.

body.text: Use the present simple when the sentence is about how things are, not about what is going on at this moment.

body.lead_in: None of these is happening at the moment of speaking.

items.text: Night buses run every forty minutes at weekends.
items.gloss: That is the pattern, whether one is running now or not.

items.text: My flat faces the railway, so mornings are noisy.
items.gloss: That is where the windows point.

items.text: The trust employs eleven people across the two sites.
items.gloss: That is the size of the staff.

body.so_what: Each one is true today, was true last month, and says nothing about this minute.

body.text: Where the *-s* goes missing, and where it goes twice

body.wrong: The scheme costs very little and help two hundred families.
body.right: The scheme costs very little and helps two hundred families.
body.why_it_happens: You put the *-s* on the first verb and then move on. By the time the second verb arrives, the subject is several words behind and out of mind.
body.smallest_fix: Check every verb in the sentence, not only the one nearest the subject.

body.wrong: Does the council knows about the leak?
body.right: Does the council know about the leak?
body.why_it_happens: The subject is one thing, so the *-s* feels compulsory. *Does* has already taken it, and English marks it in one place only.
body.smallest_fix: After *do*, *does* or *did*, go back to the base form.

body.wrong: The new bins collects more waste than the old ones.
body.right: The new bins collect more waste than the old ones.
body.why_it_happens: An *-s* on the noun and an *-s* on the verb look as though they belong together. They are opposites: the *-s* on the verb means one, and on the noun it means more than one.
body.smallest_fix: Count the subject. More than one means no *-s* on the verb.

body.heard: The present simple is the tense for things you do every day.
also_known_as: the habit tense
the everyday tense
body.truth: Habits are one of its five jobs. It also carries facts, states, rules and timetables. *The last ferry leaves at eleven* is about tomorrow evening, not about every day of your life.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the sentence is about how things are rather than what is under way now. If it is, this is the form, however often the thing happens.

body.mechanism: Chinese verbs keep one shape whatever the subject is, and who is doing the action is shown by the words in front of the verb.
body.wrong: My neighbour repair bicycles at the weekend.
body.right: My neighbour repairs bicycles at the weekend.
body.fix: Add *-s* whenever the subject is *he*, *she*, *it* or a single thing.

body.headline: Base form everywhere, plus *-s* for one thing.

title: Saying what is going on around now

article_json.also_called: The present continuous (present progressive)
article_json.one_line: This is the form for something under way, so you can say what is happening now and what is only temporary.
article_json.short_answer: Use *am*, *is* or *are* with the *-ing* form. *The crew is painting the bridge this week.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say that something is going on at the moment?

body.text: This form says: it has started and it has not finished
Use it when the event has a middle and you are standing in it. Nothing in the form says the job will be finished, so it is the natural way to talk about a temporary arrangement.
Around now counts as well as right now. *House prices are rising* is true this year, even though nothing is going up as you read it.
Build it from *be* and the *-ing* form

body.caption: Only *be* changes. The *-ing* form never moves.
body.form_line: *am*, *is* or *are* plus the *-ing* form of the main verb

rows.note: Only one short form here. *Amn't* is not standard English.

sub_tables.caption: A positive short answer never uses a short form.
*He's* has two expansions, and the next word tells you which.

examples.text: They're painting the Verdon bridge this week.
examples.gloss: The work started and it is not done yet.

examples.text: She is writing the Norland report at the moment.
examples.gloss: That is the job in front of her today.

examples.text: We aren't painting the west span until the funding lands.
examples.gloss: That part of the work is on hold.

examples.text: Is he writing the summary or the covering note?
examples.gloss: The question is which piece he has in hand.

notes: *I'm not* is the only short form for the *I* row. The *am* contracts, never the *not*.
Never *Yes, I'm.* A short answer cannot end on a short form.
The negative question for *I* is *Aren't I painting?*, which is irregular and standard.

body.caption: The event started before now and has not reached its end.

spec.caption: A bar across now, with no end marked

body.text: The four jobs this form does

body.caption: Four meanings, and only the first is about this minute.
headers: Words that turn up with it
rows: it is going on right now
The lift is stuck between floors.
I am covering the late shift this month.
it is a change still under way
Rents in the old quarter are climbing again.
it is fixed in a diary
We are meeting the contractor on Thursday.
footnotes: The fourth row is about the future. The full set of future forms is in [th_the_futures].

body.lead_in: One example per row above, in the same order.
body.dimension: the job the form is doing

items.text: The alarm is going off again in the stairwell.
items.gloss: You can hear it as you speak.

items.text: She is staying with her sister until the flat is ready.
items.gloss: It is an arrangement with an end in sight.

items.text: Fewer households are heating with gas each winter.
items.gloss: The pattern is shifting and has not settled.

items.text: I am seeing the housing officer on Friday morning.
items.gloss: The appointment is already made.

body.so_what: Only the first one is happening at this minute, and all four use the same form.

body.text: Use *be* plus the *-ing* form when the event has a middle and you are inside it, or when the situation has an end in sight.

body.lead_in: Each of these has an end the speaker can see coming.

items.text: The library is running reduced hours during the repairs.
items.gloss: It will go back to normal when the work ends.

items.text: I'm cycling in while the bus route is closed.
items.gloss: It is not how I normally travel.

items.text: Two of the wards are taking patients from the north site.
items.gloss: It is an arrangement for the moment.

body.so_what: In every one of them, things will go back to how they were.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The number of cyclists rising every year since the lane opened.
body.right: The number of cyclists is rising every year since the lane opened.
body.why_it_happens: The *-ing* form looks like a verb and feels like enough. On its own it carries no time, so the group of words is not yet a sentence.
body.smallest_fix: Put *is* or *are* in front of the *-ing* form.

body.wrong: I am wanting a room away from the road.
body.right: I want a room away from the road.
body.why_it_happens: The want is real at this minute, and this is the form for this minute. Wanting is a state, and a state has no middle to stand in.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the helping verb and the *-ing*: *I want*.

body.wrong: The council is repair the footbridge this month.
body.right: The council is repairing the footbridge this month.
body.why_it_happens: *Is* already feels like the verb of the sentence, so the second word is left in its dictionary shape. After *be*, the main verb always takes *-ing*.
body.smallest_fix: Add *-ing* to the word after *am*, *is* or *are*.

body.label: Two uses that look like errors and are not

items.text: *Always* with this form is a complaint, not a habit.
items.example: The upstairs tap is always dripping.

items.text: A state verb takes this form when it names something you are doing.
items.example: The technician is testing how the sample tastes.

body.heard: The present continuous means it is happening at this exact moment.
also_known_as: the now tense
present continuous equals now
body.truth: Right now is one of its four jobs. *Rents are climbing again* is not happening this second, and *We are meeting the contractor on Thursday* has not happened at all yet.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the situation is temporary rather than whether it is happening this second. Keep *now* as the commonest case of temporary, not as the rule.

body.headline: *Be* plus *-ing*. Started, not finished.

title: Saying that something belongs to something

article_json.also_called: The possessive *'s* and the *of*-phrase
article_json.one_line: This gives you the two ways English shows that one thing belongs to another, and tells you which one this sentence needs.
article_json.short_answer: For people and organisations use *'s*: *the council's decision*. For things use *of*: *the cost of the scheme*. Plural already ending in *-s* takes only an apostrophe.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Do I write *the council's plan* or *the plan of the council*?

body.text: Two ways to say the same thing, and they are not equal

English has two ways to link an owner to what it owns. One puts the owner first with an apostrophe. The other puts the thing first and joins the owner on with *of*. Both are correct, and each sounds right in different places.

body.gloss: the form that says something belongs to somebody: *the council's*, *my*

show_first.text: The council's decision was published on Friday.
My supervisor's comments arrived a week late.
The students' union voted against the fee.

body.name_line: The marked part is the **possessive**.
body.anchor_line: The apostrophe is doing the work of a whole phrase. *The council's decision* is a shorter way of saying *the decision belonging to the council*.

body.text: Where the apostrophe goes

body.caption: Look at the owner word first. Its ending decides the apostrophe.
footnotes: The rule is about the owner word, never about the thing owned.

body.lead_in: One owner or several. Only the apostrophe moves.

items.text: The driver's account of the collision was recorded.
items.gloss: One driver said what happened.

items.text: The drivers' accounts of the collision were recorded.
items.gloss: Several drivers each said what happened.

items.text: The women's changing rooms reopened in April.
items.gloss: The rooms for women are usable again.

items.text: I borrowed my sister's bike for the week.
items.gloss: The bike belongs to my sister and I am using it.

body.so_what: The apostrophe sits after the owner word. Where it sits tells the reader whether there is one owner or several.

body.text: Which of the two forms this sentence wants

body.question: Is the owner alive, or an organisation of people?

options.label: *'s*
options.use_it_when: The owner is a person, an animal, a group of people, a country, or a length of time.
options.example: The committee's report runs to ninety pages.

options.label: *of*
options.use_it_when: The owner is a thing or an idea, or the owner phrase is long.
options.example: The cost of the flood defences has doubled.

a.text: The surveyor's report arrived on Thursday.
a.means: A person wrote it, and she is the one you are pointing at.

b.text: The report of the survey arrived on Thursday.
b.means: The report came out of a piece of work, not out of a named person.

a.text: The town's population fell by four per cent.
a.means: You are treating the town as a body of people.

b.text: The population of the town fell by four per cent.
b.means: The same fact, written in the flatter form a report would use.

a.text: The roof of the sports hall leaks in two places.
a.means: The building has a leaking roof.
a.span: The roof of the sports hall

b.text: The sports hall's roof leaks in two places.
b.means: The same fact, and it sounds ordinary rather than formal.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: of the sports hall / sports hall's

a.text: She gave two weeks' notice before leaving.
a.means: She told them two weeks before her last day.

b.text: She gave notice two weeks before leaving.
b.means: The same fact, with the time as an ordinary time phrase.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: two weeks' notice / notice two weeks

body.deciding_factor: If the owner could sign its name, use *'s*. If it could not, use *of*, unless *'s* sounds ordinary to you.
body.trap: You were taught that *'s* is for people and *of* is for things, so you avoid *'s* with anything that is not a human being. Towns, companies, committees and lengths of time all take *'s* freely.
body.register_note: *Of* is the flatter, more formal choice and it carries most academic writing. *'s* is shorter and it is what speech uses. Both belong in Task 2.

body.text: The two forms overlap widely, so most of the time either is correct. The one place the choice is forced is length: a long owner phrase goes after *of*, because a reader cannot hold six words and then meet an apostrophe.
Use *'s* when the owner is a person, a group or a length of time. Use *of* when the owner phrase is long.

body.lead_in: The owner phrase gets longer each time. Watch where it has to move.

items.text: The tenant's letter was passed to the housing office.
items.gloss: One tenant wrote in and the letter was sent on.

items.text: The letter of the tenant who reported the damp was passed on.
items.gloss: The person who wrote it is identified by what she did.

marks.span: of the tenant who reported the damp

items.text: Next year's budget has already been agreed.
items.gloss: The money for the coming year is settled.

items.text: That's my flatmate's laptop, not mine.
items.gloss: The laptop belongs to the person I live with.

body.so_what: As the owner phrase grows, the apostrophe stops working and *of* takes over.

body.text: *A friend of mine*, and why *a friend of me* is wrong
When you want to say *one of the ones belonging to me*, English uses *of* plus the possessive form, not the object form. So it is *a friend of mine* and *a colleague of my sister's*.

body.lead_in: Only the word after *of* changes, and only one version is English.

items.text: A colleague of mine reviewed the drainage plan.
items.gloss: Somebody I work with looked at the plan.

items.text: Two neighbours of ours objected to the extension.
items.gloss: Two people who live near us wrote in against it.

items.text: That old photograph of my grandmother's is in the hall.
items.gloss: The photograph belongs to my grandmother.

body.so_what: The word after *of* is always the belonging form: *mine*, *ours*, *theirs*, or a noun with *'s*.

body.text: What goes wrong with the apostrophe

body.wrong: The tenant's on the third floor all reported the same fault.
body.right: The tenants on the third floor all reported the same fault.
body.why_it_happens: The word ends in *-s* and an apostrophe often goes with *-s*, so the two get joined. An apostrophe never makes a plural. It only ever marks belonging or a missing letter.
body.smallest_fix: Ask whether anything belongs to the tenants. If not, delete the apostrophe.

body.wrong: The scheme lost it's funding halfway through the year.
body.right: The scheme lost its funding halfway through the year.
body.why_it_happens: Every other belonging form takes an apostrophe, so *its* looks as though it should too. *It's* is already taken: it is the short form of *it is* and *it has*.
body.smallest_fix: Read it aloud as *it is*. If that makes no sense, write *its* with no apostrophe.

body.wrong: A friend of me works at the recycling centre.
body.right: A friend of mine works at the recycling centre.
body.why_it_happens: *Of* is followed by the object form everywhere else, so *me* looks right. In this one pattern *of* is followed by the belonging form instead.
body.smallest_fix: Change *me* to *mine*, *us* to *ours*, *them* to *theirs*.

body.heard: You can only use *'s* with people. Everything else takes *of*.
also_known_as: the apostrophe is for living things
body.truth: Organisations, places, vehicles and lengths of time all take *'s* in ordinary written English: *the government's response*, *the city's transport plan*, *a day's work*, *the train's arrival time*.
body.what_to_do: Use *'s* for people, groups, places and time. Use *of* when the owner is an idea or when the owner phrase is more than about three words long.

body.headline: Look at the owner word. Its ending decides the apostrophe.

title: Always, or just now?

article_json.also_called: Present simple or present continuous?
article_json.one_line: This lets you choose between two present forms that are both correct, so the sentence says whether the situation lasts.
article_json.short_answer: Ask whether it lasts. Permanent or repeated, use *she teaches*. Temporary or still moving, use *she is teaching*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I choose between *I work* and *I am working*?

body.text: Both are correct, and they say different things
*He lectures at the college* and *He is lecturing at the college* are both good English. Neither is more advanced than the other. A reader hears a real difference between them.
So the choice is not about the form. It is about whether the situation is set to last, or has an end somewhere in view.
Is this permanent, or is there an end in sight?

body.question: Does this situation last, or does it have an end in sight?

options.label: present simple
options.use_it_when: It lasts, it repeats, or it is a fact, a rule, a state or a timetable.
options.example: The market opens at six on Saturdays.

options.label: present continuous
options.use_it_when: It is temporary, it is under way at the moment, or it is a change that has not settled.
options.example: The market is opening later while the road is dug up.

a.text: He lectures at the Brackenfield college.
a.means: That is his job, and it is not about to change.

b.text: He is lecturing at the Brackenfield college.
b.means: He is there for this term, and after that who knows.

a.text: The tap leaks.
a.means: The tap has a fault, and it has had it for a while.

b.text: The tap is leaking.
b.means: Water is coming out of it while you stand there.

a.text: Fewer families rent in the town centre.
a.means: That is how the housing market is, stated as a fact.

b.text: Fewer families are renting in the town centre.
b.means: The shift is happening now and has not finished.

a.text: The ferry leaves at six.
a.means: That is the time printed in the timetable.

b.text: The ferry is leaving.
b.means: It is pulling away from the quay this moment.

body.deciding_factor: Permanent or repeated, use the plain form. Temporary or still moving, use *be* plus the *-ing* form.
body.trap: You were told that the *-ing* form means now, so anything true at this minute seems to need it. Plenty of things are true now without being under way now.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The choice pays hardest in Speaking Part 1, where *I usually cycle in* and *I am cycling more at the moment* answer two different questions.

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

steps.ask: Would this still be true in six months?

verdict.example: The clinic opens at eight on weekdays.
verdict.why: Nothing about it depends on today, so the plain form is right.

steps.ask: Can you see an end to it?

branches.answer: Yes — this term, until March, while the road is closed

verdict.example: I am covering the late shift this month.
verdict.why: An end in sight is what this form is for.

steps.ask: Is it a change that is still moving?

verdict.example: Rents in the old quarter are climbing again.
verdict.why: The change has not settled, so the verb stays open.

branches.answer: No — you are stating how things stand

verdict.example: Rents in the north of the town are lower.
verdict.why: You are reporting a fact, not a movement.

body.text: Most sentences stop at the first question. The second and third exist because a change and a temporary arrangement both fail the six-month test for different reasons.
The two forms, side by side

body.caption: One adds an ending. The other adds a helping verb and an ending.
rows: the base form on its own
footnotes: Both forms are built in full, with negatives and questions, in [th_present_simple] and [th_present_continuous].

body.lead_in: The same speaker, the same job, and only the length of the arrangement changes.

items.text: I work in the records office on the second floor.
items.gloss: That is where the speaker is based.

items.text: I am working in the records office until the audit ends.
items.gloss: The speaker has been moved there for a while.

items.text: She teaches two evening classes a week.
items.gloss: That is her normal timetable.

items.text: She's teaching two evening classes while the tutor is away.
items.gloss: It is cover, and it will stop when he comes back.

body.so_what: Adding an end date dragged the verb across to the other form every time.

body.text: Use the present simple for what lasts. Use the present continuous for what is temporary or still moving.

body.lead_in: No time expression in any of these. The verb is doing the work alone.

items.text: The heating comes on at five in the morning.
items.gloss: That is how the timer is set.

items.text: The heating is coming on far too early.
items.gloss: Something is wrong with it at the moment.

items.text: Public transport carries most of the city centre traffic.
items.gloss: That is how the city moves people.

body.so_what: Nothing in the words around the verb decided these. The verb itself carried the meaning.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: At the moment I am preferring the earlier train.
body.right: At the moment I prefer the earlier train.
body.why_it_happens: *At the moment* looks like a signal for the *-ing* form, so it drags the verb with it. Preferring is a state, and a state stays in the plain form even when the time word says now.
body.smallest_fix: Leave the time words alone and put the state verb in the plain form.

body.wrong: Since the charge came in, traffic in the centre falls steadily.
body.right: Since the charge came in, traffic in the centre is falling steadily.
body.why_it_happens: A fall in traffic sounds like a fact, and facts take the plain form. This one is a movement that has not stopped, and a movement takes the *-ing* form.
body.smallest_fix: Ask whether the number has settled. If it is still moving, use *is* plus *-ing*.

body.heard: Present continuous is for now, and present simple is for every day.
also_known_as: now versus every day
the two present tenses rule
body.truth: It breaks in both directions. *Rents are climbing again* is not happening this second, and *The ferry leaves at six* is about one departure tomorrow rather than every day.
body.what_to_do: Swap the pair for permanent against temporary. Treat right now as the commonest kind of temporary, which is why the old rule works often enough to survive.

body.headline: Does it last? Plain form. Does it end? *-ing* form.

table.caption: One row per situation.
rows: temporary, with an end in sight
a state rather than an action

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Which one is right? *My sister lives in Sandmouth.* / *My sister is living in Sandmouth.*
items.answer: Both, and they mean different things.
items.why: The first is where she lives. The second means she is there for now and will move on.

items.prompt: Why is *These days I am owning two bicycles* wrong?
items.answer: Owning is a state. Write *These days I own two bicycles.*
items.why: *These days* does not force the *-ing* form. A state verb keeps the plain form.

how the *-ing* form is built, in full
the verbs that settle the choice on their own

title: The word *a* in front of a noun

article_json.also_called: The indefinite article *a* / *an*
article_json.one_line: This tells you when a noun needs *a* in front of it, and whether to write *a* or *an* before this particular word.
article_json.short_answer: Use *a* the first time you mention one countable thing. Write *an* only when the next word starts with a vowel sound: *an hour*, *a university*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When do I put *a* in front of a word, and when is it *an*?

body.text: What *a* tells your reader

*A* means one, and it means the reader does not yet know which one. You are introducing something for the first time. That is why the next sentence can switch to *the*: by then the reader knows which one you mean.

body.lead_in: Watch the same noun come back in the second sentence with a different word in front of it.

items.text: A cycle lane was added last summer.
items.gloss: There is a cycle lane there now, and this is the first you have heard of it.

items.text: The cycle lane has already been resurfaced twice.
items.gloss: The same lane, which you now know about, has been repaired twice.

items.text: She has taken a job at the recycling centre.
items.gloss: She works there now, and you did not know about the job.

items.text: A second survey was commissioned in the same year.
items.gloss: They paid for another survey, and this is its first mention.

body.so_what: *A* opens the door on something new. *The* is what you use once the reader is already inside.

body.text: The four jobs *a* does

body.caption: Four different sentences, one word doing four different things.
headers: What the reader takes from it
rows: a leak was reported on Monday
you have not heard about this leak
she is a governor at the college
a bicycle costs less to run than a car
this is true of bicycles in general
footnotes: The fourth job is the one that surprises people. *A* can make a general statement about a whole kind of thing.

body.text: *A* or *an* is decided by sound, not by spelling
Say the next word out loud. Vowel sound at the start, write *an*. Consonant sound at the start, write *a*.

body.lead_in: Every one of these has a first letter that points the wrong way. Say them and you get the right answer.

items.text: She waited an hour outside the housing office.
items.gloss: She was there for sixty minutes.

items.text: He is applying to a university in the north.
items.gloss: He wants a place there.

items.text: The tenant wrote to an MP about the damp.
items.gloss: She contacted the person who represents her.

items.text: It is a one-way street, so the lorry had to reverse.
items.gloss: Traffic only goes in one direction there.

items.text: The panel gave an honest account of the delay.
items.gloss: They said what really happened.

body.so_what: *Hour* begins with a written *h* and a spoken vowel, so it takes *an*. *University* begins with a written vowel and a spoken *y*, so it takes *a*.

body.caption: The letter at the front lies in both directions.
footnotes: Some older writing uses *an hotel* and *an historic*. Both are dated. *A hotel* and *a historic* are the ordinary forms now.

body.text: Where a singular noun is left bare and should not be

body.wrong: Government should invest more in public transport.
body.right: Governments should invest more in public transport.
body.why_it_happens: You mean governments in general, and a general statement feels as though it needs no word in front of it. English only allows that with plurals and with uncountable nouns, so the singular has to change.
body.smallest_fix: Make the noun plural, or put *the* or *a* in front of it.

body.wrong: The report describes a new measures for reducing waste.
body.right: The report describes new measures for reducing waste.
body.why_it_happens: *A* is the word you reach for when something is new to the reader, and these measures are new. *A* also means one, so it cannot sit in front of a plural noun.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *a* in front of a plural, or make the noun singular.

body.wrong: She is studying for an university degree in engineering.
body.right: She is studying for a university degree in engineering.
body.why_it_happens: *U* is a vowel letter, so *an* looks correct. The choice runs on sound, and *university* starts with the sound of *y*.
body.smallest_fix: Say the word out loud. If it starts with a *y* or *w* sound, use *a*.

body.mechanism: Chinese marks how many with a counting word between the number and the noun, and it has no separate word that means *one of a kind not yet known*.
body.wrong: She is teacher at the college in Norland.
body.right: She is a teacher at the college in Norland.
body.fix: Put *a* in front of a singular job or role, even when the sentence feels complete.

body.heard: Use *an* before a vowel: *a*, *e*, *i*, *o*, *u*.
also_known_as: an goes before the five vowel letters
body.truth: That is a rule about letters, and the choice runs on sound. It gets *an hour* wrong, because the *h* is silent, and it gets *a university* wrong, because the *u* is said like *you*.
body.what_to_do: Say the next word out loud and listen to the first sound. Use the letters only when you cannot hear the word in your head.

body.headline: *A* introduces. The sound of the next word picks *a* or *an*.
