title: Talking about a finished event

article_json.also_called: The past simple
article_json.one_line: This is the form for something that happened and finished, so you can tell somebody what took place.
article_json.short_answer: Use the past form. Regular verbs add *-ed*: *painted*. Irregular verbs change shape: *wrote*. One form for every subject.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say what happened and finished?

body.text: This form says: it happened, and it is over
Use it when the event sits inside a stretch of time that has closed. The stretch is often named, and often just understood by both of you.
It is the spine of any story. One finished event after another, in the order they happened, is what a listener expects to hear.
One form for every subject, and *did* for the rest

body.caption: Every row is identical. The past simple does not change for the subject.
body.form_line: the past form of the verb, and *did* plus the base form for a negative or a question

rows.note: No *-s* anywhere. The past simple has no person endings.

sub_tables.caption: A short answer repeats *did* and stops.
A regular verb hides a difference that an irregular verb shows.
*Be* is the one verb that still changes for the subject.

examples.text: The depot painted the railings in 2019.
examples.gloss: The work was done that year.

examples.text: She wrote the Marlow chapter last winter.
examples.gloss: That chapter is finished.

examples.text: We didn't paint the lower panels at all.
examples.gloss: Those panels were left as they were.

examples.text: Did they write to every household on the estate?
examples.gloss: The question is how wide the letter went.

notes: After *did*, the main verb goes back to the base form. Never *he didn't wrote*.
There is no positive short form. *I'd painted* is a different form altogether.
Add *did* to a positive sentence to contradict somebody: *The council did approve it.*
The full list of irregular past forms is grouped by pattern in [th_irregular_verbs].

body.caption: One point, back there, with nothing joining it to now.

spec.caption: A single closed point in past time

body.text: The stretch of time is closed, however recent it is
Use the past simple when the stretch of time you have in mind is over, whether that stretch ended a decade ago or a minute ago.

body.lead_in: The time words move from very recent to very distant. The verb does not care.

items.text: The lights went out about ten seconds ago.
items.gloss: It has just happened, and it is over.

items.text: The council approved the parking scheme last March.
items.gloss: The decision was taken then.

items.text: Both mills closed before my grandmother was born.
items.gloss: They shut a very long time ago.

items.text: I dropped the keys somewhere between the gate and the door.
items.gloss: It happened on the walk in.

body.so_what: Ten seconds and a hundred years took the same form, because in both the stretch of time has closed.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The inspector didn't wrote anything in the log.
body.right: The inspector didn't write anything in the log.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is about the past, so the past form of the verb feels required. *Did* has already carried the past, and English carries it once.
body.smallest_fix: After *did* or *didn't*, use the base form: *write*, *paint*, *go*.

body.wrong: Nobody knowed about the second entrance.
body.right: Nobody knew about the second entrance.
body.why_it_happens: Adding *-ed* is the rule, and it works for most verbs. A few hundred common verbs change shape instead, and they are the ones you use most often.
body.smallest_fix: Look the verb up in [th_irregular_verbs] once, and learn it in its group.

body.wrong: The two engineers was still on site at eight.
body.right: The two engineers were still on site at eight.
body.why_it_happens: *Was* is the form you hear most, so it comes first. *Be* is the only verb left with a past ending, and it needs *were* for more than one.
body.smallest_fix: Count the subject. More than one takes *were*.

body.heard: The past simple is for things that happened a long time ago.
also_known_as: the distant past tense
past simple means finished long ago
body.truth: Distance has nothing to do with it. *The lights went out ten seconds ago* is past simple. What decides it is that the stretch of time has closed, not how far away it is.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the stretch of time is over. If it is over, use the past simple, even if it closed a minute ago.

body.mechanism: Spanish marks the past on the end of the verb and changes that ending for each person, so a separate helping verb is not needed for a question.
body.wrong: Wrote you the covering note?
body.right: Did you write the covering note?
body.fix: Build a past question with *did* plus the base form, and leave the main verb alone.

body.headline: One past form for everybody, and *did* for the rest.

rows: they did not paint the gates

title: The word *the*, and what it promises the reader

article_json.also_called: The definite article *the*
article_json.one_line: This tells you when to put *the* in front of a noun, by asking one question about what your reader already knows.
article_json.short_answer: Use *the* when your reader can tell which one you mean. They can tell if you already mentioned it, if there is only one, or if the words after it say which.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I know whether this noun needs *the*?

body.text: *The* is a promise that your reader can identify it

*The* does not mean the noun is important, and it does not mean the noun is specific in your head. It means the reader can work out which one you mean. If they cannot, *the* leaves them looking for something they have never been shown.
So the question is never about the thing. It is about the reader. Ask yourself: could they point at it?

body.lead_in: Every one of these uses *the*, and in each one the reader can point at what it means.
body.dimension: why the reader can identify it

items.text: The lift has been out of order since Tuesday.
items.gloss: There is one lift in this building, and we both know it.

items.text: The cost of the repairs came to nine thousand pounds.
items.gloss: The repairs we are discussing cost that much.

items.text: The government withdrew the funding in October.
items.gloss: The country's government stopped paying.

items.text: The first stage of the scheme finished ahead of time.
items.gloss: Stage one was done early.

body.so_what: In each one you could ask *which one?* and the answer is already on the page or in the room.

body.text: The four reasons a reader can identify it

body.caption: Four different ways the reader gets told which one.
rows: a leak appeared. the leak spread.
you told them in the last sentence
the sun, the internet, the coast
there is nothing else it could be
the kitchen, the manager, the deadline
one per building, per office, per task
the words after it say which
*of the repairs* narrows it to one
it is the top or the first
the highest figure, the second stage
only one thing can be highest
footnotes: *Same*, *only*, *next*, *last* and *right* behave like the top-or-first row: *the same result*, *the only option*.

body.text: Use *the* when your reader can already tell which one you mean, whether from your last sentence, from the situation, or from the words that follow.

body.lead_in: The words after the noun are what makes it identifiable each time.

items.text: The report I sent you on Friday has been withdrawn.
items.gloss: One particular report is no longer valid, and you know which.

marks.span: The report I sent you on Friday

items.text: The rise in energy prices hit rural households hardest.
items.gloss: Energy prices went up and it was worse for people in the country.

items.text: The bus that stops outside the library runs every ten minutes.
items.gloss: One particular bus is frequent.

items.text: The effect on local shops was immediate.
items.gloss: Shops nearby felt it straight away.

body.so_what: *Of*, *in*, *on* and a *that*-clause after the noun all do the same job: they tell the reader which one, so *the* becomes correct.

body.text: *The* with superlatives, ordinals and groups of people

Three patterns take *the* automatically, because in each of them only one answer is possible. Nothing else can be the highest, nothing else can be second, and there is only one group of unemployed people in the country you are writing about.

body.caption: In each of these there is only one possible answer, so *the* is fixed.
rows: the largest employer in the district
the first, the third, the last
the second stage began in May
footnotes: *The* is dropped after a belonging word: *her best result*, not *her the best result*.

body.label: Four sorts of name that keep *the*, and this is the whole list

items.text: Rivers, seas, oceans, deserts, canals and mountain ranges.
items.example: The canal was drained for two weeks in February.

items.text: Country names that are plural or that contain an ordinary noun.
items.example: The Netherlands has one of the densest cycle networks in Europe.

items.text: Newspapers, hotels, cinemas, museums and theatres.
items.example: The Marlow Museum opens at ten on weekdays.

items.text: Organisations named with *of*, and most named with initials read as words.
items.example: The University of Sandmouth published the figures last month.

body.stop_line: That is the whole list for names. Every other town, country, street, person and single mountain takes no word in front of it.

body.text: What goes wrong once *the* has been learnt

body.wrong: The technology has changed the way the people work.
body.right: Technology has changed the way people work.
body.why_it_happens: You are making a big claim, and a big claim feels as though it deserves a strong word in front of the noun. *The* narrows things down instead, so it turns a statement about everybody into a statement about one particular group.
body.smallest_fix: Take *the* out of any noun that means the whole kind rather than a particular set.

body.wrong: Cost of the new footbridge rose by a third.
body.right: The cost of the new footbridge rose by a third.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence starts with the noun, and a sentence-opening noun often needs no word in front of it. *Of the new footbridge* has already told the reader which cost, so *the* is required.
body.smallest_fix: If an *of*-phrase follows the noun, put *the* in front of it.

body.wrong: I want to describe the problem that many cities now face.
body.right: I want to describe a problem that many cities now face.
body.why_it_happens: You know exactly which problem you mean, so *the* feels right. Your reader has not met it yet, so the first mention needs *a*.
body.smallest_fix: Ask whether the reader has met this thing. If not, use *a* and switch to *the* afterwards.

body.heard: Use *the* when you are talking about something specific.
also_known_as: the is for particular things
body.truth: You always have something specific in mind, so that rule says use *the* every time. The test is whether your **reader** can tell which one. *I bought a laptop* is about one specific laptop, and it still takes *a*.
body.what_to_do: Ask *can my reader point at it?* rather than *do I mean a particular one?* If they cannot point at it yet, use *a* or no word at all.

body.headline: *The* means your reader can already tell which one.

rows: the words after it say which

items.prompt: Which is right? *Number of applicants fell.* or *The number of applicants fell.*
items.answer: *The number of applicants fell.*
items.why: *Of applicants* tells the reader which number, so the noun is identified and takes *the*.

items.prompt: Why is *The pollution is a problem in the big cities* usually wrong?
items.answer: Both nouns are meant in general, so neither takes *the*: *Pollution is a problem in big cities.*
items.why: *The* narrows a noun down to a particular set, and a general claim is about all of them.

title: The background an event happened against

article_json.also_called: The past continuous (past progressive)
article_json.one_line: This is the form for something already under way at a past moment, so a shorter event can cut across it.
article_json.short_answer: Use *was* or *were* with the *-ing* form. *We were painting the hall when the pipe burst.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say what was already going on when something else happened?

body.text: This form paints the scene. It does not move the story on
Something was already running when the moment you care about arrived. That is the whole job. The shorter event that lands in the middle of it takes the past simple.
So the two forms work as a pair. One is the picture, and the other is the thing that happens in front of it.
Build it from *was* or *were* and the *-ing* form

body.caption: Only *be* changes, and it changes in one place: *was* against *were*.
body.form_line: *was* or *were* plus the *-ing* form of the main verb

sub_tables.caption: A short answer repeats *was* or *were* and stops.
Two frames, one meaning. Pick whichever fits your sentence.
rows: While I was waiting, the power went out.
I was waiting when the power went out.

gaps.note: The past of *be* has no positive short form. *I's painting* and *they're painting* for *were* do not exist.

examples.text: They were painting the north span when the storm arrived.
examples.gloss: The work had already started when the weather turned.

examples.text: She was writing the summary while the survey team packed up.
examples.gloss: Two things were going on at the same time.

examples.text: We weren't painting that morning, so nobody was on the scaffold.
examples.gloss: No work was under way when it happened.

examples.text: Was he writing it up as the meeting went on?
examples.gloss: The question is whether he took notes live.

notes: *Was* goes with *I*, *he*, *she* and *it*. *Were* goes with *you*, *we* and *they*.
A state verb stays in the past simple here as well: *I knew*, never *I was knowing*.

body.caption: A long bar back there, with a short event landing inside it.

spec.caption: The background runs; the event cuts in

body.text: Was it the whole event, or the background to one?

body.question: Is this the event itself, or the situation the event landed in?

options.label: past simple
options.use_it_when: The event is complete and it moves the story on to the next thing.
options.example: The surveyor arrived at nine and left before lunch.

options.label: past continuous
options.use_it_when: The situation was already running, and you are setting the scene rather than moving it on.
options.example: The surveyor was measuring the roof when the rain started.

a.text: When the manager arrived, the crew left.
a.means: The crew went after she got there, and probably because she did.

b.text: When the manager arrived, the crew were leaving.
b.means: They were already on their way out when she walked in.

a.text: I read the tenancy agreement on the train.
a.means: I got to the end of it before I arrived.

b.text: I was reading the tenancy agreement on the train.
b.means: That is what I had in my hands. It says nothing about finishing.

a.text: The kettle boiled and the fuse went.
a.means: The kettle finished boiling, and then the fuse blew.

b.text: The kettle was boiling and the fuse went.
b.means: The kettle was still going when the fuse blew.

a.text: She cooked while I laid the table.
a.means: Two finished jobs, one after the other or side by side.

b.text: She was cooking while I laid the table.
b.means: The cooking was the longer job, running underneath mine.

body.deciding_factor: Short, finished and moving the story on, use the past simple. Longer, unfinished and setting the scene, use *was* plus *-ing*.
body.trap: The *-ing* form feels more descriptive, so it looks like the better choice for a story. Put a whole story in it and nothing ever happens, because the form never finishes anything.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The pair pays hardest in Speaking Part 2, where a two-minute story needs a scene as well as a sequence of events.

body.text: Use the past continuous for the situation that was already running. Use the past simple for the event that landed inside it.

body.lead_in: Each sentence has one of each. The longer thing takes the *-ing* form.

items.text: I was locking up when the alarm panel started beeping.
items.gloss: The locking up had begun; the beeping cut across it.

items.text: While the ward was moving beds, two ambulances arrived.
items.gloss: The move was under way when they turned up.

items.text: The bus was pulling away as she reached the stop.
items.gloss: She missed it by a few seconds.

body.so_what: In each one, the *-ing* form is the longer thing and the plain past form is the moment.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: Last summer I was travelling to Marlow, I was visiting the museum and I was buying a ticket.
body.right: Last summer I travelled to Marlow, visited the museum and bought a ticket.
body.why_it_happens: The *-ing* form sounds richer, so it gets used for everything. Nothing in it ever finishes, so the story stops moving and the listener waits for the point.
body.smallest_fix: Keep the *-ing* form for the scene. Put every event that moves the story on in the past simple.

body.wrong: The volunteers was clearing the towpath all morning.
body.right: The volunteers were clearing the towpath all morning.
body.why_it_happens: *Was* is the commoner word, so it arrives first. This is the one past form left in English that still changes for the subject.
body.smallest_fix: Count the subject. More than one takes *were*.

body.wrong: I was knowing the answer before she finished the question.
body.right: I knew the answer before she finished the question.
body.why_it_happens: The knowing lasted through the moment, and this is the form for things that last through a moment. Knowing is a state, so there is no middle of it to stand in.
body.smallest_fix: Put the state verb in the past simple: *I knew*, *I wanted*, *I owned*.

body.heard: *While* always takes the past continuous and *when* always takes the past simple.
also_known_as: the when and while rule
body.truth: It is a useful habit, not a rule. *While I was waiting* and *when the power went out* are the common shapes, but *While she checked the meter, I held the torch* is correct, and so is *When I was living in Norland, rents were lower*.
body.what_to_do: Choose the form by asking which event is the longer one. Then put *when* or *while* in front of whichever clause needs it.

body.headline: The long thing gets *-ing*. The moment gets the plain past.

table.caption: One row per job in the sentence.
rows: the event that lands in it
she was cooking while I was clearing up

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: What is the difference between *When I called, she left* and *When I called, she was leaving*?
items.answer: In the first she went after the call. In the second she was already on her way out.
items.why: The plain past form puts the two events in order. The *-ing* form overlaps them.

items.prompt: Why is *The tenants was waiting outside* wrong?
items.answer: *Tenants* is more than one, so it takes *were*: *The tenants were waiting outside.*
items.why: *Be* is the only verb whose past form still changes for the subject.

title: When a noun needs nothing in front of it

article_json.also_called: No article, and how English makes a generalisation
article_json.one_line: This tells you when a noun stands on its own, which is what a general statement in an essay almost always needs.
article_json.short_answer: To talk about something in general, use a plural or an uncountable noun with nothing in front of it: *Electric cars are expensive.* *Research takes time.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When do I leave the noun with no word in front of it?

body.text: A general statement takes a bare noun

Most sentences in an essay are about a whole kind of thing, not about a particular set of them. English writes those with nothing in front of the noun. Adding *the* points at a particular group instead, and that changes the claim.

body.lead_in: Nothing sits in front of these nouns, and each sentence is about the whole kind.

items.text: Electric vehicles are still expensive to insure.
items.gloss: Insurance costs more for electric cars than for other cars.

items.text: Renewable energy is getting cheaper every year.
items.gloss: The price of power from wind and sun keeps falling.

items.text: Governments rarely fund research that takes twenty years.
items.gloss: Long projects find it hard to get public money.

items.text: Traffic gets worse every time they close the bypass.
items.gloss: Closing that road makes the jams worse.

body.so_what: Each sentence is about the whole kind of thing, and none of them has a word in front of the noun.

body.text: To talk about a whole kind of thing, use a plural noun or an uncountable noun, with nothing in front of it.

body.lead_in: Only the word in front of the noun changes, and the claim changes with it.

items.text: Cyclists are more exposed to air pollution than drivers.
items.gloss: This is true of cyclists as a whole.

items.text: The cyclists were held up for an hour at the junction.
items.gloss: One particular group of cyclists was delayed.

items.text: Public transport works best when it runs late at night.
items.gloss: Buses and trains in general are more useful with late services.

items.text: The public transport in Sandmouth stops at half past ten.
items.gloss: One town's buses and trains finish early.

body.so_what: *The* narrowed each sentence down from everybody to one particular set.

body.text: Three ways to say something in general, and what each sounds like
English has three patterns for a general claim, and they are not interchangeable. The bare plural is the one an essay wants. The other two carry a flavour, so use them on purpose.

body.caption: Three ways to generalise, and the bare plural is the safe one.
rows: neutral, and right in almost any essay
electric vehicles cost more to insure
any typical one, good for a definition
an electric vehicle costs more to insure
formal or technical, the thing as an invention
the bicycle changed how cities grew
footnotes: *The* + plural is not on this list, because it is not a generalisation. It points at a particular set.

body.lead_in: The same claim in three patterns. Watch the flavour change, not the fact.

items.text: Heat pumps cost less to run than gas boilers.
items.gloss: Running a heat pump is cheaper.

items.text: A heat pump costs less to run than a gas boiler.
items.gloss: The same fact, stated about one typical example of each.

items.text: The heat pump has changed how new houses are heated.
items.gloss: The invention itself changed building practice.

items.text: Heat pumps are noisy, though, aren't they?
items.gloss: You are asking whether that is generally true of them.

body.so_what: All four are correct. The bare plural is the one that never sounds odd, which is why it carries an essay.

body.text: The fixed phrases that take no word in front

body.caption: In each pair, the bare noun means the purpose and *the* means the building.
rows: the lunch they served was cold
by train, by bus, on foot
at university, in prison, at work, in bed
the university has a new library
in March, on Friday, in 2019, at night
footnotes: The purpose row is the one that carries meaning. *In hospital* means as a patient; *in the hospital* means inside the building.

body.text: What goes wrong when the bare noun is skipped

body.wrong: In the modern society, the technology changes very fast.
body.right: In modern society, technology changes very fast.
body.why_it_happens: The opening of an essay feels formal, and *the* feels like the formal choice. Both nouns here mean the whole kind, so both need to stand bare.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *the* in front of any noun that means the whole kind of thing.

body.wrong: The young people today spend too long on their phones.
body.right: Young people today spend too long on their phones.
body.why_it_happens: You mean all of them, and *the* feels as though it makes the group complete. *The* + a plural noun points at one particular set of people, so it shrinks the claim rather than widening it.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *the*. Keep it only if you have already named which group you mean.

body.wrong: Student needs somewhere quiet to work in the evening.
body.right: Students need somewhere quiet to work in the evening.
body.why_it_happens: Bare nouns are correct for general statements, so a singular one looks correct too. Only plural and uncountable nouns can stand bare, so a singular one has to change or take a word in front.
body.smallest_fix: Make the noun plural, or write *a student needs*.

body.mechanism: Arabic marks a general statement with the definite marker on the noun, so the general form and the identified form look alike.
body.wrong: The pollution is a serious problem in the cities.
body.right: Pollution is a serious problem in cities.
body.fix: For a claim about the whole kind, take the word in front of the noun away.

body.heard: Every noun needs a word in front of it.
also_known_as: never start a sentence with a bare noun
body.truth: That is true only of singular countable nouns. Plural nouns and uncountable nouns stand bare whenever the claim is general, and in an essay that is most sentences.
body.what_to_do: Check the noun first. Singular and countable, it needs something. Plural or uncountable, leave it bare unless the reader needs to know which ones.

body.headline: General claim, plural or uncountable noun, nothing in front.

title: Talking about what you used to do

article_json.also_called: *Used to*, *would* and the past simple for past habits
article_json.one_line: This lets you pick between three ways of talking about the past, so the sentence says whether things have changed.
article_json.short_answer: Use *used to* when the point is that it is not true now. *Would* works for repeated actions only, never for states.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say that something was true then and is not true now?

body.text: Three ways to talk about the past, and they are not the same
*We used to live above the shop*, *We lived above the shop* and *Every summer we would repaint the boat* are all correct. What separates them is whether you are pointing at a change.
There is also a fourth structure that looks identical and means something else entirely. *I am used to working nights* is about now, not about the past.
Is it a state, a repeated action, or one event?

body.question: Was this a state, a repeated action, or a single event?

options.label: *used to* + base form
options.use_it_when: It was true then and is not true now, and that change is the point. It works for states and for actions.
options.example: The station used to have a waiting room.

options.label: *would* + base form
options.use_it_when: It is a repeated action inside a past time you have already set up. Never use it for a state.
options.example: Every August the yard would close for two weeks.

options.label: past simple
options.use_it_when: It is one finished event, or a habit where you are making no claim about now.
options.example: We lived above the shop for six years.

a.text: I used to walk to the depot.
a.means: I do not walk there any more, and that change is the news.

b.text: I walked to the depot.
b.means: That is what I did then. Nothing is claimed about now.

a.text: Every winter the pond used to freeze.
a.means: It froze then and it does not any more.

b.text: Every winter the pond would freeze.
b.means: You are remembering those winters from inside the story.

a.text: He used to have a motorbike.
a.means: He owned one then and he does not now.

b.text: He had a motorbike.
b.means: He owned one at the time you are talking about.

a.text: I used to work nights.
a.means: I worked nights then and I do not now.

b.text: I am used to working nights.
b.means: I work nights now and it feels normal to me.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: used to work / am used to working

body.deciding_factor: *Used to* for anything that was true then and is not now. *Would* for repeated actions only, once the past time is already set.
body.trap: *Used to* and *would* are taught as swappable, so *would* gets used for states. *She would be shy* is grammatical and means something completely different.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere, and *used to* is one of the strongest Speaking Part 3 moves for saying how things have changed.

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

steps.ask: Is it a state, such as having, being, knowing or living somewhere?

verdict.example: The yard used to belong to the railway.
verdict.why: *Would* cannot carry a state. It turns the sentence into something else.

steps.ask: Is the point that it does not happen any more?

verdict.example: The trust used to run a bus to the coast.
verdict.why: *Used to* carries the contrast with now on its own, with no extra words.

steps.ask: Have you already told the reader which past time you mean?

branches.answer: Yes, and it happened again and again

verdict.example: Every August the yard would close for two weeks.
verdict.why: *Would* leans on a past time frame that is already in place.

verdict.example: The yard closed for two weeks that August.
verdict.why: One finished event in closed time is what the past simple is for.

body.text: The first question does most of the work. States are where *would* goes wrong, and states are common, because having, being and living somewhere are all states.
The four shapes, side by side

body.caption: Two take the base form. The last two take the *-ing* form.
rows: happened again and again back then
it feels normal to me now
I am becoming accustomed to it
footnotes: The *to* in the last two rows is a small placing word, which is why an *-ing* form follows it.
*Used to* has no present form. For a present habit use the present simple with *usually*.

body.lead_in: One example per row above, in the same order.

items.text: The library used to open on Sunday afternoons.
items.gloss: It does not open on Sundays any more.

items.text: On wet mornings my father would drive us in.
items.gloss: That is what happened whenever it rained, back then.

items.text: I am used to cycling in the rain by now.
items.gloss: It does not bother me, because I do it often.

items.text: New staff take a month to get used to the shift pattern.
items.gloss: It takes them that long to settle into it.

body.so_what: The first two are about the past. The last two are about how something feels now.

body.text: Use *used to* whenever the sentence says that something was true then and is not true now. Use *would* for repeated actions only.

body.lead_in: Every one of these is a state, so *would* is unavailable in all of them.

items.text: The building used to belong to the water company.
items.gloss: Somebody else owns it now.

items.text: There used to be a chemist on the corner.
items.gloss: It has gone.

items.text: I used to know everybody on the street.
items.gloss: Most of them have moved away.

body.so_what: Belonging, being there and knowing people are all states, and none of them is something you repeatedly did.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: I didn't used to cycle in the winter.
body.right: I didn't use to cycle in the winter.
body.why_it_happens: *Used to* is learned as one block, so the *d* travels with it everywhere. *Did* has already taken the past, so what follows goes back to the base form.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the *d* after *did* and *didn't*: *Did you use to…?*

body.wrong: She would be very shy as a child.
body.right: She used to be very shy as a child.
body.why_it_happens: *Would* and *used to* look interchangeable, so the swap seems free. *Would* cannot carry a state, and the sentence turns into a guess about what she is like.
body.smallest_fix: If the verb names a state, use *used to* or the past simple.

body.wrong: I am used to live near the station before the move.
body.right: I used to live near the station before the move.
body.why_it_happens: The two structures share four letters and sound almost the same. One is about the past and takes the base form; the other is about now and takes the *-ing* form.
body.smallest_fix: For the past, drop *am* and keep the base form: *I used to live*.

body.heard: *Used to* and *would* mean the same thing, so you can use whichever sounds better.
also_known_as: would is the more advanced used to
body.truth: They overlap for repeated actions and nowhere else. *Would* cannot carry a state, so *I would have a motorbike* does not mean that you owned one. It reads as a guess about a situation that is not real.
body.what_to_do: Check what the verb names. A state takes *used to* or the past simple. A repeated action takes any of the three, and *would* needs the past time already set up.

body.headline: *Used to* for a change. *Would* for actions only.

items.answer: *There used to be a market here.*
items.why: *Be* names a state, and *would* cannot carry a state.

items.prompt: What is the difference between *I used to drive* and *I am used to driving*?
items.answer: The first means you drove then and do not now. The second means you drive now and it feels normal.
items.why: One is a past habit; the other is a feeling about the present.

title: Which little word goes in front of this noun?

article_json.also_called: The article decision procedure: *a* / *an* / *the* / nothing
article_json.one_line: This gives you a three-question procedure you can run inside a sentence, instead of a rule list you have to remember all of.
article_json.short_answer: Ask three things, in order. General claim? Nothing. Reader knows which one? *The*. Otherwise, singular countable? *A*. That covers most sentences.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: I am halfway through a sentence. Do I write *a*, *the*, or nothing?

body.text: Why a list of rules does not help mid-sentence

You already know the rules. The trouble is that you are writing, and a list of fourteen rules cannot be checked in the second and a half you have. What works is a short procedure that always runs in the same order.
Three questions do most of the work. Run them in order and stop at the first one that answers. The rest of the article is those three questions, and what to do when none of them fires.

body.question: Can my reader already tell which one I mean?

options.label: nothing
options.use_it_when: The noun is plural or uncountable, and you mean the whole kind rather than a particular set.
options.example: Rural bus services have been cut in most counties.

options.label: *the*
options.use_it_when: The reader can point at it: you mentioned it, there is only one, or the words after it say which.
options.example: The bus service to Marlow was cut in April.

options.label: *a* / *an*
options.use_it_when: The noun is singular and countable, and the reader has not met this one yet.
options.example: A bus service was withdrawn without any consultation.

a.text: Libraries are closing across the county.
a.means: Libraries in general are shutting. You are making a claim about all of them.

b.text: The libraries are closing across the county.
b.means: A particular set of libraries that you have already named is shutting.

a.text: She has taken a laptop from the store cupboard.
a.means: She took one of the laptops. You are not saying which.

b.text: She has taken the laptop from the store cupboard.
b.means: She took the one particular laptop we both know about.

a.text: He went to school in Norland until he was sixteen.
a.means: He was a pupil there. You are talking about his education.

b.text: He went to the school in Norland to collect a form.
b.means: He walked to the building for another reason entirely.

a.text: Water is charged by the cubic metre in this district.
a.means: Water in general is billed that way here.

b.text: The water in the storage tank has not been tested.
b.means: One particular quantity of water has not been checked.

body.deciding_factor: Ask what your reader knows, not what you know. If they cannot point at it, *the* is wrong.
body.trap: You were taught that *the* is for specific things, and you always have a specific thing in mind, so *the* creeps into every noun. The test is about the reader, not about you.
body.register_note: The same procedure runs in speech and in writing. It pays hardest in Task 2, where a single wrong *the* turns a claim about everybody into a claim about one group.

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

steps.ask: Is the noun plural or uncountable, and do you mean the whole kind?

verdict.example: Rural bus services have been cut in most counties.
verdict.why: A claim about the whole kind takes a bare plural or a bare uncountable noun.

branches.answer: No, or the noun is singular

steps.ask: Can your reader already tell which one you mean?

branches.answer: Yes — mentioned, unique, or named by the words after it

verdict.example: The bus service to Marlow was cut in April.
verdict.why: *The* is a promise that the reader can identify it, and here they can.

branches.answer: No — this is new to them

steps.ask: Is the noun singular and countable?

verdict.example: A bus service was withdrawn without any consultation.
verdict.why: A singular countable noun is never left bare, and the reader has not met this one.

branches.answer: No — it is plural or uncountable

verdict.example: The depot has taken delivery of new equipment.
verdict.why: Plural and uncountable nouns can stand bare, and *some* adds a vague amount.

body.text: Most sentences stop at the first or the second question. The third only runs when the noun is new to the reader, which is why the commonest error is a *the* that should have been an *a*.
The three rules underneath the procedure

body.lead_in: Three statements carry most of the article system:
items: A singular countable noun is never bare. It takes *a*, *the*, *this*, *my*, *each* or something.
A general claim takes a bare plural or a bare uncountable noun.
*The* goes on once the thing has been identified, by earlier mention, by uniqueness, or by the words that follow.

body.caption: The same noun, run through the procedure four times.
footnotes: Row three follows row two in a real paragraph. That switch from *a* to *the* is the commonest article move in English.

body.lead_in: One short paragraph. Watch the word in front of *scheme* change as the reader learns about it.

items.text: Councils across the region have tried car-free schemes.
items.gloss: This sort of scheme has been tried in lots of places.

items.text: Sandmouth launched a scheme of this kind in 2021.
items.gloss: One town started one, and this is its first mention.

items.text: The scheme cut traffic in the centre by a fifth.
items.gloss: That same scheme reduced the traffic.

items.text: So the scheme worked, and nobody expected that.
items.gloss: It succeeded, which was a surprise.

body.so_what: Nothing about the scheme changed. What changed is how much the reader had been told.

body.text: What goes wrong when the procedure is skipped

body.wrong: The children who grow up near a main road have more asthma.
body.right: Children who grow up near a main road have more asthma.
body.why_it_happens: The words after the noun look as though they identify which children, so *the* feels earned. Here they describe a kind of child rather than pointing at a known group, so the claim is general and the noun stands bare.
body.smallest_fix: Ask whether you mean all of them or a known set. All of them, delete *the*.

body.wrong: Results of the second trial were published in June.
body.right: The results of the second trial were published in June.
body.why_it_happens: You have been told that general statements take a bare noun, and this looks like one. *Of the second trial* names which results, so the reader can identify them and *the* is required.
body.smallest_fix: If an *of*-phrase or a *that*-clause follows the noun, put *the* in front.

body.wrong: Solution to this problem will take several years.
body.right: A solution to this problem will take several years.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence opens on the noun, and opening nouns often stand bare. *Solution* is singular and countable, and English never leaves that bare.
body.smallest_fix: Put *a* in front, or make the noun plural.

body.what_varies: Whether *the* appears in front of an institution named by its purpose.

option_a.label: British English
option_a.example: She spent three days in hospital after the fall.

option_b.label: American English
option_b.example: She spent three days in the hospital after the fall.

body.why_this_default: Our examples use British conventions throughout. Both forms are standard, and neither is an error. This is a house choice, not a rule of English.

body.heard: Use *a* the first time and *the* every time after that.
also_known_as: first mention a, second mention the
body.truth: That half works, and it is the reason for a whole class of errors. It says nothing about the general claims that fill an essay, where the correct answer is nothing at all, and nothing about the *the* that comes from an *of*-phrase on a first mention.
body.what_to_do: Run the general-claim question first, before you think about first or second mention. *Governments should act* has no first mention and no word in front of it.

items.answer: *Air quality in city centres has improved since 2015.*
items.why: The noun is uncountable and the claim is general, so question one answers and nothing goes in front.

items.prompt: Run the procedure: *___ decision to close the depot was taken in March.*
items.answer: *The decision to close the depot was taken in March.*
items.why: The words after the noun say which decision, so question two answers and it takes *the*.

items.prompt: Why is *Council must act on housing* wrong?
items.answer: *Council* is singular and countable, so it needs a word in front: *The council must act on housing.*
items.why: A singular countable noun is never left bare, whatever the claim is about.

title: The idea behind every *have* plus third form

article_json.also_called: Perfect aspect
article_json.one_line: This is the one idea behind four of the twelve tenses, so you can learn them as a single thing instead of four.
article_json.short_answer: *Have* plus the third form stands at one point and looks back at an earlier one. Move the *have* and you move the standing point.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: What do all the *have* forms have in common?

body.text: Every perfect form has two points in it, not one
A plain past form gives you one point: it happened. A perfect form gives you two. There is the point where the thing happened, and the point you are standing at when you mention it.
That is why these forms feel harder. You are not choosing when something happened. You are choosing where to stand while you talk about it.
Move the *have*, and you move where you stand

body.caption: The third form never moves. Only the word in front of it changes.
rows: The trust has repaired the west span.
at a past moment, looking back
By April the trust had repaired it.
at a future moment, looking back
By June the trust will have repaired it.
footnotes: The fourth member of the family adds *been* and an *-ing* form, and measures how long: *has been repairing*.

body.lead_in: One event, three standing points. Only the word in front of *repaired* changes.

items.text: The council has repaired both footbridges.
items.gloss: They are usable now. That is the situation today.

items.text: By the inspection the council had repaired both footbridges.
items.gloss: The work was already finished when the inspector came.

items.text: By September the council will have repaired both footbridges.
items.gloss: The work will be behind them by then.

items.text: They've repaired the handrail twice this winter.
items.gloss: It keeps breaking, and the winter is not over.

body.so_what: The repair happened once. What moved is the moment from which you are looking at it.

body.caption: An arrow from the event to the point you are standing at.

body.text: The second word is the third form, and it never changes
Whatever the first word is, the word behind it is always the third form of the main verb. For a regular verb that looks exactly like the past form. For an irregular verb it does not.
Put *have*, *has*, *had* or *will have* in front, and the third form of the main verb behind. The main verb takes no other shape.

body.lead_in: Two verbs, one regular and one irregular, in the same three shapes.

items.text: The crew has painted the whole span.
items.gloss: The span is painted now.

items.text: The crew has written up the inspection notes.
items.gloss: The notes exist and are ready to read.

items.text: By Friday they had painted every railing on the bridge.
items.gloss: That job was finished before Friday.

items.text: They'd written to the residents before the work started.
items.gloss: The letters went out first.

body.so_what: *Painted* looks the same as the past form and *written* does not. The grammar is identical in both.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The panel has wrote to every household on the estate.
body.right: The panel has written to every household on the estate.
body.why_it_happens: With a regular verb the past form and the third form are the same word, so the two never need telling apart. With an irregular verb they are different, and the past form comes to hand first.
body.smallest_fix: After *have*, *has*, *had* or *will have*, use the third form: *written*, *taken*, *gone*.

body.wrong: The surveyor has gone to the site twice this month, so she knows it well.
body.right: The surveyor has been to the site twice this month, so she knows it well.
body.why_it_happens: *Gone* is the ordinary third form of *go*, so it looks like the right choice. *Has gone* means the person is still away; *has been* means they went and came back.
body.smallest_fix: Use *been* when the person has returned, and *gone* when they have not.

body.wrong: The tenants would of noticed a leak that size.
body.right: The tenants would have noticed a leak that size.
body.why_it_happens: *Would have* is squeezed to *would've* in speech, and that sounds exactly like *would of*. There is no verb *of*, so the word is always *have*.
body.smallest_fix: Write *have* every time. The same goes for *should have* and *could have*.

body.label: Two things that look like this family and are not

items.text: *Have got* means *have*. It is not a perfect form at all.
items.example: They've got two more sites to inspect.

items.text: *'d* stands for *had* in front of a third form and for *would* in front of a base form.
items.example: They'd painted it. They'd paint it.

body.heard: The present perfect is one of the past tenses.
also_known_as: have done is a past tense
the perfect tenses are past tenses
body.truth: *Has repaired* is built on *has*, which is a present form. That is why the sentence is about how things stand now. A perfect form always reports from where you are standing, and *has* puts you at now.
body.what_to_do: Read the first word rather than the second. *Has* means you are standing at now, *had* at a past moment, and *will have* at a future one.

body.headline: The first word says where you stand. The second never moves.

rows: the site has been closing early

title: Saying that something before now still matters

article_json.also_called: The present perfect
article_json.one_line: This is the form for something that happened earlier and still counts today, so the sentence stays about now.
article_json.short_answer: Use *have* or *has* with the third form. *The ward has closed to visitors.* Something happened, and it matters now.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say that something happened and it still matters?

body.text: This form keeps the sentence about now
The event is behind you. The point of the sentence is in front of you. That is what this form buys: something happened, and here is where it leaves us.
So it is the form for reporting a position rather than telling a story. Nothing in it says when, and that is deliberate.
Build it from *have* or *has* and the third form

body.caption: Only *have* changes, and only in the *he* row. The third form never moves.
body.form_line: *have* or *has* plus the third form of the main verb

rows.note: The only row where the helping verb changes.

sub_tables.caption: A short answer repeats the helping verb and stops there.
The word after *have* is the third form, not the past form.
Two ways to shorten the negative, and both are correct.

examples.text: The contractors have painted the Verdon river bridge.
examples.gloss: The bridge is painted, and that is where things stand.

examples.text: The inspector has written to both landlords.
examples.gloss: The letters are with them now.

examples.text: We haven't painted the lamp posts yet.
examples.gloss: That part of the job is still waiting.

examples.text: Has she written up the meter readings?
examples.gloss: The question is whether they are recorded.

notes: *He's painted* is *he has painted*. The third form behind it is the clue.
Never *Yes, I've.* A short answer cannot end on a short form.
The *'ve not* and *'s not* negatives are commoner in British English than in American English. Both are correct everywhere.

body.text: The four jobs this form does

body.caption: Four contexts, and in all four the answer to *when* is not the point.
headers: Words that turn up with it
rows: it happened and it matters now
The board has withdrawn the proposal.
it has happened at some point in my life
I have never sat an exam that long.
it started earlier and is still true
The trust has managed the woodland since 2011.
it is news that still counts
Both of the smaller depots have already shut.
footnotes: In every row the reader can still ask *when?* and be told that it does not matter.

body.lead_in: One example per row above, in the same order.
body.dimension: the job the form is doing

items.text: The water company has cut off the supply to the block.
items.gloss: There is no water in the taps at the moment.

items.text: I have never worked a night shift before.
items.gloss: In my whole working life it has not happened.

items.text: The charity has run the food bank since the mill closed.
items.gloss: It started then and it is still running it.

items.text: Two of the tutors have already handed in their notice.
items.gloss: The department is going to be short.

body.so_what: Not one of those sentences tells you the date, and not one of them needs to.

body.caption: The event sits back there; the arrow lands on now.

spec.caption: Back there, but pointing at today

body.text: Use the present perfect when the point of the sentence is where things stand now, or when the stretch of time is still open.

body.lead_in: No time expression in any of these. The verb is carrying the meaning alone.

items.text: The lift has broken down again.
items.gloss: It is out of order, and that is the problem.

items.text: The committee has agreed the new route.
items.gloss: The route is settled. That is where things stand.

items.text: Two of the surveyors have resigned.
items.gloss: They are gone, and the team is two people short.

body.so_what: Each one reports a position rather than an event, which is why no date is needed.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: Since the new timetable came in, journey times improved.
body.right: Since the new timetable came in, journey times have improved.
body.why_it_happens: *Since* points backwards, so a past form feels like the natural partner. *Since* opens a stretch that runs up to today, and the verb inside it has to stay open too.
body.smallest_fix: Change *improved* to *have improved*. The stretch from the timetable change is still running.

body.wrong: The office has took on two more apprentices.
body.right: The office has taken on two more apprentices.
body.why_it_happens: For a regular verb the past form and the third form are the same word, so the two never need separating. *Take* separates them, and the past form is the one you say more often.
body.smallest_fix: After *have* or *has*, use the third form: *taken*, *written*, *gone*.

body.wrong: The two clinics has moved to the new health centre.
body.right: The two clinics have moved to the new health centre.
body.why_it_happens: The word nearest the verb is a single building, so *has* sounds right. The subject is the two clinics, and the helping verb matches the subject.
body.smallest_fix: Find the subject, count it, and pick *have* or *has* from that.

body.label: Three cases where this looks broken and is not

items.text: After *this is the first time*, English uses this form even though the frame is present.
items.example: This is the first time the ward has closed to visitors.

items.text: *Since* can give a reason rather than a start point, and then no perfect form is needed.
items.example: Since the ward is short-staffed, visiting hours are limited.

items.text: *Have got* means *have*. It is not a perfect form at all.
items.example: I've got the spare keys in my bag.

body.heard: *Since* always needs the present perfect.
also_known_as: since goes with have done
if you see since, use the perfect
body.truth: It holds when *since* marks a start point. *Since* has a second job: it can mean *because*, as in *Since the ward is short-staffed, visiting hours are limited*, and then the verb is whatever the sentence needs.
body.what_to_do: Ask what *since* is doing. Marking a start point takes *have* plus the third form. Giving a reason takes no special form at all.

body.headline: *Have* or *has*, then the third form. It happened; it counts now.

table.caption: One row per shape you need.

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Which one is right? *He has forgot the code.* / *He has forgotten the code.*
items.answer: *He has forgotten the code.*
items.why: After *has*, the verb takes its third form, and for *forget* that is *forgotten*.

items.prompt: Why does *Since April the queue got longer* need changing?
items.answer: *Since April* is still running, so the verb stays open: *has got longer*.
items.why: A stretch that reaches today needs a verb that reaches today.

title: Pointing at things, and saying whose they are

article_json.also_called: Demonstrative and possessive determiners
article_json.one_line: This gives you the words that point at a thing and the words that say who it belongs to, and shows why they cannot stack.
article_json.short_answer: *This* and *these* are near or just mentioned. *That* and *those* are further off. *My*, *your*, *their* say whose, and they replace *the*, never join it.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When do I write *this* and when *that*, and can I say *the my house*?

body.text: Words that point, and words that say whose

Two small families of words go in the same slot as *a* and *the*. One family points at something. The other says who it belongs to. They fill the same slot, so only one of them can be there at a time.

body.caption: Near or far, one or several: four words cover the whole grid.
footnotes: Distance can be in space, in time, or in the text. *This morning* is now; *that morning* was some time ago.

body.caption: One word per owner, and none of them changes for a plural noun.
footnotes: *Its* has no apostrophe. *It's* is the short form of *it is*.
These words never take *-s* and never change for a plural noun after them.

body.lead_in: Only the pointing word changes. Watch the distance move.

items.text: This bus goes to the station; that one does not.
items.gloss: The bus in front of us is the right one.

items.text: These figures come from the 2019 survey.
items.gloss: The numbers you are looking at now come from that survey.

items.text: Those delays were caused by a burst water main.
items.gloss: The delays we talked about earlier had that cause.

items.text: Her application arrived before the deadline.
items.gloss: The application belonging to her was on time.

body.so_what: *This* and *these* pull the thing close. *That* and *those* push it away, in space or in time.

body.text: One slot, one word: they cannot stack
Only one of *a*, *the*, *this*, *that*, *my* or *your* goes in front of a noun. They fill the same slot, so they never appear together.

body.lead_in: One word in the slot each time, and each one gives the reader something different.

items.text: A survey found damp in nineteen flats.
items.gloss: Some survey found it, and you have not met the survey before.

items.text: The survey found damp in nineteen flats.
items.gloss: The survey we already know about found it.

items.text: This survey found damp in nineteen flats.
items.gloss: The one in front of you, or the one just named, found it.

items.text: Our survey found damp in nineteen flats.
items.gloss: The one we carried out found it.

body.so_what: The slot in front of the noun holds exactly one word, and which word you choose is what the reader reads.

body.text: To say both *whose* and *which one*, English uses *of* instead of stacking. So *a friend of mine* does the job of *a my friend*, and *that car of theirs* does the job of *that their car*.
*This* in writing, where the distance is in the text

In an essay, *this* usually points back at your own last sentence rather than at anything in the room. It works best with a noun after it, because a bare *this* leaves the reader guessing what you mean.

body.lead_in: Only the noun after *this* changes, and the reader gets more each time.

items.text: This has caused problems for rural households.
items.gloss: Something in the last sentence caused problems, and the reader has to guess which part.

items.text: This shift has caused problems for rural households.
items.gloss: The change you just described is what caused them.

items.text: This funding cut has caused problems for rural households.
items.gloss: The cut in money you just described is the cause.

items.text: That's the bit I don't follow, to be honest.
items.gloss: You are pointing at something the other person just said.

body.so_what: A noun after *this* tells the reader exactly which part of your last sentence you mean.

body.text: What goes wrong in the slot

body.wrong: The my colleague sent the figures on Tuesday.
body.right: My colleague sent the figures on Tuesday.
body.why_it_happens: You know exactly which colleague, so *the* feels needed as well. *My* already tells the reader which one, so the two words are competing for one slot.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *the*. A word like *my* or *this* does the identifying on its own.

body.wrong: This findings suggest that the scheme had little effect.
body.right: These findings suggest that the scheme had little effect.
body.why_it_happens: The set of findings feels like one thing, so the singular word comes out. *This* and *that* only go with one thing; more than one takes *these* and *those*.
body.smallest_fix: Count the noun. Plural noun, use *these* or *those*.

body.wrong: The tutor marked the essay and gave his feedback on Friday.
body.right: The tutor marked the essay and gave her feedback on Friday.
body.why_it_happens: In many languages the belonging word matches the thing owned, not the owner. In English it matches the owner, so *feedback* has no say in the choice.
body.smallest_fix: Look at the owner, not at the thing owned, and pick *his*, *her*, *its* or *their*.

body.mechanism: Spanish matches the belonging word to the thing owned, so one form covers both a male and a female owner.
body.wrong: My sister sent his notes from the seminar.
body.right: My sister sent her notes from the seminar.
body.fix: Choose the word by looking at who owns it, not at what is owned.

body.heard: *This* is for things that are physically close and *that* is for things far away.
also_known_as: this means here and that means there
body.truth: Distance is only one of the three things these words measure. In writing they mark distance in the text, and in speech they often mark distance in time: *this week* is the one we are in, *that week* is one we have left behind.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the thing is current or already behind you. Current takes *this*; finished or earlier takes *that*.

title: Words for amount

article_json.also_called: Quantifiers: *some* / *any*, *much* / *many*, *few* / *a few*, *little* / *a little*
article_json.one_line: This gives you every word for how much or how many, tells you which sort of noun each one takes, and shows the pair that reverses the meaning.
article_json.short_answer: Count the noun first. Countable takes *many* and *a few*. Uncountable takes *much* and *a little*. Drop the *a* and *few* turns negative.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Which word for amount goes with this noun?

body.text: The noun picks the word, not the other way round
Every word for amount belongs to one of three groups: countable nouns only, uncountable nouns only, or both. So the decision starts with the noun. Count it, then pick from the right column.

body.gloss: a word for how much or how many: *some*, *many*, *a few*

show_first.text: Many households were affected by the closure.
There isn't much evidence for that claim.
A few colleges have already adopted the scheme.

body.name_line: A word like that is called a **quantifier**.
body.anchor_line: It sits in the same place as *the* and *a*, and it answers a different question: not which one, but how many or how much.

body.caption: Count the noun, then read down the column it belongs to.
footnotes: *A lot of*, *plenty of* and *some* go with both, which makes them the safe choice when you are unsure.

body.lead_in: Only the noun changes. Watch the word in front of it change with it.

items.text: Many households switched supplier during the price rise.
items.gloss: A lot of homes changed who supplied their energy.

items.text: Much of the damage was done in the first hour.
items.gloss: Most of the harm happened early on.

items.text: A large number of applicants withdrew before the interview.
items.gloss: Lots of people pulled out.

items.text: There's plenty of space in the back room.
items.gloss: That room has more room than you need.

body.so_what: *Many* went with a noun you can count, *much* with one you measure, and *plenty of* with either.

body.text: *Much* is awkward in a plain positive sentence
*Much* is normal in negatives, in questions, and after *so*, *too*, *as* and *how*. In a plain positive statement it sounds stiff and old, so a formal phrase does the job instead.

body.caption: One fact, three registers, and the middle one is what an essay wants.
rows: a great deal of research supports this
there isn't much research on this
footnotes: The same split does not affect *many*, which is fine in positives, negatives and questions alike.

body.text: *Some* and *any*, and the offer that breaks the pattern
Use *some* in positive statements and in offers and requests. Use *any* in negatives, in most questions, and to mean *it does not matter which*.

body.lead_in: Only *some* or *any* changes, and what the sentence is doing changes with it.

items.text: There are some errors in the third column.
items.gloss: The column has mistakes in it.

items.text: There aren't any errors in the third column.
items.gloss: The column is clean.

items.text: Would you like some help with the references?
items.gloss: You are offering, and you expect the answer to be yes.

items.text: Any student on the course can borrow the equipment.
items.gloss: It does not matter which student. All of them can.

body.so_what: *Some* in a question is an offer. *Any* in a positive sentence means it does not matter which one.

body.text: *A few* and *few* mean opposite things

This is the one place where a single letter reverses the point of a sentence. With *a*, you are saying there are some, and that is good news. Without it, you are saying there are hardly any, and that is the complaint.

body.caption: With *a*, some and positive. Without *a*, hardly any and negative.
rows: a few colleges have adopted it
hardly any, and that is the problem
hardly any, and that is the problem
footnotes: Bare *few* and *little* are formal. In speech people say *not many* and *not much* instead.

body.lead_in: The only change is the word *a*, and the conclusion flips each time.

items.text: A few residents objected to the parking scheme.
items.gloss: Some people complained, so there was opposition.

items.text: Few residents objected to the parking scheme.
items.gloss: Almost nobody complained, so the scheme went ahead easily.

items.text: There is a little support for a night bus service.
items.gloss: Some people want one, so the idea is alive.

items.text: There is little support for a night bus service.
items.gloss: Almost nobody wants one, so it will not happen.

body.so_what: One letter, and the reader draws the opposite conclusion. This one is worth reading twice.

body.text: What goes wrong with words for amount

body.wrong: The study drew on many research from three universities.
body.right: The study drew on a great deal of research from three universities.
body.why_it_happens: *Research* arrives in separate studies, so it feels countable, and *many* is the word for a lot of countable things. English measures research rather than counting it.
body.smallest_fix: Change *many* to *a great deal of* or *a lot of*, and leave the noun singular.

body.wrong: The office doesn't have some spare keys for the side door.
body.right: The office doesn't have any spare keys for the side door.
body.why_it_happens: You have been told that *some* is used for offers and requests, and this feels like a polite sentence. That exception covers questions, not negatives, so a negative takes *any*.
body.smallest_fix: In a sentence with *not* in it, change *some* to *any*.

body.wrong: Few of my classmates helped me, so the work was finished quickly.
body.right: A few of my classmates helped me, so the work was finished quickly.
body.why_it_happens: Both forms mean a small number, so they look interchangeable. Bare *few* is a complaint, and it contradicts the second half of this sentence.
body.smallest_fix: If the small number is good news, put *a* in front.

body.heard: Use *any* in questions and *some* in statements.
also_known_as: some for positive, any for question
body.truth: That half works. *Some* is normal in a question when you are offering or requesting, because you expect the answer to be yes: *Would you like some tea?* And *any* is normal in a statement when it means *it does not matter which*: *Any bus will get you there.*
body.what_to_do: Ask what the sentence is doing. Offering or requesting takes *some*, whatever the punctuation. Meaning *whichever* takes *any*, even in a statement.

body.headline: Count the noun first. Then read down the right column.

table.caption: One row per meaning.

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Which one means the campaign failed? *Few people signed.* or *A few people signed.*
items.answer: *Few people signed.*
items.why: Without *a*, the word means hardly any, and it carries a complaint with it.

items.prompt: Fix this: *There were many traffics on the ring road.*
items.answer: *There was a lot of traffic on the ring road.*
items.why: *Traffic* is measured, not counted, so it takes no *-s* and no *many*.

title: Saying how long something has been going on

article_json.also_called: The present perfect continuous
article_json.one_line: This is the form for measuring how long an activity has run up to now, so the length becomes the point.
article_json.short_answer: Use *have been* or *has been* with the *-ing* form. *The crew has been painting since April.* The length is the point.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say how long something has been going on?

body.text: This form measures the activity, not the result
Something has been running for a while and it reaches up to now. The sentence is about the running of it, so it often explains why things look the way they do.
It does not promise that the activity is finished, and it does not promise that it has stopped. It only tells you how long it went on.
Build it from *have been* and the *-ing* form

body.caption: Only *have* changes. *Been* and the *-ing* form never move.
body.form_line: *have been* or *has been* plus the *-ing* form of the main verb

rows.note: The only row where the helping verb changes.

sub_tables.caption: The short answer drops everything except the helping verb.
*How long* and this form are a standing partnership.
rows: How long have you been painting?
How long has she been writing it?

examples.text: The contractors have been painting the bridge since April.
examples.gloss: The job started in April and it is still going.

examples.text: She's been writing the Ashfield chapter all morning.
examples.gloss: That is what she has been doing since she sat down.

examples.text: The team has not been painting in this weather.
examples.gloss: Work has been held up by the rain.

examples.text: Have they been writing to residents about the closure?
examples.gloss: The question is whether letters have been going out.

notes: *He's been painting* is *he has been painting*. The *been* is what tells you.
A state verb has no form here. Write *I have known her for years*, never *I have been knowing her*.
*How long* pulls this form more strongly than any other words in English.

body.caption: A bar that starts back there and is still running at now.

spec.caption: The length of the bar is the point

body.text: The two jobs this form does

body.caption: Two meanings, and the second one is the reason nobody teaches this form well.
headers: Words that turn up with it
rows: how long it has run, and it is still running
The pump has been running since Tuesday.
why things look the way they do now
You can tell he has been decorating.
footnotes: In the second row the activity has usually stopped. What is left behind is the evidence.

body.lead_in: The first two measure the length. The last two explain what you can see.

items.text: The council has been consulting residents since the spring.
items.gloss: The consultation started then and is not over.

items.text: I've been waiting at this stop for forty minutes.
items.gloss: The wait started forty minutes ago and it goes on.

items.text: Her eyes are red because she has been staring at figures.
items.gloss: That is what has made her eyes sore.

items.text: The corridor smells of paint. Somebody has been decorating.
items.gloss: The smell is the evidence of the work.

body.so_what: In the last two the work has stopped, and the sentence is still correct.

body.text: Use *have been* plus the *-ing* form when the length of an activity is the point, or when its traces explain the present situation.

body.lead_in: Each one answers the question *how long*, with a different kind of answer.

items.text: The clinic has been running Saturday sessions for a year.
items.gloss: They started a year ago and they are still on.

items.text: We've been sharing an office since the refit started.
items.gloss: The sharing began with the refit and continues.

items.text: Fares have been rising steadily since the fuel levy.
items.gloss: The rise began then and has not stopped.

body.so_what: Each one names a starting point, and the stretch from it reaches today.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: I have been reading four chapters this morning.
body.right: I have read four chapters this morning.
body.why_it_happens: The reading went on all morning, so the form for a long activity looks right. A counted amount is a finished result, and a finished result needs the plain third form.
body.smallest_fix: Drop *been* and the *-ing* whenever the sentence gives a number.

body.wrong: They have been knowing each other since college.
body.right: They have known each other since college.
body.why_it_happens: The knowing has lasted for years, and this is the form for something that lasts. Knowing is a state, and a state cannot be shown in the middle of happening.
body.smallest_fix: Use *have* plus the third form: *have known*, *have owned*, *have believed*.

body.wrong: The pump has running since Tuesday without a break.
body.right: The pump has been running since Tuesday without a break.
body.why_it_happens: *Has running* sounds close enough to be missed, especially in speech where *been* is unstressed. The form needs all three words, in that order.
body.smallest_fix: Put *been* between the helping verb and the *-ing* form.

body.heard: The present perfect continuous means the activity is still going on.
also_known_as: have been doing means it has not stopped
body.truth: It often is still going on, and it does not have to be. *Somebody has been decorating* is normally said about a job that finished an hour ago, because the point is the smell of paint rather than the painting.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the length or the traces of the activity are the point. If they are, this form is right, whether the activity has stopped or not.

body.headline: *Have been* plus *-ing*. The length is the message.
