title: Words for the whole, and for every part of it

article_json.also_called: *All*, *both*, *each*, *every*, *either*, *neither*, *no*, *none*, and the order of determiners
article_json.one_line: This gives you the words that cover a whole group, tells you which verb each one takes, and fixes the *of* that goes missing.
article_json.short_answer: *All* and *both* take a plural verb. *Every* and *each* take a singular one. Add *of* only when a word like *the* or *these* follows.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Is it *every student is* or *every student are*, and when do I need *of*?

body.text: Same group, four ways of looking at it
*All*, *every*, *each* and *both* can describe the same set of people. They differ in whether you are seeing the group together or one member at a time, and that difference decides the verb.

body.caption: Together takes a plural verb. One at a time takes a singular one.
rows: one at a time, small set
either noun, verb follows the noun
footnotes: *Every* means all of them and still takes a singular verb. That mismatch is the commonest trap in this group.

body.lead_in: Same fact each time. Only the word for the group changes, and the verb follows it.

items.text: All the rooms were checked before the inspection.
items.gloss: The checking got done, and you are treating it as one job.

items.text: Each room was checked before the inspection.
items.gloss: The rooms were checked one by one, and that is the point.

items.text: Every room has a smoke alarm now.
items.gloss: There is not a single room without one.

items.text: Both lifts are out of order again.
items.gloss: There are two lifts and neither is working.

body.so_what: *All* and *both* see the group together and take a plural verb. *Every* and *each* see it one at a time and take a singular one.

body.text: When these words need *of*, and when they must not have it
The word *of* is not decoration. It appears when the noun already has *the*, *these*, *my* or a pronoun after it, and it stays away when the noun is bare.
Add *of* when a word like *the*, *these*, *my* or a pronoun comes next. Leave *of* out when the noun stands bare.

body.lead_in: The same word each time. Only what follows it decides whether *of* appears.

items.text: Most students take the bus rather than drive.
items.gloss: You are talking about students in general.

items.text: Most of the students on this course take the bus.
items.gloss: You are talking about one particular group of students.

items.text: All applicants must supply two references.
items.gloss: The rule covers everybody who applies.

items.text: All of them missed the deadline by a week.
items.gloss: Every person in the group we were discussing was late.

body.so_what: *Of* turns a claim about everybody into a claim about one named group. It is never optional decoration.

body.caption: Bare noun, no *of*. A word like *the* after it, *of* is required.
rows: all of the students, all the students
both of the proposals, both the proposals
footnotes: *All* and *both* may drop the *of* in front of *the*: *all the students* and *all of the students* are both correct.
A dash means the pattern does not exist. *Every* cannot take *of*, and *none* cannot stand in front of a bare noun.

body.text: The order these little words go in
Three of these words can sit in front of *the* rather than instead of it. That gives a fixed order, and it is the reason a phrase like *the all reasons* sounds wrong.

body.caption: Front slot, middle slot, number slot, then the noun.
footnotes: A dash means the slot is empty in that row. Every slot is optional; the order is not.
*Such*, *what*, *quite* and *rather* go in the front slot and push *a* to the right: *such a delay*, *quite a change*, *rather a shame*.

body.lead_in: Words are added one slot at a time, and none of them moves.

items.text: The reasons for the delay were never made public.
items.gloss: Nobody explained why it was late.

items.text: All the reasons for the delay were never made public.
items.gloss: Not one of the reasons was explained.

items.text: All the many reasons for the delay were listed in the appendix.
items.gloss: There were a lot of reasons and every one was written down.

items.text: It was such a delay that half the audience left.
items.gloss: The wait was so long that many people gave up.

body.so_what: The slots fill from the left. Nothing ever moves in front of *all*, and nothing ever squeezes between *the* and the number.

body.text: What goes wrong with the whole-group words

body.wrong: Every students on the course have to register by Friday.
body.right: Every student on the course has to register by Friday.
body.why_it_happens: *Every* means all of them, so a plural noun and a plural verb feel right. *Every* looks at them one at a time, so the noun and the verb both stay singular.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the *-s* from the noun and match the verb to it.

body.wrong: Most of students in the survey cycled to work at least once.
body.right: Most of the students in the survey cycled to work at least once.
body.why_it_happens: *Most of* is a fixed phrase in your ear, so it gets used in front of a bare noun. *Of* needs a word like *the* or *these* after it, so either add one or take *of* out.
body.smallest_fix: Write *most students* or *most of the students*. Never *most of students*.

body.wrong: All of applicants were interviewed within two weeks.
body.right: All applicants were interviewed within two weeks.
body.why_it_happens: The same fixed phrase problem as *most of*. *All* goes straight in front of a bare noun, and *of* is only for when a word like *the* follows.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *of*, or write *all of the applicants*.

body.label: Three agreement points where careful writing and speech differ

items.text: *Neither of* and *either of* take a singular verb in careful writing. A plural verb after them is very common in speech.
items.example: Neither of the reports is complete.

items.text: *None of* takes either a singular or a plural verb, and both are standard. Be consistent.
items.example: None of the proposals were affordable.

items.text: *All of* and *both of* follow the noun after them, so the verb is plural with a plural noun.
items.example: All of the equipment was returned undamaged.

body.heard: *Every* means all of them, so it takes a plural verb.
also_known_as: every is the same as all
body.truth: *Every* covers the whole group in meaning and stays singular in shape. English looks at the members one at a time here, so it is *every student receives*, never *every students receive*.
body.what_to_do: Use *all* with a plural noun and a plural verb. Use *every* with a singular noun and a singular verb. They mean the same and they behave differently.

body.headline: Together takes a plural verb. One at a time takes a singular one.

title: Words that stand in for a noun

article_json.also_called: Subject, object, possessive, reflexive and reciprocal pronouns
article_json.one_line: This puts every form of every English pronoun in one table, so you can see which slot each one belongs in.
article_json.short_answer: Before the verb use *I*, *he*, *they*. After a verb or a preposition use *me*, *him*, *them*. When the doer and the receiver are the same, use *myself*, *himself*, *themselves*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Is it *me* or *I* here, and when do I need *myself*?

body.text: Five forms of the same word, one per slot

English changes the shape of a pronoun depending on where it sits. Before the verb it takes one shape, after the verb another, and in front of a noun a third. The table has all five shapes for every person.
Read it across a row, not down a column. Each row is one person, and the five cells are the five places that person can appear in a sentence.

body.caption: One row per person. Five slots, and each slot has its own shape.
body.form_line: the person, in the shape the slot requires

rows.note: The first three cells are the same word. Only the last two change.
*His* fills two slots and does not change between them.
*Her* fills two slots: after a verb, and in front of a noun.
Written English uses the same *you* for one person and for several.

sub_tables.caption: When two people do the same thing to each other, use these two.
rows: the two departments email each other daily
the same, and slightly more formal
each person acts on himself or herself
the students taught themselves the software

sub_tables.caption: The same *-self* words also do a second job: emphasis.
rows: she cut herself on the broken glass
the doer and the receiver are the same
the minister herself signed the order
emphasis: nobody more junior signed it
emphasis: we did not pay anybody
emphasis: the problem is somewhere else

sub_tables.caption: After every preposition, English uses the after-the-verb form.

gaps.note: English has no standing-alone form for *it*. Use *its own*, or rewrite the sentence with a noun.

examples.text: I sent the figures to her on Monday morning.
examples.gloss: You emailed one person the numbers at the start of the week.

examples.text: The delay affected them more than it affected us.
examples.gloss: One group suffered more from the delay than the other.

examples.text: Their bid was cheaper than ours by four thousand pounds.
examples.gloss: The other side asked for less money than we did.

examples.text: She taught herself to use the mapping software.
examples.gloss: Nobody trained her. She worked it out alone.

examples.text: The two teams check each other's calculations every month.
examples.gloss: Each team looks at the other team's sums.

examples.text: That's mine, I think — the blue one on the end.
examples.gloss: You are claiming one particular item as yours.

examples.text: The council itself admitted that the survey was rushed.
examples.gloss: Even the council, which had every reason not to, said so.

notes: *Ours*, *yours*, *theirs*, *hers* and *its* never take an apostrophe. *It's* means *it is*.
*Myself* is not a polite version of *me*. Never *please contact myself*.
*Each other* is for two sides acting on each other. *Themselves* is for each person acting on himself or herself.
The emphasis use can move to the end: *we repaired the fence ourselves*, or *we ourselves repaired the fence*.

body.caption: The slot decides the shape, not the meaning.

spec.caption: One person in each slot, and each slot has its own shape.

body.text: Seeing the two forms that get swapped

body.lead_in: Only the position in the sentence changes. Watch the shape follow it.

items.text: She reviewed the drainage plan last week.
items.gloss: One person read the plan.

items.text: The engineer sent her the drainage plan last week.
items.gloss: The plan went to that same person.

items.text: The plan was reviewed by her and two colleagues.
items.gloss: Three people read it, and she was one of them.

items.text: Give it to him and me before Friday, could you?
items.gloss: Two of us need a copy by the end of the week.

body.so_what: The same person appears four times in four shapes. The slot chose the shape every time.

body.headline: The slot picks the shape. Before the verb, or after it.

title: Making sure the reader knows what a pronoun points at

article_json.also_called: Demonstrative and indefinite pronouns, reference, and substitution with *one*
article_json.one_line: This covers the pronouns that stand alone, the ones built from *some* and *any*, and how to stop a pronoun pointing at the wrong thing.
article_json.short_answer: A pronoun must have exactly one noun it can point back to. If two are possible, name the noun again instead: *this shift*, not *this*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I stop *it* and *this* being confusing in my writing?

body.text: A pronoun is a promise that the reader can fill it in

A pronoun saves you from repeating a noun. It only works when the reader can put the noun back. If two nouns in the last sentence could fit, the reader has to guess, and half the time they guess wrong.

body.gloss: the noun a pronoun points back to

show_first.text: The survey was delayed because it needed new funding.
Two tenants complained, and they were both ignored.
The bridge reopened after they had reinforced it.

body.name_line: The marked noun is the pronoun's **antecedent**.
body.anchor_line: Every pronoun needs one, and it needs to be the only one that fits. When two nouns fit, the sentence has stopped saying anything definite.

body.text: The pronouns that stand on their own

body.caption: These work with no noun after them, and each points somewhere different.
rows: this is the problem we came to solve
that was the year the depot closed
part of an amount already named
none of them arrived on time
a person or thing you cannot name
footnotes: *One* and *ones* only replace countable nouns. There is no *one* for *water* or *advice*.

body.lead_in: Only the standing-alone word changes, and each one sends the reader somewhere different.

items.text: We looked at two routes and chose the shorter one.
items.gloss: There were two options and you took the shorter route.

items.text: The older buses were noisy; the new ones are not.
items.gloss: The replacement buses are quieter than the ones before.

items.text: Nobody from the depot attended the meeting.
items.gloss: Not one person from there came.

items.text: That's the bit I'd cut, if it were up to me.
items.gloss: You are pointing at a section somebody just showed you.

body.so_what: *One* replaces a countable noun. *This* and *that* replace a whole idea. *Nobody* stands for a person who does not exist.

body.text: The words built from *some*, *any*, *no* and *every*

body.caption: Sixteen words from four starts and four endings, and all of them are singular.
footnotes: *-one* and *-body* mean the same. *-one* is slightly more formal in writing.
*No one* is two words in British English. *Nobody* is one word.
The *some* and *any* split works exactly as it does with the nouns: *some* in positives and offers, *any* in negatives and most questions.

body.text: Every one of these sixteen words takes a singular verb, including *everyone* and *everybody*.

body.lead_in: Only the pronoun changes, and the verb after it stays singular every time.

items.text: Everyone on the committee has read the report.
items.gloss: All the committee members have read it.

items.text: Nothing in the survey suggests that costs will fall.
items.gloss: The survey gives no reason to expect cheaper prices.

items.text: Somebody has left a bike across the fire exit.
items.gloss: A bike is blocking the exit and you do not know whose.

items.text: Anyone with a valid pass is allowed through.
items.gloss: A pass is all you need to get in.

body.so_what: *Everyone* means all of them and still takes a singular verb, exactly like *every student*.

body.text: How to stop a pronoun pointing at two things at once
The fix is not a rule about pronouns. It is a habit: when the noun you mean is not the only one that fits, put a noun after the pointing word. *This shift*, *these findings*, *that decision*.

body.lead_in: The same sentence three times. Each version tells the reader more about what *this* means.

items.text: Fares rose and services were cut. This angered commuters.
items.gloss: Something angered them, and the reader cannot tell which of the two.

items.text: Fares rose and services were cut. This combination angered commuters.
items.gloss: Both things together are what made people angry.

items.text: Fares rose and services were cut. These cuts angered commuters.
items.gloss: The reduction in services is what made people angry.

items.text: So that's why they're annoyed, then.
items.gloss: You are summing up a reason somebody just gave you.

body.so_what: One noun after *this* removes the guess, and it costs you one word.

body.text: What goes wrong when a pronoun is left loose

body.wrong: The council wrote to the contractor after it missed the deadline.
body.right: The council wrote to the contractor after the contractor missed the deadline.
body.why_it_happens: You know which one missed the deadline, so the pronoun feels clear. Two nouns in the sentence can both take *it*, and the reader has no way to choose between them.
body.smallest_fix: Repeat the noun, or rewrite so only one noun comes before the pronoun.

body.wrong: Rents rose and wages stayed flat. This is the main cause of the problem.
body.right: Rents rose and wages stayed flat. This gap is the main cause of the problem.
body.why_it_happens: *This* feels like a link back to the whole of the last sentence, and often it is. When the last sentence contains two ideas, the reader cannot tell which one you have picked up.
body.smallest_fix: Put a noun after *this*: *this gap*, *this rise*, *this pattern*.

body.wrong: Everyone in the department have been asked to comment.
body.right: Everyone in the department has been asked to comment.
body.why_it_happens: *Everyone* covers a whole group, and *department* is plural in your ear, so the plural verb comes out. *Everyone* is singular in shape, and the words in between do not change the verb.
body.smallest_fix: Cover the words between the pronoun and the verb. *Everyone has* is what is left.

body.heard: Never repeat a noun. Use a pronoun instead, or the writing looks repetitive.
also_known_as: repeating a word is bad style
body.truth: Repeating a key noun is what holds a paragraph together. Reaching for a pronoun every time is what produces sentences where nobody can tell what *it* means, and that costs far more than repetition does.
body.what_to_do: Use a pronoun when only one noun can fit it. When two could, repeat the noun, or put it after *this* or *these*.

body.headline: One noun must fit the pronoun. If two do, name it.

title: How *can*, *must* and *should* behave

article_json.also_called: Modal verbs: the nine central modals and their grammar
article_json.one_line: This shows you how the nine modal verbs behave, so you can use any of them without a form mistake.
article_json.short_answer: A modal never changes shape, and the verb after it is the base form with no *to*: *she must go*, *must she go?*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: What is a modal, and what shape does the verb after it take?

body.text: Nine verbs that follow none of the usual rules

Nine verbs in English add an attitude to another verb. They are *can*, *could*, *may*, *might*, *will*, *would*, *shall*, *should* and *must*. Each one says how sure you are, how necessary something is, or what you are allowed to do.

body.lead_in: A modal verb behaves in five ways that no ordinary verb does:
items: the verb after it is the base form, with no *to*
it never takes *-s*, whoever the subject is
it has no *-ing* form and no third form of its own
it makes its own questions and negatives, with no *do*
two modals never stand together in one verb group

body.caption: One shape for every person. No *-s*, no *do*, no *to* after it.
body.form_line: a modal + the base form of the verb, with no *to*

rows.note: The full negative is written as one word: *cannot*.
*May I…?* asks permission. *May she…?* is rare.
*mightn't* is British and rare. *might not* is safe everywhere.
In everyday English *shall* survives mainly in offers and suggestions.

sub_tables.caption: The modal keeps one shape, and so does the verb behind it.
Where a modal has no form, a helper of two or more words fills the gap.
A short answer repeats the modal and stops there.

gaps.cell: positive short form, seven of the nine rows
gaps.note: Only *will*, *would* and *shall* run together with the subject. The others shorten with *not* instead.
*may not* has no short form in use today. Write and say the two words.

examples.text: Every applicant must upload a scan of the certificate.
examples.gloss: There is no way round it. That is the rule.

examples.text: The Verdon depot can process four hundred parcels an hour.
examples.gloss: That is what the depot is capable of doing.

examples.text: Should we move the meeting to Thursday?
examples.gloss: You are asking whether Thursday is a better idea.

examples.text: The bus won't stop at the hospital after seven.
examples.gloss: After seven the hospital stop is closed.

examples.text: Residents may not park along the towpath.
examples.gloss: Parking there is not allowed.

notes: A modal never takes *-s*. Write *she must*, never *she musts*.
The verb behind a modal is the base form: *must go*, never *must to go*.
Questions and negatives need no *do*: *Can you drive?*, not *Do you can drive?*
*she'd paint* is *she would paint*. Only *will*, *would* and *shall* shorten this way.

body.caption: Three boxes, and the middle one never changes shape.

body.text: The same modal, whoever you are talking about

body.lead_in: Only the subject changes here. Watch what does not happen to *can*.

items.text: I can read the meter from the doorway.
items.gloss: Standing at the door is enough. I do not have to go in.

items.text: The technician can read the meter from the doorway.
items.gloss: Same thing, one person doing it.

items.text: Both technicians can read the meter from the doorway.
items.gloss: Two people, and the reading still works from the door.

items.text: Nobody can read the meter once the cover is locked.
items.gloss: With the cover locked the reading is impossible.

body.so_what: The subject changed four times and *can* never moved. No other English verb behaves like that.

title: Helpers made of more than one word

article_json.also_called: Semi-modals: *have to*, *be able to*, *ought to*, *had better*, *used to*
article_json.one_line: This gives you the past, the future and the *to*-forms that the nine modals cannot build for themselves.
article_json.short_answer: When a modal has no form you need, use a helper made of words: *had to*, *will be able to*, *ought to check*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say *must* in the past, or *can* in the future?

body.text: The gaps the nine modals leave, and what fills them

A modal has one shape and no others. So there is no past *must*, no future *can*, and no way to put a modal after another modal. English fills every one of those gaps with a helper made of two or three words.

body.gloss: a helper made of more than one word: *have to*, *be able to*

show_first.text: Drivers have to renew the permit every spring.
The clinic was able to see everybody before six.
You had better keep the receipt.

body.name_line: A helper like that is called a **semi-modal**.
body.anchor_line: It means what a modal means, and it changes shape like an ordinary verb. That is the point of it.

body.text: The whole set, and what each one takes after it

body.caption: Some take *to* + the base form. Four take the base form on its own.
rows: the coach is due to arrive
footnotes: *had better* and *would rather* look past but point at now or later.
The negative sits after the whole helper: *had better not go*, *would rather not go*.

body.lead_in: One meaning, four times. Only the time changes, and the helper carries it.

items.text: Volunteers are able to book a slot online.
items.gloss: Booking online is open to them now.

items.text: Volunteers were able to book a slot online last winter.
items.gloss: Online booking worked for them then.

items.text: Volunteers will be able to book a slot online from March.
items.gloss: From March onwards online booking opens to them.

items.text: It is good to be able to book a slot online.
items.gloss: Having the online option is a good thing.

body.so_what: *Can* could not have gone in three of those four sentences. The two-word helper goes in all of them.

body.text: When the modal you want has no form for the time or the position you need, use the semi-modal with the same meaning.

body.lead_in: The modal is impossible in each of these, so the helper does the work.

items.text: Staff had to move the whole archive in one weekend.
items.gloss: The move was forced on them, and it is over.

items.text: Nobody wants to have to queue twice for the same form.
items.gloss: Queuing twice for one form is a waste of everybody's morning.

items.text: The scheme is likely to be extended for another year.
items.gloss: Another year of the scheme looks probable.

items.text: You will have to bring the original, not a copy.
items.gloss: A copy will not get you in when you go.

body.so_what: Each sentence needs a past, a *to*-form or a second helper, and a modal cannot supply any of the three.

body.text: Three helpers that look the same and are not

body.caption: *Used to* is about the past. *Be used to* is about how normal something feels.
rows: she is used to cycling in
she is getting used to cycling in
footnotes: In the last two, *to* is the small placing word, which is why an *-ing* form follows it.

body.lead_in: The same person and the same journey, with the three structures in turn.

items.text: My tutor used to work at the Norland campus.
items.gloss: She worked there before. She does not now.

items.text: My tutor is used to working across two campuses.
items.gloss: She does it, and it gives her no trouble.

items.text: My tutor is getting used to working across two campuses.
items.gloss: It is new, and it is starting to feel normal.

body.so_what: The first sentence is about a past that has ended. The other two are about how a present arrangement feels.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: You had better to book the coach seat early.
body.right: You had better book the coach seat early.
body.why_it_happens: *Have to*, *need to* and *ought to* all end in *to*, so *to* starts to look like part of every helper. *Had better* is one of the four that take the base form on its own.
body.smallest_fix: Delete the *to*. Four helpers take no *to*: *had better*, *would rather*, *be going to*, *be about to*.

body.wrong: The panel ought publish the raw figures as well.
body.right: The panel ought to publish the raw figures as well.
body.why_it_happens: *Ought* means what *should* means, and *should* takes no *to*, so the *to* gets dropped along with the meaning it came with.
body.smallest_fix: Keep *ought* and *to* together. They are one helper and they never separate.

body.wrong: I am used to live in Sandmouth, but I moved away in 2019.
body.right: I used to live in Sandmouth, but I moved away in 2019.
body.why_it_happens: *Used to* and *be used to* are spelled the same, so one gets reached for when the other is meant. Adding *am* switches the sentence from a finished past to a present feeling.
body.smallest_fix: For a finished past, drop the *be*: *I used to live*. Keep *be used to* for what feels normal now.

body.label: Three oddities in this set, one of them worth learning today

items.text: In the negative and the question, *used* loses its *-d*, because *did* already carries the past.
items.example: Did you use to cycle in, or did you always drive?

items.text: *Didn't used to* is written and said by many people, and plenty of reference books now list it. *Didn't use to* is the safer form to write.
items.example: The library didn't use to open on Sundays.

items.text: *Need* and *dare* work as ordinary verbs and, in questions and negatives only, as modals. The modal versions are formal and mainly British.
items.example: You needn't send the second reference.

body.stop_line: That is the whole list for this article. Everything else in the table above follows the pattern shown in its own row.

body.what_varies: How common *have got* and *have got to* are, and where they belong.

option_a.label: British English
option_a.example: We've got to hand the keys back by Friday.

option_b.label: American English
option_b.example: We have to hand the keys back by Friday.

body.house_default: *have to* in writing, *have got to* shown as speech
body.why_this_default: *Have to* is right in every country and every register. That is a house choice for our examples, not a rule of English.
body.costs_marks: yes in an essay — write *have to* there

body.heard: *Have got to* is bad English. Say *must* instead.
also_known_as: *have got* is incorrect
*got* is lazy English
body.truth: *Have got to* is ordinary spoken English, chiefly British, and it is correct. It is marked as speech, not as error. What it is wrong for is an essay, where it reads as conversation on the page.
body.what_to_do: Say *we've got to* in Speaking if it comes naturally. Write *have to* or *must* in Task 1 and Task 2.

title: Saying how certain you are

article_json.also_called: Modality of certainty: deduction and possibility in the present
article_json.one_line: This lets you say how sure you are about something, instead of stating everything as a flat fact.
article_json.short_answer: Sure it is true, use *must*. Sure it is not, use *can't*. Anything in between, use *may*, *might* or *could*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say I think something is true without saying it is?

body.text: Every modal here answers one question: how sure are you?

*The lights are on in the office* is a fact you can see. *Somebody must be working late* is not a fact. It is what you work out from the fact, and the modal is what tells your reader you worked it out.
So the choice is not really between words. It is a choice about how far you are prepared to go on the evidence you have.

body.caption: One line from certain-yes to certain-no, with the middle left open.

steps.gloss: I am confident this is true
I expect it to be true

steps.text: may be, might be, could be
may not be, might not be

steps.gloss: I am confident this is not true

body.text: How to build it, and where the negative goes

body.caption: *Can't* is the opposite of *must*. *May not* is the opposite of nothing.
rows: you expect it not to be so
footnotes: *Could not be* does not mean *possibly not*. It means the same as *can't be*.

body.lead_in: One situation, five degrees of confidence. Only the modal changes.

items.text: The lift is out again, so the engineer must be on site.
items.gloss: You are confident the engineer is there.

items.text: The engineer should be on site by now.
items.gloss: You expect him to be there, from the usual timings.

items.text: The engineer may be on site already.
items.gloss: It is possible that he is there.

items.text: The engineer might not be on site until Thursday.
items.gloss: Possibly he will not be there before Thursday.

items.text: The van has gone, so the engineer can't be on site.
items.gloss: You are confident he is not there.

body.so_what: Nothing about the office changed across those five sentences. What changed is how much the speaker is willing to claim.

body.text: Use *must* when you are confident something is true, *can't* when you are confident it is not, and *may*, *might* or *could* in between.

body.lead_in: Each of these draws a conclusion from something visible in the sentence before it.

items.text: Her coat is still here, so she must be in the building.
items.gloss: The coat is the evidence. You are confident she is inside.

items.text: The figures could be out of date, so check the source first.
items.gloss: Old figures are one real possibility here.

items.text: That can't be the final total, because it is smaller than the first quarter.
items.gloss: The number is impossible, so it is not the final one.

items.text: The rise may reflect a change in how the data is collected.
items.gloss: A change in method is one possible reason for the rise.

body.so_what: Each sentence names its evidence and then says how far that evidence goes. That is the whole job of the modal.

body.text: So which of *may*, *might* and *could* do I write?

body.question: How formal am I being, and am I offering one option among several?

options.label: *may*
options.use_it_when: You are writing, and you want a careful, formal way of saying that something is possible.
options.example: The shortfall may be the result of a slower spring.

options.label: *might*
options.use_it_when: You are speaking or writing, and you want the everyday word for a possibility.
options.example: The shortfall might be the result of a slower spring.

options.label: *could*
options.use_it_when: You are naming one possibility out of two or three that you can see.
options.example: The shortfall could be a slower spring, or simply a counting error.

a.text: The delay may be weather-related.
a.means: Bad weather is a real possible cause, and you are being careful about saying so.

b.text: The delay can be weather-related.
b.means: Delays of this kind are sometimes caused by weather. You are describing what happens in general.

a.text: The results might not arrive before Friday.
a.means: Possibly they will not come by Friday.

b.text: The results couldn't arrive before Friday.
b.means: Friday is impossible. There is no way of getting them sooner.

a.text: You may leave your bag at the desk.
a.means: You are allowed to leave it there.

b.text: You may lose your bag at the desk.
b.means: Losing it there is possible, so be careful.

a.text: The council could fund the repair.
a.means: Funding it is one option open to them.

b.text: The council should fund the repair.
b.means: You expect them to, or you think they ought to.

body.deciding_factor: *May* is the formal one, *might* the everyday one, and *could* the one that offers an option. All three mean it is possible.
body.trap: You were told *might* is less likely than *may*, so you spend time weighing the two when the real difference is how formal the sentence is.
body.register_note: *May* is the safer choice in Task 1 and Task 2 when you explain a cause. *Might* and *could* are natural in Speaking Part 3 speculation.

body.text: *May* and *might* are very close in meaning, and speakers do not agree about which is weaker. What is reliable is that *may* is the more formal of the two, and that *might* is the form you use when you report what somebody said.
The word *may* is doing two different jobs

body.lead_in: The same word twice, once about possibility and once about permission.

items.text: The scheme may run for a second year.
items.gloss: A second year is possible. Nobody has decided.

items.text: Students may use the west entrance after six.
items.gloss: They are allowed to use it after six.

items.text: The hall may be booked for private events.
items.gloss: Booking it privately is permitted — or possible. The sentence alone does not say which.

items.text: May I take one of these leaflets?
items.gloss: You are asking for permission.

body.so_what: In a question, *may* always asks permission. In a statement, the sentence around it tells you which job it is doing.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The windows are dark, so the family mustn't be at home.
body.right: The windows are dark, so the family can't be at home.
body.why_it_happens: *Must* is the confident word, so its negative looks like the confident negative. *Mustn't* was never about certainty at all — it forbids something.
body.smallest_fix: Swap *mustn't* for *can't*. The opposite of *must be* is *can't be*.

body.wrong: I have not seen the report, so the fall must be caused by the new charge.
body.right: I have not seen the report, so the fall may be caused by the new charge.
body.why_it_happens: *Must* feels like a strong, academic word, so it gets used to sound confident. It claims that you are sure, and the first half of the sentence has just said you are not.
body.smallest_fix: Use *may* or *might* whenever you have not seen the evidence yourself.

body.wrong: She is not answering her phone, so she can be in the meeting.
body.right: She is not answering her phone, so she may be in the meeting.
body.why_it_happens: *Can* does mean possible, but only about what happens in general — *evenings here can be cold*. For one occasion happening now, English uses *may*, *might* or *could*.
body.smallest_fix: For a guess about this moment, write *may*, *might* or *could*, never *can*.

body.heard: *Might* means it is less likely than *may*.
also_known_as: *may* is 50 per cent and *might* is 30 per cent
body.truth: Many speakers do feel *might* as slightly more remote, but they do not agree with each other, and no reader can tell the two apart in your writing. The reliable difference is that *may* is the more formal word.
body.what_to_do: Stop weighing them. Write *may* in an essay, say *might* in speech, and put the real strength in the words around the modal if it matters.

body.mechanism: Russian carries this meaning with small separate words placed near the verb, such as the words for *probably* and *perhaps*.
body.wrong: Probably the engineer is on site now.
body.right: The engineer may be on site now.
body.fix: Put the doubt in the verb group with a modal. English prefers that to an added word.

body.headline: *Must* for yes, *can't* for no, *may* or *might* for anything between.

items.prompt: Which one is right? *His bike has gone, so he mustn't be here.* / *His bike has gone, so he can't be here.*
items.answer: *His bike has gone, so he can't be here.*
items.why: *Mustn't* forbids something. For a confident no, English uses *can't*.

items.prompt: Why does *The fee can be higher next year* sound wrong?
items.answer: *Can* is about what is possible in general. For one future case, use *may*, *might* or *could*.
items.why: The sentence is a guess about one year, not a statement about what fees do.

title: *Must have*, *can't have*, *might have*

article_json.also_called: The modal perfect: modal + *have* + the third form
article_json.one_line: This lets you say how sure you are about something that happened before now, instead of avoiding the guess.
article_json.short_answer: Put *have* and the third form after the modal: *must have risen* if you are sure, *can't have risen* if you are sure it did not.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I guess about the past without saying I know?

body.text: Working out what happened, when you were not there

You come back to the site and the trench is full of water. You did not see it fill. *The pump must have failed overnight* says what you have worked out, and it says openly that you are working it out.
Learners usually avoid this whole structure and write *maybe the pump failed* instead. That is understandable English, and it throws away the difference between what you saw and what you concluded.
How to build it: modal, then *have*, then the third form

body.caption: The modal never changes. *Have* never changes. Only the third form varies.
body.form_line: a modal + *have* + the third form of the verb

rows.note: For the negative of this row, use the *can't have* row.

cells: they may not have painted it
rows.note: *May* is the formal one. *May have* is common in academic writing.

cells: they might not have painted it
they could not have painted it
rows.note: *Couldn't have* means impossible, not *possibly not*.

sub_tables.caption: The third word is the third form, not the past form.
The same shape does three unrelated jobs. Read the meaning column.
rows: it did not happen, and that was wrong
we would have finished by six
it happened, and it was unnecessary

gaps.note: English does not use *mustn't have* for a guess. The confident negative is *can't have*.
*May* does not shorten, and *May they have…?* is not used. Ask with *might* or *could*.

examples.text: The road was already clear, so the tide must have turned early.
examples.gloss: You are confident the tide turned before you arrived.

examples.text: They can't have finished the survey; the equipment is still out there.
examples.gloss: You are confident the survey is not done.

examples.text: The drop may have begun before the new charge was introduced.
examples.gloss: It is possible the fall started earlier than people assume.

examples.text: The file might not have reached the second reviewer at all.
examples.gloss: Possibly the second reviewer never got it.

examples.text: They could've taken the coast road instead.
examples.gloss: The coast road was an option they had.

notes: *must've* and *might've* are what you hear. They sound like *must of*, and *must of* is never written.
The word after *have* is the third form: *written*, *taken*, *begun*, never the past form.
There is no *to* anywhere in this structure.

body.caption: The event is back there. The guessing is happening now.

body.text: To guess about the past, keep the modal you would use about now, and put *have* plus the third form behind it.

body.lead_in: The same guess about now, then about earlier. Only the second half of the verb group moves.

items.text: The heating must be broken.
items.gloss: You are confident it is broken at this moment.

items.text: The heating must have broken during the night.
items.gloss: You are confident it broke while nobody was there.

items.text: The panel may be using last year's figures.
items.gloss: Possibly they are working from old figures right now.

items.text: The panel may have used last year's figures.
items.gloss: Possibly the figures they worked from were the old ones.

body.so_what: The modal did not change in either pair. *Have* plus the third form is what moved the guess into the past.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The subsidy must contributed to the rise in applications.
body.right: The subsidy must have contributed to the rise in applications.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is about the past, so the past form of the verb goes in and feels like enough. The modal cannot carry past time by itself, and *have* is the part that does it.
body.smallest_fix: Put *have* in, and change the verb to the third form: *must have contributed*.

body.wrong: She might have wrote to the department in March.
body.right: She might have written to the department in March.
body.why_it_happens: For most verbs the past form and the third form are the same word, so the difference never comes up. It comes up on the irregular verbs, and those are the commonest ones.
body.smallest_fix: After *have*, use the third form: *written*, *taken*, *done*, *seen*.

body.wrong: The gate was locked, so the delivery mustn't have arrived.
body.right: The gate was locked, so the delivery can't have arrived.
body.why_it_happens: You want the negative of *must have*, and *mustn't have* looks like it. *Mustn't* forbids things and cannot make a guess at all.
body.smallest_fix: Write *can't have* or *couldn't have* for a confident negative guess about the past.

body.label: Three cases that behave differently, one of them a real meaning difference

items.text: *Needn't have* + third form says the thing was done and was unnecessary. *Didn't need to* says only that it was not necessary.
items.example: You needn't have queued — the tickets were emailed that morning.

items.text: American English also uses *must not have* for a confident negative guess. British English uses *can't have* there. Both are correct at home.
items.example: He must not have seen the second notice.

items.text: *Could have* + third form has a second meaning: it was possible and it did not happen.
items.example: The council could have funded the repair, but the money went elsewhere.

body.stop_line: That is the whole list. Anything else that looks like a fourth case is one of these three wearing different words.

body.heard: *Must have gone* is the past tense of *must go*.
also_known_as: *must have* is how you say *must* in the past
body.truth: They are two different meanings. *Must go* is an obligation, and its past is *had to go*. *Must have gone* is a confident guess about something that already happened, and it has nothing to do with obligation.
body.what_to_do: For a past obligation write *had to*. Keep *must have* for guesses: *the notice must have gone out on Monday*.

body.headline: Modal + *have* + the third form. *Can't have* is the confident no.

title: Rules, obligation, and where it comes from

article_json.also_called: Obligation and necessity: *must*, *have to*, *need to*, *be required to*
article_json.one_line: This lets you say that something is necessary, and show whether the rule is yours or somebody else's.
article_json.short_answer: Use *must* when the rule is yours, *have to* when it comes from outside. For the past there is only *had to*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When do I write *must*, and when do I write *have to*?

body.text: Saying something is necessary, and saying who says so
*Applicants submit two references* is a description of what happens. *Applicants must submit two references* is a rule. The modal is what turns the description into the rule.
English then gives you a second decision, and it is the one this article is really about. The word you pick tells your reader where the rule came from.

body.caption: From no choice at all down to a free choice.

body.text: How to build it in every tense

body.caption: *Must* has one form only. *Have to* goes anywhere a verb can go.
footnotes: The two empty cells are the reason *had to* and *will have to* exist.
The three negatives do not all mean the same thing. That is the next article.

body.lead_in: One rule, four times, with only the time of the sentence changing.

items.text: Cyclists have to use the marked lane through the tunnel.
items.gloss: In the tunnel the marked lane is the only option.

items.text: Cyclists had to use the marked lane while the tunnel was narrowed.
items.gloss: During the narrowing there was nowhere else to ride.

items.text: Cyclists will have to use the marked lane from Monday.
items.gloss: From Monday the lane becomes the only route.

items.text: Nobody likes having to use that lane in the rain.
items.gloss: Riding there in wet weather is unpleasant.

body.so_what: *Must* would fit only the first of those four sentences. Everywhere else the two-word helper is the only way in.

body.text: Use *must* when the obligation is yours to impose, and *have to* when it comes from outside you. For any past obligation, use *had to*.

body.lead_in: Each of these names the source of the rule in the words around the modal.

items.text: I must sort out the insurance before the trip.
items.gloss: Nobody is making you. You have decided it matters.

items.text: I have to renew the permit every March.
items.gloss: The rule is somebody else's, and March is when they want it.

items.text: All visitors must sign in at the west gate.
items.gloss: This is the notice speaking. It is the rule of the place.

items.text: Governments need to plan for a much older population.
items.gloss: Planning for it is necessary, and you are saying so gently.

body.so_what: Read the four again without the modal and the difference disappears. The modal is carrying the source of the rule on its own.

body.text: Whose rule is this — mine, or somebody else's?

body.question: Whose rule is this — mine, or somebody else's?

options.label: *must*
options.use_it_when: You are the one imposing it: your own decision, your own strong recommendation, or a notice or regulation you are writing.
options.example: Entries must reach the office by the last Friday in May.

options.label: *have to*
options.use_it_when: The rule comes from outside: the law, an employer, the timetable, the facts of the situation.
options.example: We have to leave by six, because the last ferry goes at seven.

a.text: I must cut down on the amount I drive.
a.means: You have decided it yourself. Nobody has told you to.

b.text: I have to cut down on the amount I drive.
b.means: Something outside you has forced it: the cost, a rule, a health warning.

a.text: Students must keep a copy of every submission.
a.means: The department is stating its own rule to the students.

b.text: Students have to keep a copy of every submission.
b.means: Somebody is explaining a rule that exists, from outside it.

a.text: You must see the new footbridge while you are here.
a.means: You are recommending it strongly. There is no rule at all.

b.text: You have to see the surveyor before the work starts.
b.means: Seeing the surveyor is a requirement somebody else has set.

a.text: Drivers must not exceed twenty in the market square.
a.means: Going faster is forbidden.

b.text: Drivers do not have to pay after six in the market square.
b.means: Paying after six is optional.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: must not / do not have to

body.deciding_factor: *Must* means the rule is mine. *Have to* means the rule is somebody else's. In the past there is only *had to*.
body.trap: *Must* looks like the stronger and more academic word, so it gets used for every requirement in an essay, including the ones nobody is imposing.
body.register_note: *Have to* does nearly all the work in speech. *Must* belongs in written rules, notices and Task 2 recommendations, used sparingly.

body.text: The difference is a strong tendency, not a border. Speakers cross it often, and *have to* is slowly taking over in speech. Where the two really part company is the past, and there the choice is made for you.
What goes wrong

body.wrong: Last winter we must close the path for three weeks.
body.right: Last winter we had to close the path for three weeks.
body.why_it_happens: *Must* is a verb, so it looks as though it should have a past like any other verb. It has none, and *must have closed* is a guess, not an obligation.
body.smallest_fix: Every past obligation is *had to*, whoever imposed it.

body.wrong: Applicants must to provide a second form of identification.
body.right: Applicants must provide a second form of identification.
body.why_it_happens: *Have to*, *need to* and *ought to* all carry a *to*, so *to* starts to look like part of every word in this family. *Must* is a modal, and no modal takes it.
body.smallest_fix: Delete the *to* after *must*, *should*, *can*, *may* and *will*.

body.wrong: Students must study a foreign language, because it broadens their thinking.
body.right: Students should study a foreign language, because it broadens their thinking.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is a recommendation and *must* sounds forceful, so it reads as more committed. It commits you to an absolute claim that the rest of the paragraph then has to defend.
body.smallest_fix: Keep *must* for real requirements. Recommend with *should* or *need to*.

body.heard: *Must* and *have to* mean exactly the same thing, so use whichever you like.
also_known_as: *have to* is just the informal *must*
body.truth: In the plain present they are close, and swapping them rarely produces a wrong sentence. They still differ: *must* puts the rule in your own mouth, and *have to* puts it outside. And *must* has no past at all.
body.what_to_do: Swap freely in the present if you must, but never write *must* for a past obligation. That one is *had to* every time.

body.mechanism: Mandarin marks time with words such as the ones for *yesterday* and *already*, and leaves the verb itself unchanged.
body.wrong: Yesterday I must work until nine.
body.right: Yesterday I had to work until nine.
body.fix: In English the past has to show on the verb group as well: *had to*, not *must*.

body.headline: *Must* is my rule, *have to* is theirs, *had to* is all of the past.

we have to renew it yearly
we had to close the path

title: Two negatives that mean opposite things

article_json.also_called: Prohibition against absence of obligation: *mustn't* and *don't have to*
article_json.one_line: This keeps you from writing the opposite of what you mean, in a sentence that will look completely correct.
article_json.short_answer: *Mustn't* forbids it. *Don't have to* means you may choose. *You mustn't apply* and *you don't have to apply* are opposites.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Is *don't have to* the negative of *must*?

body.text: The same six words, and two opposite instructions
*You mustn't tell them* and *you don't have to tell them* look like two versions of one sentence. One of them forbids you from telling. The other says telling is up to you.
That is why this is the most expensive negative in the modal system. Both sentences are correct English, so nothing looks wrong, and the reader takes away the instruction you did not give.
Is it forbidden, or is it just not necessary?

body.question: Do I want to stop them, or to release them?

options.label: *mustn't*
options.use_it_when: You are forbidding it. Doing it is not allowed, and there will be a consequence.
options.example: Staff mustn't share the login with contractors.

options.label: *don't have to*
options.use_it_when: You are releasing them. Doing it is not necessary, and they may do it if they want.
options.example: Staff don't have to attend the Friday briefing.

a.text: You mustn't park in the loading bay.
a.means: Parking there is forbidden. Expect a fine.

b.text: You don't have to park in the loading bay.
b.means: The loading bay is free to you, and so is everywhere else.

a.text: Candidates mustn't bring a phone into the hall.
a.means: Phones are banned in the hall.

b.text: Candidates don't have to bring a pen into the hall.
b.means: Pens are provided. Bring one if you prefer your own.

a.text: We mustn't move the boxes before the survey.
a.means: Moving them first is not permitted.

b.text: We needn't move the boxes before the survey.
b.means: Moving them first is unnecessary. We can if it helps.

a.text: Residents can't use the side gate after nine.
a.means: The side gate is closed to them after nine.

b.text: Residents don't need to use the side gate after nine.
b.means: The side gate is one option, and the main gate is open too.

body.deciding_factor: Ask whether you are closing a door or opening one. Closing it is *mustn't*. Opening it is *don't have to*.
body.trap: *Have to* means what *must* means, so its negative looks as though it must mean what *mustn't* means. The negative attaches to different parts of the two phrases.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. In notices and instructions the difference is the whole message, so it is worth a second look before you send anything.

body.intro: Two questions, in this order. The first one usually settles it.

steps.ask: If they do it, is that a problem?

verdict.example: Visitors mustn't take photographs in the reading room.
verdict.why: You are forbidding the action, so the negative goes on the whole action.

branches.answer: No — it is fine either way

steps.ask: Are you saying it is a waste of their time, or that it was already done for them?

verdict.example: You don't have to book a slot for the drop-in session.
verdict.why: You are removing the requirement, not the permission.

branches.answer: They already did it, and it turned out to be pointless

verdict.example: You needn't have printed the form; the desk had spare copies.
verdict.why: The action happened, and this is the form that says it was unnecessary.

body.text: The whole family of negatives, in one place

body.caption: Three of these forbid. Three release. Read the middle column first.
rows: forbids it, or says it is impossible
visitors may not enter the yard
footnotes: *Mustn't* is chiefly British. American English tends to forbid with *can't* or *may not*.
*Needn't* is British and slightly formal. *Don't need to* works everywhere.

body.lead_in: One notice, written six ways. Watch which three close the door.

items.text: Cyclists mustn't ride through the covered market.
items.gloss: Riding through is banned.

items.text: Cyclists may not ride through the covered market.
items.gloss: The same ban, in the language of a formal notice.

items.text: Cyclists can't ride through the covered market.
items.gloss: The same ban, in ordinary speech.

items.text: Cyclists don't have to ride through the covered market.
items.gloss: There is another route, and either one is fine.

items.text: Cyclists needn't ride through the covered market.
items.gloss: The same choice, in slightly more formal words.

body.so_what: The first three stop people riding through. The last two tell them nobody is making them.

body.text: In the past: *needn't have* against *didn't need to*
*Needn't have* plus the third form is reliable. It says the thing was done and turned out to be unnecessary. *You needn't have queued* means you queued.

*Didn't need to* says only that the necessity was absent. British speakers often use it when the action did not happen, but that comes from the situation and not from the form, so check the sentence around it before you read anything into it.

body.lead_in: The same morning, told with each of the two past forms.

items.text: We needn't have arrived so early; the doors opened at ten.
items.gloss: You arrived early, and the early start bought you nothing.

items.text: We didn't need to arrive early, so we had breakfast first.
items.gloss: There was no requirement, so you took your time.

items.text: She needn't have written a covering letter.
items.gloss: She wrote one, and nobody asked for it.

body.so_what: The first and third sentences tell you the action happened. The second one leaves it open.

body.wrong: You mustn't bring your own laptop; there are machines in every room.
body.right: You don't have to bring your own laptop; there are machines in every room.
body.why_it_happens: You mean to remove a requirement, and *mustn't* is the negative form of the requirement word. The negative in *mustn't* lands on the action, so it bans laptops instead of releasing you.
body.smallest_fix: If the person may still do it, write *don't have to* or *don't need to*.

body.wrong: Passengers don't have to lean out of the window while the train is moving.
body.right: Passengers mustn't lean out of the window while the train is moving.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is meant as a safety rule, and *don't have to* looks like a polite way of stating one. It says leaning out is optional, which is the opposite of a safety rule.
body.smallest_fix: For anything that is genuinely banned, use *mustn't*, *can't* or *may not*.

body.heard: The negative of *must* is *don't have to*.
also_known_as: *must* becomes *don't have to* in the negative
body.truth: The negative of *must* is *mustn't*, and it forbids. *Don't have to* is the negative of *have to*, and it releases. The two positives are close in meaning, and their negatives are not.
body.what_to_do: Do not build these two from each other. Decide first whether you are forbidding or releasing, then pick from the table above.

body.headline: *Mustn't* closes the door. *Don't have to* opens it.

table.caption: One row per thing you might want to say.
rows: you don't have to sign in
it was done, and it was pointless
it was not required at the time

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: A form is optional. Which do you write? *You mustn't complete section four.* / *You don't have to complete section four.*
items.answer: *You don't have to complete section four.*
items.why: *Mustn't* would ban people from completing it, which is not what optional means.

items.prompt: What does *He needn't have paid the deposit* tell you about the deposit?
items.answer: He paid it, and paying it was unnecessary.
items.why: *Needn't have* plus the third form says the action happened and was pointless.

*needn't have* beside the other modal-plus-*have* forms

title: *Should*, *ought to*, and the one that is a warning

article_json.also_called: Advice and expectation: *should*, *ought to*, *had better*, *be supposed to*
article_json.one_line: This lets you recommend something without ordering it, and shows you which word turns advice into a warning.
article_json.short_answer: Use *should* for advice. *Had better* is not politer or stronger — it warns that something bad follows if you ignore it.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I tell somebody what is a good idea without sounding like a boss?

body.text: Advice sits between an order and a suggestion
*Keep a copy* is an instruction. *You could keep a copy* is one option among several. *You should keep a copy* sits between them: you are recommending it, and the other person still decides.
Three other helpers live in the same area, and one of them is not advice at all. Getting that one wrong changes a friendly sentence into a threat.
How to build the four, including the negatives

body.caption: Two take *to*. *Had better* takes none, and its *not* comes last.
footnotes: *Had better* is nearly always shortened in speech to *'d better*.
*Ought not to* is rare. Most people write *shouldn't*.

body.lead_in: One piece of advice, given four ways. Only the helper changes.

items.text: You should keep the receipt until the warranty runs out.
items.gloss: Keeping it is sensible. It is up to you.

items.text: You ought to keep the receipt until the warranty runs out.
items.gloss: The same advice, with a small nod to what is proper.

items.text: You'd better keep the receipt — they will ask for it.
items.gloss: If you lose it, there will be trouble at the counter.

items.text: You're supposed to keep the receipt for two years.
items.gloss: That is the arrangement, and plenty of people ignore it.

body.so_what: Only the third one carries a threat. The other three are ordinary advice at different levels of formality.

body.text: Use *should* for advice. Use *had better* only when ignoring the advice leads to a specific bad outcome.

body.lead_in: Each of these names the bad outcome that makes *had better* the right word.

items.text: We'd better leave now, or we'll miss the last train back.
items.gloss: Staying longer means walking home.

items.text: You'd better not lend him the drill again.
items.gloss: Last time it came back broken.

items.text: They'd better fix the leak before the frost comes.
items.gloss: A frost on a wet wall will split the brickwork.

body.so_what: Take the second half off each sentence and *had better* still carries the threat. That is what makes it different from *should*.

body.text: General advice, or this time and or else?

body.question: Am I giving general advice, or warning about one specific bad outcome?

options.label: *should*
options.use_it_when: You are recommending something in general, to anybody in that situation. This is the default.
options.example: Councils should publish the consultation figures in full.

options.label: *had better*
options.use_it_when: You are talking about one occasion, and something bad happens if the person ignores you.
options.example: You'd better book the seat now — the coach fills up by Thursday.

a.text: You should back up your files.
a.means: Sensible general advice, for anybody, at any time.

b.text: You'd better back up your files.
b.means: Something is about to go wrong, and you will lose them.

a.text: Students should arrive fifteen minutes early.
a.means: Arriving early is the recommended thing to do.

b.text: Students are supposed to arrive fifteen minutes early.
b.means: That is the arrangement, and it is not always kept.

a.text: The parcel should arrive on Tuesday.
a.means: You expect it on Tuesday. Nobody is being advised of anything.

b.text: The parcel must arrive on Tuesday.
b.means: Tuesday is a requirement. Later than that is a problem.

a.text: You shouldn't cross before the light changes.
a.means: Crossing early is a bad idea.

b.text: You'd better not cross before the light changes.
b.means: Cross early and you will be hit by something.

body.deciding_factor: *Should* is general advice. *Had better* is this time, or else. If you cannot name the bad outcome, use *should*.
body.trap: *Had better* sounds like a softer, more polite *should*, because it is longer and it contains *better*. It is the harder of the two.
body.register_note: *Should* is the workhorse of Task 2 recommendations. *Had better* is spoken and too informal for an essay. *Ought to* fits both and is rare.

body.text: *Should* has a second job, and learners meet it and think it is a mistake. *The results should be out by Friday* gives nobody advice. It says what you expect to happen.
What goes wrong

body.wrong: You had better to check the timetable before you set off.
body.right: You had better check the timetable before you set off.
body.why_it_happens: *Ought to* and *have to* both carry a *to*, and *had better* sits beside them in meaning, so the *to* travels across. *Had better* takes the base form with nothing in front of it.
body.smallest_fix: Delete the *to*: *had better check*.

body.wrong: You hadn't better leave the bikes outside overnight.
body.right: You'd better not leave the bikes outside overnight.
body.why_it_happens: *Had* looks like the helping verb it usually is, so the *not* goes where a *not* normally goes. *Had better* is one fixed piece, and the *not* comes after all of it.
body.smallest_fix: Put *not* after *better*: *had better not*.

body.wrong: People must reduce the number of flights they take each year.
body.right: People should reduce the number of flights they take each year.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is a recommendation, and *must* sounds committed and academic. *Must* states a requirement, so the sentence now claims an authority you do not have and cannot defend.
body.smallest_fix: Recommend with *should* or *need to*, and keep *must* for real requirements.

body.heard: *Had better* is a stronger, more polite way of saying *should*.
also_known_as: *had better* is the polite form of *should*
body.truth: It is not politer. *Had better* carries a warning: do this, or something bad follows. *You'd better speak to your tutor* sounds far more serious than *you should speak to your tutor*, and to some ears it sounds like a threat.
body.what_to_do: Use *should* for advice, including polite advice. Save *had better* for the occasions where you could finish the sentence with *or else*.

body.headline: *Should* for advice. *Had better* only when you can name the consequence.

rows: the results were supposed to arrive

title: Saying what you can do, and what you are allowed to do

article_json.also_called: Ability and permission: *can*, *could*, *be able to*, *may*, *be allowed to*
article_json.one_line: This lets you say what somebody is capable of and what somebody is permitted to do, in any tense you need.
article_json.short_answer: *Can* for now, *could* for general past ability, *was able to* for one past success: *we were able to reach the airport*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When is it *could* and when is it *was able to*?

body.text: Two different things, and English uses one word for both
*She can drive* says she has the skill. *You can park here* says nobody will stop you. English uses *can* for both, and the sentence around it tells you which one is meant.
The hard part is not the present. It is the past, because English splits past ability into two forms and most learners are given only one of them.
How to build it, in every tense

body.caption: *Can* covers now. Everything else is *be able to*.
rows: she was allowed to go in
she was allowed to go in
she will be able to swim
she will be allowed to go in
she has been able to swim
she has been allowed to go in
she might be able to swim
she might be allowed to go in
footnotes: *Can* has no past for one occasion, no future and no form after another modal.
*May* is used for permission in the present, mainly in formal writing and notices.

body.lead_in: The same ability, moved through five different times.

items.text: The clinic can see forty patients a day.
items.gloss: Forty a day is what the clinic manages now.

items.text: The clinic could see forty patients a day before the refit.
items.gloss: Forty a day was normal for it in those years.

items.text: The clinic was able to see everybody on the storm weekend.
items.gloss: That one weekend, everybody got seen.

items.text: The clinic will be able to see sixty a day from June.
items.gloss: From June its capacity rises to sixty.

items.text: The clinic has been able to keep the evening service open.
items.gloss: The evening service is still running, and that took some doing.

body.so_what: *Can* fits only the first sentence. The two-word helper fits all five, which is why it exists.

body.text: Use *could* for a general ability in the past. Use *was able to* or *managed to* for one occasion where somebody actually succeeded.

body.lead_in: Each of these is one occasion, so the general past form will not do.

items.text: Despite the strike, we were able to get everybody to the airport.
items.gloss: The strike was on, and everybody still arrived.

items.text: She managed to reach the site office before it closed.
items.gloss: She got there in time, and it was not easy.

items.text: The team was able to finish the survey in a single afternoon.
items.gloss: One afternoon was enough on that occasion.

items.text: We couldn't get a signal anywhere in the valley.
items.gloss: There was no signal that day, wherever you stood.

body.so_what: The first three succeeded on one occasion, so they take *was able to* or *managed to*. The fourth failed, and a failure keeps *couldn't*.

body.text: Was it a general ability, or did it happen once?

body.question: Am I talking about what somebody could do generally, or about one time they succeeded?

options.label: *could*
options.use_it_when: The ability ran over a stretch of the past: a skill, a capacity, something that was true for years.
options.example: At that age I could read a page of small print without glasses.

options.label: *was able to* / *managed to*
options.use_it_when: One occasion, and the person actually did the thing.
options.example: After two hours of queuing we were able to change the tickets.

a.text: He could persuade the committee.
a.means: He had the knack of persuading them. It says nothing about any particular meeting.

b.text: He was able to persuade the committee.
b.means: At that meeting he did persuade them.

a.text: As a student she could work through the night.
a.means: Working through the night was something she was capable of then.

b.text: The night the pipe burst, she was able to work until it was fixed.
b.means: On that one night she stayed with it until the job was done.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: could work / was able to work

a.text: We couldn't reach the depot before six.
a.means: That day, six o'clock beat you.

b.text: We were able to reach the depot before six.
b.means: That day, you got there in time.

a.text: You can leave your bag at the desk.
a.means: You are allowed to leave it there.

b.text: You could leave your bag at the desk.
b.means: Leaving it there is one thing you might do. It is a suggestion.

body.deciding_factor: General ability takes *could*. One successful occasion takes *was able to* or *managed to*. A failure can keep *couldn't*.
body.trap: *Could* is taught as the past of *can*, so it looks like the past of every *can*. It is the past of the general one only.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. *Managed to* is warmer and more spoken; *was able to* fits an essay or a report.

body.text: Asking whether you are allowed

body.caption: All four ask the same thing. They differ in how formal you sound.
rows: Can I take one of these?
Could I take one of these?
May I take one of these?
plain, and works in any tense
Am I allowed to take one?
footnotes: In notices, permission is usually given with *may* or with *be allowed to*.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The road was flooded, but we could reach the ferry in time.
body.right: The road was flooded, but we were able to reach the ferry in time.
body.why_it_happens: *Could* is presented as the past of *can*, so it gets used for every past ability. Used on one occasion it reads as *we would have been able to*, and the reader cannot tell whether you got there.
body.smallest_fix: For one occasion that worked out, write *were able to* or *managed to*.

body.wrong: After the training, staff will can use the new system.
body.right: After the training, staff will be able to use the new system.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence needs a future ability, and English has no future of *can*. Two modals cannot stand together, so the two-word helper takes over.
body.smallest_fix: Write *will be able to*. The same repair works after *might*, *should* and *must*.

body.wrong: The new pump can able to move twice the volume.
body.right: The new pump can move twice the volume.
body.why_it_happens: *Can* and *be able to* mean the same thing, so both get written into one verb group for safety. Only one of the two is needed, and *can* is the shorter.
body.smallest_fix: Delete one of them. Use *can* on its own for the present.

body.heard: *Can* means only ability. If you are asking permission you have to use *may*.
also_known_as: *Can I go?* is wrong; say *May I go?*
body.truth: *Can I…?* is standard English for asking permission and has been for a very long time. *May* is not more correct — it is more formal, and in speech it can sound stiff. Some readers were taught the older rule and still prefer *may* in writing.
body.what_to_do: Ask with *can* or *could* in speech. Use *may* in a formal letter or a written notice, where the extra distance suits the page.

body.mechanism: Arabic often builds ability with a verb meaning *to be able*, followed by a full clause with its own marking.
body.wrong: She can that she finishes the report today.
body.right: She can finish the report today.
body.fix: After a modal, put the base form straight in. No second clause and no joining word.

body.headline: *Could* for a general past. *Was able to* for one time it worked.

table.caption: One row per situation you are describing.
rows: we were able to reroute the coach
they will be able to reapply

related_articles.reason: *be able to* and *be allowed to* in all their forms
using the same words to ask somebody else to do something
the other job *can*, *could* and *may* do
every modal with its past equivalent in one table

title: Asking somebody to do something

article_json.also_called: Requests, offers and suggestions with modals
article_json.one_line: This lets you ask for something, offer something or suggest something at the level of politeness the situation needs.
article_json.short_answer: Ask with *Could you…?* in most situations. Offer with *Shall I…?* Suggest with *Why don't we…?* or *Shall we…?*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I ask somebody for something without sounding rude?

body.text: Politeness in English is mostly distance

English rarely gets politer by adding polite words. It gets politer by stepping back from the other person. *Send me the file* is direct. *Could you send me the file?* asks whether they are able to, which leaves them room to say no.
That is why the past-looking modals do this work. *Could* and *would* put a small distance between you and the request, and distance is what politeness is made of here.

body.caption: The same request, from the kitchen table to a formal letter.

rungs.text: Can you send me the figures?
Could you send me the figures?
Would you mind sending me the figures?
I would be grateful if you could send me the figures.

body.text: How to build a request, an offer and a suggestion

body.caption: Three jobs, three sets of words. Only one takes an *-ing* form.
rows: Would you mind holding the door?
*I would be grateful if you could…*
I would be grateful if you could confirm the date.
Shall I carry that for you?
Would you like a copy of the map?
How about starting at the north end?
footnotes: *Would you mind* is followed by an *-ing* form, never by *to*.
*Yes* to *Would you mind…?* means the person does object. Most people answer *not at all*.

body.lead_in: One request, climbing from direct to formal. Only the opening words change.

items.text: Can you check the meter reading for me?
items.gloss: You are asking a colleague you know well.

items.text: Could you check the meter reading before you lock up?
items.gloss: The same request, and it works with almost anybody.

items.text: Would you mind checking the meter reading before you lock up?
items.gloss: You are asking a favour, and you know it is one.

items.text: I would be grateful if you could confirm the meter reading in writing.
items.gloss: This is a letter to somebody you have never met.

marks.span: would be grateful if you could

body.so_what: Nothing about the meter changed. What changed is how much room the asker leaves the other person to refuse.

body.text: Ask with *Could you…?* unless you know the person well or you are writing a formal letter. It fits almost every situation in between.

body.lead_in: Three offers and a suggestion, each with the words that job takes.

items.text: Shall I ring the depot and ask about the delivery?
items.gloss: You are offering to make the call yourself.

items.text: Would you like me to send the notes across?
items.gloss: You are offering to do it, and checking they want it.

items.text: Shall we start with the section nobody has read?
items.gloss: You are suggesting something the two of you do together.

items.text: How about moving the whole meeting to the morning?
items.gloss: You are putting an idea on the table for the group.

body.so_what: *Shall* survives mainly in these two places: offering to do something, and suggesting something together.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: Would you mind to send me the timetable?
body.right: Would you mind sending me the timetable?
body.why_it_happens: *Would you like to…* takes *to*, and the two openings look alike. *Mind* is one of the verbs that takes an *-ing* form after it.
body.smallest_fix: After *would you mind*, use the *-ing* form: *sending*, *holding*, *waiting*.

body.wrong: I want you to send me the confirmation by Friday.
body.right: I would be grateful if you could send me the confirmation by Friday.
body.why_it_happens: *I want* is honest and clear, and in many languages the equivalent is ordinary politeness. In English it takes all the distance out of the sentence and reads as an order.
body.smallest_fix: In a formal letter, ask with *I would be grateful if you could* or *Could you please*.

body.wrong: Do you can help me with the second form?
body.right: Can you help me with the second form?
body.why_it_happens: Ordinary verbs need *do* in a question, so *do* goes in for safety. A modal makes its own question by moving to the front, and it never takes *do* as well.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *do* and start with the modal: *Can you…?*, *Could you…?*

body.heard: *Can you…?* is rude. You must say *Could you…?*
also_known_as: *can* is impolite in requests
body.truth: *Can you…?* is ordinary polite English between people who know each other, and it is what most requests in a workplace sound like. *Could you…?* is a little more careful, which is why it is the safer choice with a stranger.
body.what_to_do: Use *Could you…?* when you do not know the person. Use *Can you…?* freely with people you know, and add *please* wherever it fits.

body.mechanism: Hindi carries politeness in the ending of the verb itself, so a direct instruction can already be fully polite.
body.wrong: Please give me the second form.
body.right: Could you give me the second form, please?
body.fix: In English, put the politeness in the question shape as well, not only in *please*.

body.headline: *Could you* to ask, *Shall I* to offer, *Shall we* to suggest.

rows: I would be grateful if you could…
