title: *Will* and *would* for what typically happens

article_json.also_called: *Will* and *would* for characteristic behaviour, and *won't* for refusal
article_json.one_line: This lets you describe what somebody or something typically does, and what it stubbornly refuses to do.
article_json.short_answer: *Will* says what typically happens now. *Would* says what typically happened then. *Won't* and *wouldn't* mean refuses and refused.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Why does *will* turn up in a sentence that is not about the future?

body.text: *Will* is not only about the future
*Our printer will jam if you load more than fifty sheets* is not a prediction about later. It says what the printer does, every time, because that is what it is like.
Move the same sentence back into the past and *will* becomes *would*. Make either of them negative and the meaning changes again: the thing is not failing, it is refusing.
The four jobs in one table

body.caption: Positive means typical. Negative means refuses.
rows: the barrier will stick in wet weather
the barrier would stick in wet weather
the barrier won't lift at all
the barrier wouldn't lift that morning
footnotes: In speech the *will* of typical behaviour is often stressed, which is what makes it sound like a complaint.

body.lead_in: One machine and one habit, moved between now and then, and between working and refusing.
body.dimension: now or then, typical or refusing

items.text: The old scanner will cut out if you leave it on all afternoon.
items.gloss: That is what it does. It has always done it.

items.text: The old scanner would cut out if you left it on all afternoon.
items.gloss: In those days that was what it did.

items.text: The scanner won't read anything smaller than a postcard.
items.gloss: It refuses. Small items simply do not scan.

items.text: The scanner wouldn't read the form, so we typed it in by hand.
items.gloss: On that occasion it refused, and somebody did the work instead.

items.text: My grandmother would repaint the boat every May.
items.gloss: Every May she painted it. That was her year.

body.so_what: The positives describe a pattern. The negatives describe something digging its heels in.

body.text: Use *will* and *would* for repeated actions that are typical of somebody or something. Use *won't* and *wouldn't* for refusal.

body.lead_in: Three refusals, one from a person, one from a machine and one from a door.

items.text: The site manager won't sign anything without the survey.
items.gloss: He refuses, and he has said so.

items.text: The side door wouldn't shut properly all winter.
items.gloss: All winter the door stayed slightly open however hard you pushed.

items.text: The office computer won't accept the new password.
items.gloss: You have typed it correctly and the machine still says no.

body.so_what: None of these is about the future. Each one is about something that will not do what it is asked.

body.text: Was it a state, a repeated action, or one event?

body.question: Was it something that was true, something repeated, or one event?

options.label: *used to*
options.use_it_when: Anything that was true then and is not true now, including states. This is the safe default.
options.example: There used to be a ferry across the estuary.

options.label: *would*
options.use_it_when: A repeated action, once the past setting has already been established, usually in a story or a memory.
options.example: Every August the whole street would repaint their fences.

options.label: past simple
options.use_it_when: One completed event, or a habit where you are not pointing at the contrast with now.
options.example: We lived above the shop for six years.

a.text: I used to have a motorbike.
a.means: You owned one, and you do not now.

b.text: I used to ride to work.
b.means: Riding to work was your routine then, and it is not now.

a.text: She used to be nervous about presentations.
a.means: Nerves were how she was then, and she has got past it.

b.text: She would rehearse every presentation twice.
b.means: Rehearsing twice was what she did each time.

a.text: We used to walk to the market on Saturdays.
a.means: That was the Saturday routine, and it stopped.

b.text: We walked to the market on Saturday.
b.means: On that one Saturday, you walked.

a.text: The mill would flood twice a winter.
a.means: Two floods a winter was the pattern.

b.text: The mill flooded twice that winter.
b.means: That particular winter there were two floods.

body.deciding_factor: *Used to* works for everything that has stopped. *Would* works only for repeated actions, never for states.
body.trap: *Would* looks like the more advanced word, so it gets used everywhere. Put it on a state and the sentence stops meaning the past at all.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere, and this is a strong Speaking Part 1 and Part 3 move for saying how things have changed.

body.text: *Would* also needs the past already set up around it. Open a story with it and the reader hears a different sentence, because *would* on its own points at something imaginary.
What goes wrong

body.wrong: Before the bypass opened, there would be a level crossing here.
body.right: Before the bypass opened, there used to be a level crossing here.
body.why_it_happens: *Would* and *used to* are taught as two ways of saying the same thing, so one gets swapped for the other. *Would* cannot describe a state, and the sentence turns into a guess about something imaginary.
body.smallest_fix: If the verb describes how things were rather than what somebody did, use *used to*.

body.wrong: Would my father drive us to the coast every August.
body.right: Every August my father would drive us to the coast.
body.why_it_happens: *Would* for a past habit needs the past set up first, either by an earlier sentence or by a time expression in this one. Without it, the reader reads *would* as something unreal.
body.smallest_fix: Put the past time expression in front: *every August*, *in those years*, *when we were small*.

body.wrong: In my country, people will usually eat late in the evening.
body.right: In my country, people usually eat late in the evening.
body.why_it_happens: *Will* for typical behaviour is real English, but it carries a note of complaint or resignation. Used for a plain cultural fact it sounds as though you disapprove of it.
body.smallest_fix: For a neutral general fact, use the present simple. Keep *will* for things that annoy you or surprise you.

body.heard: *Would* and *used to* are interchangeable for past habits.
also_known_as: you can always replace *used to* with *would*
body.truth: They swap freely for repeated actions. They do not swap for states. *There used to be a bus stop outside* cannot become *there would be a bus stop outside*, which means something else entirely.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the verb is something somebody did, or something that simply was. If it simply was, use *used to*.

body.headline: Positive means typical. Negative means refuses. States take *used to*.

rows: a past state that has ended

title: Putting a modal in front of a longer verb group

article_json.also_called: Modals with the continuous, the perfect, *be* + third form, and in *if*-sentences
article_json.one_line: This lets you be unsure about something that is in progress, already finished, or done to something else.
article_json.short_answer: Keep the base form after the modal, then build normally: *must be working*, *may have finished*, *can be checked*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I put *must* or *might* in front of a longer verb group?

body.text: A modal can sit in front of any verb group, not only a short one
*The pump is running* becomes *the pump must be running* when you cannot see it and you are working it out from the noise. Nothing about the verb group changed except the word in front of it.
That is the whole article. Build the verb group you would have used, then push it one step to the right and put the modal in the space.
How to build each combination

body.caption: The word straight after the modal is always the base form: *be* or *have*.
rows: she might have been waiting an hour
done to it, now or later
the figures must have been checked
footnotes: There is never a *to* anywhere in these patterns.
The last two put the thing that was done to at the front of the sentence.

body.lead_in: One modal, five verb groups. Watch the word straight after *must*.
body.dimension: the verb group behind the modal

items.text: The heating must run on a timer.
items.gloss: You are confident a timer controls it.

items.text: The heating must be running, because the radiators are warm.
items.gloss: You are confident it is on at this moment.

items.text: The heating must have run all night.
items.gloss: You are confident it stayed on while everybody was asleep.

items.text: The system must be serviced once a year.
items.gloss: A yearly service is a requirement. The rule does not say who does it.

items.text: The system must have been serviced in the spring.
items.gloss: You are confident somebody serviced it in the spring.

body.so_what: *Must* never moved and never changed. Everything that changed happened behind it.

body.text: Put the base form straight after the modal, then build the rest of the verb group as you normally would.

body.lead_in: Four different modals, each in front of a longer verb group.

items.text: The results can be downloaded from the portal after Friday.
items.gloss: From Friday, anybody with the link can get them.

items.text: Two of the readings might have been recorded twice.
items.gloss: Possibly the same reading went in the list twice.

items.text: They could be waiting at the wrong entrance.
items.gloss: The wrong entrance would explain why nobody has appeared.

items.text: The old bridge should have been replaced years ago.
items.gloss: Nobody replaced it, and that was a mistake.

body.so_what: The word straight after each modal is *be* or *have*, in the plain base form, every single time.

body.text: Where the modal goes in an *if*-sentence

body.caption: The result half takes the modal. The *if* half almost never does.
rows: the path would flood every winter
if the drain should block again
footnotes: *If the drain should block* means the same as *if the drain blocks*, with a small note of unlikeliness.

body.lead_in: The same situation, with the modal moving between the two halves.
body.dimension: which half the modal is in

items.text: If the survey is delayed, the work will start in April instead.
items.gloss: A delay pushes the start to April.

items.text: If the survey were delayed, the work might not start until June.
items.gloss: A delay is not expected, and June is what it would cost.

items.text: If the survey should be delayed, please tell the contractors at once.
items.gloss: A delay is unlikely, and here is what to do if it happens.

body.so_what: In all three, the *if* half stays plain or takes *should*. The modal that carries the meaning sits in the other half.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The samples must been collected before the frost.
body.right: The samples must have been collected before the frost.
body.why_it_happens: *Been* already sounds like the past, so it feels like enough on its own. It cannot start a verb group. *Have* is the part that moves the whole thing into the past.
body.smallest_fix: Put *have* straight after the modal, and leave *been* where it is.

body.wrong: The figures can checked against last year's return.
body.right: The figures can be checked against last year's return.
body.why_it_happens: The third form on its own looks finished, and in a short sentence it seems to say enough. Without *be*, the verb group has nothing holding it together.
body.smallest_fix: Put *be* between the modal and the third form: *can be checked*.

body.wrong: If the council would publish the figures, the debate would be shorter.
body.right: If the council published the figures, the debate would be shorter.
body.why_it_happens: Both halves are about something imaginary, so *would* looks as though it belongs in both. English marks the *if* half with the verb form alone and keeps *would* for the result.
body.smallest_fix: Take *would* out of the *if* half. One *would* per sentence, in the result.

body.heard: A modal can only be followed by one verb.
also_known_as: after a modal you use the plain verb and nothing else
body.truth: The rule is about the shape, not the length. The word straight after the modal must be a base form, and *be* and *have* are base forms. Once they are in place they carry as much as any other verb group carries.
body.what_to_do: Check only the first word after the modal. If it is a base form, the group is legal however long it gets.

body.headline: Base form first, then build the verb group as usual.

table.caption: One row per combination you are likely to need.

title: Nine modals, four columns

article_json.also_called: The modal summary table, with past forms and past equivalents
article_json.one_line: This is the page to come back to: every modal, both of its jobs, its past form, and what its negative means.
article_json.short_answer: Most modals do two jobs, one about how sure you are and one about rules. The past is *had to*, *could*, *was allowed to*, *would*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: What does each modal mean, and how do I say it in the past?

body.text: Every modal does two jobs, and the sentence decides which
*You must be tired* and *you must sign here* use one word for two unrelated things. The first says how sure the speaker is. The second states a rule. Almost every modal works this way.
The table below puts both jobs side by side, with the past form in the fourth column, because that is the column learners come looking for.

body.caption: Read across one row: how sure, what rule, how to say it in the past.
body.form_line: a modal + the base form of the verb, with no *to*

cells: *may not* — possibly not, or not permitted

rows.note: *Might* has no job in the rules column.

cells: you expect it; what typically happens

rows.note: Outside offers and legal writing, *shall* is rare today.

cells: you are confident it is true
rows.note: The two past forms mean completely different things.

sub_tables.caption: The past of a modal is usually a two-word helper, not another modal.
Weakest to strongest, for the four things modals are used for.
Where each one belongs, so speech and writing do not swap.

gaps.note: *Might I…?* for permission exists, and it is formal and rare enough to leave out of the working table.
*Shall* makes no guesses. In legal writing it states requirements, which is a separate use.

examples.text: The archive can be searched by name or by year.
examples.gloss: Both searches are possible on the site.

examples.text: Applicants may attach a second reference if they wish.
examples.gloss: A second reference is allowed and not required.

examples.text: The coach should reach Marlow by half past four.
examples.gloss: That is when you expect it, from the timetable.

examples.text: Shall I hold the lift for you?
examples.gloss: You are offering to keep the doors open.

examples.text: We had to reroute the whole service for a fortnight.
examples.gloss: For two weeks there was no other option.

examples.text: The lock won't turn once the frame swells.
examples.gloss: A swollen frame stops the lock working, every time.

notes: *Must* has two past forms and they are unrelated: *had to* for a rule, *must have* for a guess.
*Can't* is the confident negative guess. *Mustn't* forbids and never guesses.
Each modal keeps one shape. The two-word helpers supply everything else.

body.headline: Two jobs per modal, and the past is usually a two-word helper.

table.caption: The five past forms worth memorising.
rows: we had to close the path
she could read music at six
we were able to reroute it

title: Not claiming more than you can defend

article_json.also_called: Softening a claim: modality in academic and cautious writing
article_json.one_line: This lets you make a claim you can stand behind, instead of a big claim the next paragraph has to rescue.
article_json.short_answer: Match the word to your evidence. *Must* claims certainty, *should* claims a position, *may* and *tend to* claim less.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I give an opinion without claiming more than I can prove?

body.text: A big claim is easy to write and hard to defend

*Online study is better for everybody* takes one sentence to write and a whole paragraph to defend, because a single unhappy student proves it wrong. *Online study suits some learners better* costs one word more and is defensible.
The modal is where that work happens. It is the difference between saying a thing is so and saying how sure you are that it is so.
The words that carry the strength of a claim

body.caption: Strongest at the top. Each row commits you to something different.
rows: an absolute claim you now defend
a clear position, and the usual choice
a general pattern with room for exceptions
footnotes: *Appear to* and *seem to* work like *tend to* and sit at the careful level.

body.lead_in: One claim about the same policy, at four strengths. Only the modal changes.

items.text: Congestion charges must be introduced in every large city.
items.gloss: You are saying there is no acceptable alternative anywhere.

items.text: Congestion charges should be introduced in the largest cities.
items.gloss: You are taking a clear position and leaving smaller cities out of it.

items.text: Congestion charges could be trialled in two boroughs first.
items.gloss: You are putting one workable idea on the table.

items.text: Charges of this kind tend to fall hardest on low earners.
items.gloss: That is the usual pattern, and you are not claiming it always happens.

body.so_what: All four are defensible. The first one is only defensible if you can really show that no city can manage without a charge.

body.text: Pick the weakest word that still says what you mean. A claim you can defend is worth more than a claim that sounds strong.

body.lead_in: Each of these takes a claim about everybody and narrows it to something provable.

items.text: Remote work may reduce the number of short car journeys.
items.gloss: A fall in short journeys is one possible effect.

items.text: Younger workers tend to change employer more often.
items.gloss: That is the general pattern, and there are plenty of exceptions.

items.text: The rise appears to have started before the new fares.
items.gloss: From the figures, the rise looks older than the fare change.

items.text: In most cases the cost falls on the tenant rather than the owner.
items.gloss: Usually the tenant pays, and sometimes the owner does.

body.so_what: Each sentence still says something. None of them can be knocked over by a single counter-example.

body.text: How strong should this sentence be?

body.question: Could one counter-example prove this sentence wrong?

options.label: *must*, *will*
options.use_it_when: You can defend it against any counter-example, or you are stating a real requirement.
options.example: Any charge of this kind must be set out in law before it is collected.

options.label: *should*, *need to*
options.use_it_when: You are taking a clear position and you know somebody could reasonably disagree.
options.example: Councils should publish the consultation responses in full.

options.label: *may*, *tend to*, *is likely to*
options.use_it_when: You are describing a pattern or a possible effect, and exceptions exist.
options.example: Higher fares tend to push short journeys back into cars.

a.text: Working from home reduces stress.
a.means: You are claiming it reduces stress for everybody who does it.

b.text: Working from home may reduce stress.
b.means: Less stress is one possible result, and you are not promising it.

a.text: Students must attend every lecture.
a.means: Attendance is a requirement, and missing one breaks a rule.

b.text: Students should attend every lecture.
b.means: Attending is strongly recommended, and nobody is breaking a rule.

a.text: Older drivers cause more accidents at junctions.
a.means: You are stating it as a fact about older drivers as a group.

b.text: Older drivers tend to have more accidents at junctions.
b.means: That is the pattern in the figures, with many exceptions.

a.text: The new timetable will cut waiting times by half.
a.means: You are promising the cut. If it does not happen, you were wrong.

b.text: The new timetable is likely to cut waiting times.
b.means: A cut is what you expect, and you are not guaranteeing the size of it.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: will cut / is likely to cut

body.deciding_factor: Ask whether one counter-example would sink the sentence. If it would, step down one row in the table.
body.trap: A strong word feels like a strong argument, so the biggest claim goes in first. A claim that is too big is the easiest thing in an essay to argue against.
body.register_note: This belongs in writing above all. In Speaking Part 3 the same words work, and *might* and *could* sound more natural there than *may*.

body.text: Vary the strength across a piece of writing. *Should* in every sentence is not a position but a habit, and *must* in every sentence claims an authority no essay has.
What goes wrong

body.wrong: Social media destroys the concentration of every young person.
body.right: Heavy social media use may weaken concentration in some young people.
body.why_it_happens: A flat statement sounds confident, and confidence sounds like a strong argument. It also means one careful reader with one counter-example has finished your paragraph for you.
body.smallest_fix: Add a modal and narrow the group: *may*, *tend to*, *some*, *in most cases*.

body.wrong: It may possibly be the case that fares could perhaps have some effect.
body.right: Fares may have some effect on how often people travel.
body.why_it_happens: One careful word is good, so four look better. Stacked up, they cancel each other out and the sentence stops claiming anything at all.
body.smallest_fix: Keep one softening word per claim. Delete the rest.

body.wrong: Governments must ban private cars from all city centres.
body.right: Governments should restrict private cars in the busiest city centres.
body.why_it_happens: The task asks for a recommendation, and *must* sounds like the most committed way to give one. It states a requirement, so the rest of the essay has to prove that no other policy could work.
body.smallest_fix: Recommend with *should* or *need to*, and narrow the claim while you are there.

body.heard: Words like *may* and *might* make your writing sound unsure, so leave them out and write with confidence.
also_known_as: academic writing should sound certain
never say *maybe* in an essay
body.truth: Careful writing is not unsure writing. *May* and *tend to* show that you know how far your evidence goes, which is a mark of control. What does read as weak is stacking three of them into one sentence.
body.what_to_do: Keep the careful words, one per claim. Be strong about the position you are taking and careful about how far you claim it reaches.

title: Putting the thing done to first

article_json.also_called: Voice: the active and the passive
article_json.one_line: This lets you build a sentence around the thing something was done to, instead of around the person who did it.
article_json.short_answer: Put the thing done to first, then a form of *be*, then the third form: *the road was widened*.

body.text: Two ways to say the same event
One event, two sentences. *The council widened the road.* *The road was widened.* Both are true and both are correct English. What differs is what the sentence is about.
English puts the thing a sentence is about in front of the verb. So this is not a choice about sounding formal. You pick the shape that starts with what you are talking about.

body.gloss: which one the sentence puts first: the doer, or the thing done to

show_first.text: The inspectors closed the pool.
The pool was closed.
Storm damage closed the pool.

body.name_line: The choice between those two shapes is called **voice**.
body.anchor_line: Look at what stands in front of each verb. Two of them start with a doer, and one starts with the thing it happened to.

body.text: How to turn a doer-first sentence around

body.caption: Move the object to the front, add *be*, use the third form.
rows: Take a sentence with an object
Put the object at the front
Add *be* in the same time as before
Put the main verb in its third form
Add *by* and the doer, if it is news
The footpath was resurfaced by volunteers.
footnotes: Step 1 needs an object, so only a verb that takes one can be turned round this way.

body.text: After step 3 the main verb never moves again. Only *be* changes, because *be* is carrying the time: *is resurfaced*, *was resurfaced*, *has been resurfaced*.

body.lead_in: Three events, each written twice. Only the order of the parts changes.

body.text: Every passive has two parts, and the second never changes
Build a passive with a form of *be* and the third form of the main verb. Only *be* changes.

body.lead_in: Four different times, and only the *be* part moves.

items.gloss: Somebody cleans them every morning and every evening.

items.gloss: They were clean by the time the match started.

items.gloss: They are clean now, so nobody needs to do it.

body.text: Which shape does this sentence need?
Ask what the sentence is about. If it is about the person or group who acted, start there. If it is about the thing that was acted on, start there instead.

body.question: Is this sentence about the doer, or about the thing it happened to?

options.label: doer first
options.use_it_when: The doer is the point, or you are telling somebody what a person or a group did.
options.example: Two engineers checked every bolt on the walkway.

options.label: thing first, with *be* and the third form
options.use_it_when: The thing it happened to is the point, or the doer is unknown, obvious or beside the point.
options.example: Every bolt on the walkway was checked.

a.means: You are telling the reader about the sensor and what it did.

b.text: The production line was stopped by a faulty sensor.
b.means: You are telling the reader about the line and what happened to it.

a.text: The committee rejected the funding bid.
a.means: You are saying what the committee did, and it sounds like their decision.

b.text: The funding bid was rejected.
b.means: You are saying what happened to the bid, and nobody is blamed.

a.text: Somebody has moved the recycling bins again.
a.means: You do not know who moved them, so you fill the gap with *somebody*.

b.text: The recycling bins have been moved again.
b.means: The same fact, with no empty word standing in for a doer.

body.deciding_factor: Whatever the sentence is about belongs in front of the verb. Choose the shape that puts it there.
body.trap: You were told that the passive sounds academic, so you use it to lift the level of an essay instead of to decide what each sentence is about.
body.register_note: Both belong in speech and in writing. The passive earns most in Task 1 process descriptions and in Task 2 background sentences.

body.text: A passive is not a higher-level sentence than a doer-first one. Reach for it because the thing done to is what you are talking about, and for no other reason.
What goes wrong

body.wrong: The forms checked by two members of staff.
body.right: The forms were checked by two members of staff.
body.why_it_happens: The third form already looks like a past verb, so the group of words feels finished. Nothing in it says when the checking happened, because the word that carries the time is missing.
body.smallest_fix: Put *was* or *were* in front of the third form.

body.wrong: The report was wrote by a panel of three.
body.right: The report was written by a panel of three.
body.why_it_happens: *Wrote* is the form you meet first and use most, so it comes out under pressure. After *be*, English wants the third form, and for *write* that is a different word.
body.smallest_fix: After *be*, use the third form: *written*, *taken*, *chosen*.

body.label: Two cases where *be* plus a third form is not a passive at all

items.text: *Be* plus a third form can describe how something is, rather than what happened to it.
items.example: The side gate was locked all weekend.

items.text: Add *being* and only the event reading is left.
items.example: The side gate was being locked when I arrived.

body.heard: The passive is one of the English tenses, so you learn it after the twelve tenses.
also_known_as: the passive tense
body.truth: The passive is not a tense. It is a choice about which part of the event goes first. The tense is still carried by *be*, which is why there is a passive for each one: *is checked*, *was checked*, *has been checked*.
body.what_to_do: Settle the time first, the way you always do. Then settle which part of the event you want in front. Those are two separate decisions.

body.mechanism: Mandarin puts the topic first, and the topic does not have to be the subject.
body.wrong: The old library, they demolished it last year.
body.right: The old library was demolished last year.
body.fix: Make the topic the subject. A passive is what lets you do that.

body.text: One word carries the time, and it is always *be*
A passive is two words or more, and the last one never changes. The main verb sits in its third form and stays there. Every piece of time information is carried by *be*.
So there is only ever one thing to choose. The table below holds all of it, and you can come back to it.

*It's been painted* is *it has been painted*. The word *been* tells you which one you heard.

body.anchor_line: Each sentence starts with the thing, and *by* adds the doer at the end. Most passive sentences stop before they get there.

body.text: Keep the agent only when the doer is news. If your reader would not care who did it, the sentence is already finished without it.

body.text: Both shapes are correct, so something else has to decide
Nothing about a passive is more academic than a doer-first sentence. The choice between them is a choice about what the sentence is about, and a reader feels it straight away.
The strongest reason for using one is also the one least often taught. A passive lets the next sentence begin where the last one ended.
What should this sentence start with?

body.question: Is the doer the point of this sentence?

options.label: the ordinary doer-first sentence
options.use_it_when: The doer is the point, or you are telling somebody what a person or a group actually did.
options.example: The planning team rejected all four designs.

options.label: the passive
options.use_it_when: The doer is unknown, obvious or beside the point, or the thing done to is what the paragraph is about.
options.example: All four designs were rejected.

body.trap: You were taught that the passive is the formal one, so you use it to lift the level of an essay instead of to control what each sentence is about.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The passive earns most in Task 1 and in Task 2 background sentences; the doer-first shape earns most in Speaking.

body.text: Five situations call for the passive. Four of them are about the doer. The fifth is about the sentence before it, and it is the one that changes how a paragraph reads.

body.lead_in: Choose the passive in five situations:
items: nobody knows who did it
the doer is obvious from the situation
the doer makes no difference to your point

body.text: The strongest reason: keeping the same topic at the front
Read the two versions below. The facts are identical and no word in the second one is harder. One version is easier to follow, and the passive is the reason.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: In my opinion, it is believed that traffic charges should be introduced.
body.right: In my opinion, traffic charges should be introduced.
body.why_it_happens: You were taught that impersonal openings sound academic, so one gets attached even to a sentence stating your own view. *It is believed* hands that view to somebody else.
body.smallest_fix: When the view is yours, say so and drop the impersonal opening.

body.wrong: The scheme was criticised, and later the funding was withdrawn.
body.right: Two councils criticised the scheme, and the government later withdrew the funding.
body.why_it_happens: Leaving the doer out is comfortable, so it becomes a habit. Once several sentences in a row name nobody, the reader cannot tell who is doing anything.
body.smallest_fix: Where the doer is new information, name it: with *by*, or by going back to the doer-first shape.

body.wrong: My holiday was spent in Sandmouth with my cousins.
body.right: I spent my holiday in Sandmouth with my cousins.
body.why_it_happens: You are trying to sound careful, and the passive feels careful. In a personal story you are the doer, and taking yourself out of it makes the answer sound evasive.
body.smallest_fix: In Speaking, stay in the sentence: *I spent*, *we went*, *I chose*.

body.heard: Never use the passive. Good writing is always in the active voice.
also_known_as: the passive is weak writing
always write in the active
body.truth: The passive is the ordinary choice whenever the doer is unknown, obvious or beside the point, and that covers most of a process description. It decides what a sentence is about; it is not a weakness.
body.what_to_do: Use it on purpose. The advice was aimed at one real habit: a whole paragraph in which nobody does anything. Watch for that habit instead of avoiding the shape.

body.heard: Academic writing should be in the passive, so use it as often as you can.
also_known_as: passive equals formal
the more passives, the higher the band
body.truth: Academic English uses both and chooses one per sentence. A page of passives hides every actor and reads as heavier, not better. The question of who did it decides, not the register.
body.what_to_do: Decide sentence by sentence. Ask who did it and whether the reader needs to know. Keep the passive for process descriptions and for sentences whose topic is the thing done to.

body.text: Saying that you arranged it, not that you did it
*We repaired the roof* says you were up the ladder. Most of the time that is not what happened, and English has a separate shape for the other case.
That shape keeps *have* or *get* at the front and drops the thing into the middle. Nobody has to say who came out to do the work.
It matters most in Speaking. Almost everything that happens to a house, a car or a document is arranged rather than done.

options.example: We had the back room painted over the weekend.

a.text: They cut down the tree on Saturday.
a.means: They did the cutting themselves, with their own saw.

b.text: They had the tree cut down on Saturday.
b.means: They arranged it and somebody came out to do it.

a.text: She checked her application twice.
a.means: She read it through herself, on two occasions.

b.text: She had her application checked twice.
b.means: Two other people read it through for her.

a.text: He lost his passport in Marlow.
a.means: He mislaid it himself and could not find it.

b.text: He had his passport stolen in Marlow.
b.means: Somebody took it from him.

body.deciding_factor: Ask whether you did the job. If you only arranged it, or it happened to you, put the thing in the middle.
body.trap: The shape looks like a past perfect, so *we had the roof repaired* gets read as *we had repaired the roof*, and the meaning flips straight back.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. *Have* is safe in writing and *get* leans spoken. Speaking Part 1 and Part 2 use this shape constantly.

body.text: Both sentences in each pair describe the same finished job. What changes is who was holding the brush, and a listener hears it at once.
Making somebody do something

body.caption: Four ways to say you got a person to act, and four different verb shapes.
rows: We had the surveyor look again.
We got the surveyor to look again.
The rules make every driver stop here.
The school lets pupils leave at three.
footnotes: Only *get* takes *to*. The other three take the base form on its own.

body.text: *Make* and *let* are about pressure and permission, so they never take *to*. *Get* is the only one of the four that does, because it means you had to persuade somebody.

body.lead_in: The same request, with four different amounts of pressure behind it.
body.dimension: how much choice the other person had

items.text: The manager had the team redo the safety checks.
items.gloss: The team was told to do them again.

items.text: We got the landlord to fix the heating.
items.gloss: It took some persuading, and then he fixed it.

items.text: The new rule makes every visitor sign in.
items.gloss: Nobody can get past the door without signing.

items.text: The library lets students borrow twelve books.
items.gloss: Twelve is the limit for a student card.

body.so_what: Same event, four different relationships between the two people involved.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: We had repaired the roof by a local builder.
body.right: We had the roof repaired by a local builder.
body.why_it_happens: *Had repaired* is a shape you know well, so your hand writes it first. The thing has to sit between *had* and the third form, or the sentence says you did the work yourself.
body.smallest_fix: Move the thing in front of the third form: *had the roof repaired*.

body.wrong: She had her laptop steal at the station.
body.right: She had her laptop stolen at the station.
body.why_it_happens: The middle word is a thing, so the verb behind it feels like a plain verb starting a new action. It is the third form here, for the same reason it is in a passive.
body.smallest_fix: Use the third form after the thing: *stolen*, *taken*, *cut*.

body.wrong: My application got rejected, and my second one got turned down too.
body.right: My application was rejected, and my second one was turned down too.
body.why_it_happens: *Got* is what you say, so it is what comes out under time pressure. It is correct English and it reads as speech, which costs you in a formal essay.
body.smallest_fix: In Task 1 and Task 2, use *was* or *were* in place of *got*.

body.what_varies: Whether the passive is built on *be* or on *get*.

option_a.label: *be* + third form
option_a.example: The bid was turned down in June.

option_b.label: *get* + third form
option_b.example: The bid got turned down in June.

body.why_this_default: *Be* is right in speech and in writing, so it never costs anything. That is a house choice for our examples, not a rule of English.
body.costs_marks: yes in Task 1 and Task 2 — it reads as speech

body.label: Two things that look like this shape and are not

items.text: *Get married*, *get dressed*, *get lost*, *get started* and *get involved* are fixed phrases with no spoken flavour.
items.example: Two hundred residents got involved in the consultation.

items.text: *Get* plus a person plus *to* is a different pattern, and it is not a passive at all.
items.example: We got the council to publish the figures.

body.heard: *Got* is bad English. Never write *get* in a passive sentence.
also_known_as: *get* is lazy English
body.truth: *Get* plus a third form is correct English and completely normal in speech. What is true is that it reads as speech, so it is the wrong choice in a formal essay, where *be* does the same job.
body.what_to_do: Say it freely. Write *was* or *were* instead in Task 1 and Task 2. Keep the fixed phrases such as *get involved*, which are neutral anywhere.

items.answer: In the first you did it. In the second somebody came out and did it for you.
items.why: The thing sits between *had* and the third form, and that is what says you arranged it.

items.prompt: Why is *He got his phone steal* wrong?
items.answer: The verb after the thing has to be the third form: *He got his phone stolen.*
items.why: The middle word is the thing it happened to, so the verb behind it behaves as it does in a passive.

title: The passives that behave differently

article_json.also_called: Verbs with no passive, double objects, prepositional passives, reporting passives and non-finite passives
article_json.one_line: This covers the passives that do not follow the plain pattern, and the verbs that have no passive at all.
article_json.short_answer: Ask *…something?* after the verb. If you cannot, there is no passive: *the fault occurred*, never *was occurred*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Which verbs have no passive, and what are the odd passive shapes?
article_json.risk_note: Two of these are recognition-first. Use *it is believed that* in writing, and leave *having been checked* until the rest of the passive is automatic.

body.text: Where the plain pattern does not hold
Everything so far has been one pattern: a form of *be* and the third form. Six situations behave differently, and each one has a common error attached to it.
Start with the largest. Some verbs have no passive at all, and the sentences learners build from them are among the most frequent errors in Task 1.
If you cannot ask *…something?*, there is no passive
Only a verb that takes an object has a passive. If you cannot say *paint something*, there is nothing to move to the front.

body.lead_in: Four verbs that take no object, in the shape they actually need.

items.text: The fault occurred during the night shift.
items.gloss: Something went wrong overnight.

items.text: Rents rose by nine per cent last year.
items.gloss: People paid nine per cent more than the year before.

items.text: Two of the panels disappeared before the audit.
items.gloss: Nobody could find them when the audit began.

items.text: The scaffolding stayed up all winter.
items.gloss: It was still standing there in March.

body.so_what: None of these verbs takes an object, so none of them has anything to build a passive out of.

body.caption: These verbs have no passive. The right-hand column is what to write.
rows: The land belongs to the trust.
The plan resembles the old one.
The works cost forty thousand pounds.
footnotes: *She is suited to the role* is a different structure, and it is correct.
Only a transitive verb has a passive, and none of these twelve is one in the sense the passive needs.

body.text: Two groups sit in that table. The first takes no object at all. The second is made of state verbs, which describe how something is rather than something being done to it.
Two objects, and a small word that stays put
*Give*, *send*, *offer*, *show*, *tell*, *teach*, *lend*, *pay* and *award* can be followed by a person and a thing. Either one can move to the front, so these verbs give you two passives.

body.caption: English puts the person in front far more often than the thing.
rows: The trust gave the school a grant.
The school was given a grant.
A grant was given to the school.
The contract was offered to Verdon.
The tutor sent every student a link.
Every student was sent a link.
A link was sent to every student.
footnotes: The thing-in-front version needs *to* in front of the person.

body.text: Other verbs reach their object through a preposition: *look into*, *deal with*, *account for*, *pay for*. In the passive the preposition stays directly behind the verb, with nothing after it.

body.caption: The small word does not move and it is never dropped.
rows: A panel looked into the complaint.
Staff deal with refunds on Fridays.
Refunds are dealt with on Fridays.
Nobody accounted for the missing hours.
The missing hours were not accounted for.
Two councils paid for the survey.
The survey was paid for by two councils.
footnotes: *Look* and *look into* are two different verbs with two different meanings.

body.lead_in: Three sentences where the person went to the front.

items.text: Applicants are told the outcome within two weeks.
items.gloss: Everybody hears back inside a fortnight.

items.text: We were shown the drawings before the meeting.
items.gloss: The drawings came out beforehand.

items.text: Staff were offered a place on the training.
items.gloss: The training was open to them if they wanted it.

body.so_what: In each one the person is what the sentence is about, and that is the usual choice.

body.text: Reporting what people think, without naming them
Academic writing often has to state a widely held view before arguing with it. Two shapes do that, and both of them are passives.

body.caption: Two ways to report a view that belongs to nobody in particular.
rows: It is widely believed that costs will fall.
Costs are believed to be falling.
Emissions are estimated to have fallen.
footnotes: Both shapes come from the same doer-first sentence: *people believe that costs will fall*.

body.lead_in: These verbs fit both shapes:
items: *say*, *think* and *believe*
*know*, *report* and *claim*
*expect*, *consider* and *assume*
*estimate*, *understand* and *find*

body.lead_in: One view, reported three ways.

items.text: It is often said that rail fares deter younger travellers.
items.gloss: Many people hold that view about fares.

items.text: Rail fares are said to deter younger travellers.
items.gloss: The same view, in fewer words.

items.text: Fares are thought to have risen faster than wages.
items.gloss: People believe that fares went up faster than pay did.

body.so_what: Nobody is named in any of them, and that is exactly what the shape is for.

body.text: Passive shapes with no time on them
A non-finite verb has a passive too. You need these to fit a second event into a sentence without starting a new clause with its own subject.

body.caption: Three shapes, and the position each one takes.
rows: The wiring needs to be checked.
after a verb or a preposition
Having been repaired, the lift reopened.
at the front of a sentence
footnotes: The third shape is worth recognising long before it is worth producing.

body.lead_in: The same three shapes in ordinary sentences.
body.dimension: the shape with no time on it

items.text: The roof still has to be inspected before winter.
items.gloss: The inspection has not happened yet.

items.text: Nobody enjoys being told what to do.
items.gloss: People dislike taking orders.

items.text: Having been closed for two years, the pool reopened in May.
items.gloss: It was shut for two years and then it opened again.

body.so_what: Each one packs a second event into a sentence without a second full stop.

body.text: When the thing seems to do it itself
*Sales rose.* *The door opened.* Nobody is named, and there is no passive either. A group of English verbs describe a change as though the thing brought it about on its own.

body.question: Is somebody making it change, or is it just changing?

options.label: the plain verb: *rose*, *fell*, *opened*
options.use_it_when: You are describing what a figure or a thing did, and no doer is in the picture at all.
options.example: Attendance fell steadily after 2018.

options.label: the passive: *was raised*, *was reduced*
options.use_it_when: Somebody made the change happen, and you want the sentence to be about the thing rather than about them.
options.example: The entry fee was reduced twice.

a.text: Rents rose by twelve per cent.
a.means: Rents went up. Nothing is said about anyone pushing them up.

b.text: Rents were raised by twelve per cent.
b.means: Somebody put them up on purpose.

a.text: The waiting list shortened over the winter.
a.means: It got shorter. Why, the sentence does not say.

b.text: The waiting list was shortened over the winter.
b.means: Somebody took names off it deliberately.

a.text: The main gate opened at six.
a.means: The gate came open at that time.

b.text: The main gate was opened at six.
b.means: Somebody unlocked it and pushed it open.

body.deciding_factor: In Task 1 the figures rise and fall by themselves. Use the plain verb for the numbers and the passive for the process.
body.trap: You were told that Task 1 is formal writing and the passive is the formal shape, so the figures end up in a passive that English does not allow.
body.register_note: Both are written and spoken English. The distinction earns most in Task 1, where most sentences are about a figure going up or down.

body.text: Why a process description is almost all passive
In a process the same people carry out every stage, so naming them in each sentence tells the reader nothing new. Each stage starts with the material instead.

body.lead_in: Four stages of one process, each starting with the material.

items.text: The waste is sorted by hand on a moving belt.
items.gloss: Workers pick out whatever does not belong.

items.text: It is then washed and cut into flakes.
items.gloss: The clean material comes out in small pieces.

items.text: The flakes are dried in a heated drum.
items.gloss: The water is taken out of them.

items.text: They're finally melted down and pressed into pellets.
items.gloss: The material leaves as small hard pellets.

body.so_what: Every sentence starts where the last one ended, and the doer never has to be named at all.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The population was risen sharply between 2005 and 2015.
body.right: The population rose sharply between 2005 and 2015.
body.why_it_happens: Task 1 feels formal, and the passive is what you were told formal writing uses. *Rise* takes no object, so there is nothing to move to the front and no passive to build.
body.smallest_fix: Ask *rise something?* You cannot, so write *rose*.

body.wrong: The complaint was looked by a panel of three.
body.right: The complaint was looked into by a panel of three.
body.why_it_happens: The preposition ends up a long way from its object in a passive, so it is easy to lose. Without it the verb means something else entirely.
body.smallest_fix: Keep the small word directly behind the verb: *dealt with*, *looked into*, *paid for*.

body.wrong: It believed that fees will rise again next year.
body.right: It is believed that fees will rise again next year.
body.why_it_happens: The shape gets memorised as one phrase, and the small word in the middle carries no meaning you can hear. Without *is* the sentence has no verb holding it together.
body.smallest_fix: Put *is* or *was* between *it* and the third form.

body.label: Two places where a passive looks impossible and is not

items.text: *Be suited to* and *be lacking* look like passives. They describe how something is.
items.example: The site is not suited to heavy vehicles.

items.text: A verb with no object of its own can borrow one through a preposition, and then it does have a passive.
items.example: The proposal has been objected to twice.

body.heard: Task 1 is formal writing, so describe the changes in the passive.
also_known_as: put the trends in the passive to raise your band
body.truth: The figures in a chart rise, fall, peak and level off by themselves. Those verbs take no object, so they have no passive. The passive belongs to the process diagram, where a material really is being worked on.
body.what_to_do: Use plain verbs for the numbers: *rose*, *fell*, *peaked*. Save the passive for process and map tasks, where somebody is doing something to something.

body.mechanism: Arabic marks the passive by a regular change inside the verb, and the pattern fits a wide range of verbs.
body.wrong: Three of the deliveries were arrived late.
body.right: Three of the deliveries arrived late.
body.fix: Check that the verb can take an object before you make it passive.

body.headline: Ask *…something?* after the verb before you build any passive.

rows: a verb with a small word
It is believed that costs fell.
a shape with no time on it

items.prompt: Why is *A serious fault was occurred during testing* wrong?
items.answer: You cannot *occur something*, so *occur* has no passive: *A serious fault occurred during testing.*
items.why: Only a verb that takes an object has anything to move to the front.

items.prompt: Which is more usual? *A refund was sent to her.* / *She was sent a refund.*
items.answer: *She was sent a refund.*
items.why: When a verb has a person and a thing after it, English usually puts the person in front.

title: Questions you answer with yes or no

article_json.also_called: Yes/no questions, and the helping-verb swap
article_json.one_line: This lets you turn a statement into a question that the other person can answer with *yes* or with *no*.
article_json.short_answer: Put the helping verb in front of the subject. With no helping verb, start with *do*, *does* or *did*: *Does the bus stop here?*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I turn a statement into a question?

body.text: What this kind of question asks the other person
A yes/no question hands the other person two answers to choose from. They say yes, or they say no, and either one finishes the job.
So this question needs no question word at the front. What it needs is a change of order, and English makes that change the same way every time.
Move the helping verb in front of the subject

body.caption: The helping verb jumps in front of the subject. Nothing else moves.
rows: The results will come out today.
Will the results come out today?
The bus stops at the clinic.
Does the bus stop at the clinic?
The bus stopped at the clinic.
Did the bus stop at the clinic?
footnotes: The last two rows had no helping verb, so English put one in and the main verb went back to its plain form.

body.text: In the first four rows one word moved and everything else stayed put. In the last two there was no word to move, so *does* and *did* took the time and the person, and *stops* became *stop*.

body.caption: Three boxes. The first one is the word you moved.

body.lead_in: The statement already had a helping verb in each of these. Watch which word moved to the front.

items.text: Is the ferry running today?
items.gloss: You want to know whether it is running. Yes or no settles it.

items.text: Have the results been published?
items.gloss: You want to know whether they are out yet.

items.text: Can the council refuse the application?
items.gloss: You want to know whether refusing it is allowed.

items.text: Should we book the room in advance?
items.gloss: You want advice about booking early.

items.text: Was the site closed all week?
items.gloss: You want to know whether anybody could get on to it.

body.so_what: Every one of them starts with a word taken out of the middle of a statement.

body.lead_in: None of these statements had a helping verb, so *do*, *does* or *did* went in at the front.

items.text: Does the clinic open on Saturdays?
items.gloss: You want to know whether you can go at the weekend.

items.text: Did the survey close in March?
items.gloss: You want to know whether it is too late to take part.

items.text: Do the buses run after nine?
items.gloss: You want to know whether you can get home late.

items.text: Did the panel reach a decision?
items.gloss: You want to know whether the matter is settled.

body.so_what: *Do*, *does* and *did* carry the time and the person, so the verb behind them is the plain form.

body.text: Put the helping verb in front of the subject. If the statement has no helping verb, put *do*, *does* or *did* in front and use the plain verb.

body.lead_in: One statement, four times. Only the time changes, and only the first word shows it.

items.text: Is the depot open at weekends?
items.gloss: You are asking about how things stand now.

items.text: Was the depot open last weekend?
items.gloss: You are asking about one weekend that is over.

items.text: Has the depot been open all week?
items.gloss: You are asking about the stretch running up to today.

items.text: Will the depot be open in August?
items.gloss: You are asking about a month that has not come yet.

body.so_what: Only the first word changed. Everything behind it stayed where it was.

body.text: The verb *be* moves on its own
*Is*, *are*, *was* and *were* need no help. When one of them is the only verb in the sentence, it moves to the front by itself, and *do* never appears.

body.lead_in: There is no other verb in any of these, so *be* does the moving.

items.text: Are the seats free at the back?
items.gloss: You want to know whether you can sit there.

items.text: Was the second route cheaper?
items.gloss: You want to know which one cost less.

items.text: Is the training free for staff?
items.gloss: You want to know whether staff have to pay.

body.so_what: None of them has *do* in it, because there was already a word that could move.

body.text: Which word starts the question?

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

steps.ask: Does the statement contain *is*, *are*, *was* or *were*?

verdict.use: that word, moved to the front
verdict.example: Is the coast road open?
verdict.why: *Be* is its own helping verb, so nothing needs to be put in.

steps.ask: Does it contain *have*, *will*, *can*, *must* or another helper?

verdict.use: that word, moved to the front
verdict.example: Have the tenants replied?
verdict.why: The first helper is the one that moves. Later ones stay where they are.

steps.ask: Is the statement about the past?

verdict.example: Did the meeting finish early?
verdict.why: *Did* takes the past, so the verb behind it loses its past shape.

verdict.example: Does the office close at four?
verdict.why: Use *does* for *he*, *she*, *it* or one thing, and *do* for the rest.

body.text: Most sentences stop at the first two questions. The third one only comes up when the statement has no helping verb anywhere in it.
What goes wrong

body.wrong: Did the survey closed in March?
body.right: Did the survey close in March?
body.why_it_happens: The statement was *the survey closed*, and that past shape feels like part of the word. *Did* has already taken the past, so the verb behind it goes back to its plain form.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-ed* off the main verb. Only one word in the question carries the time.

body.wrong: Does the clinic opens on Saturdays?
body.right: Does the clinic open on Saturdays?
body.why_it_happens: The statement was *the clinic opens*, and the *-s* looks like it belongs to the verb. The *-s* has moved onto *does*, and it cannot sit in two places at once.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-s* off the main verb. *Does* is already carrying it.

body.wrong: You have sent the application form?
body.right: Have you sent the application form?
body.why_it_happens: In speech you can leave the words in statement order and raise your voice at the end, and it works. On the page there is no voice, so the order has to do the work.
body.smallest_fix: Move the helping verb to the front whenever you are writing.

body.label: One older shape you will meet in reading and should not copy

items.text: When *have* means *own*, modern English uses *do*: *Does she have a permit?*
items.example: Does the flat have a second exit?

items.text: The older British shape moves *have* itself. It sounds dated and formal.
items.example: Has she a permit?

body.heard: To make a question, put a question mark at the end and raise your voice.
also_known_as: a question mark is what makes it a question
body.truth: That works in speech and it does not work on the page. *You have sent the form?* has a question mark and is still written as a statement. What makes it a question in English is the order: the helping verb sits in front of the subject.
body.what_to_do: Move the helping verb to the front, then add the question mark. Keep the statement-with-a-question-mark shape for speech, where the rise in your voice does the same job.

body.mechanism: Chinese turns a statement into a yes/no question by adding a small word at the end, and nothing in the sentence moves.
body.wrong: The ferry is running today?
body.right: Is the ferry running today?
body.fix: Move the helping verb to the front. English has no word you can add at the end instead.

body.mechanism: Tamil marks a yes/no question with an ending added to a word, and the word order stays as it is.
body.wrong: The clinic opens on Saturdays?
body.right: Does the clinic open on Saturdays?
body.fix: Start the question with *do*, *does* or *did* when there is no other helping verb.

body.headline: One word moves to the front. If there is no such word, put one in.

title: Asking for information

article_json.also_called: *Wh*-questions: the question words, and object questions
article_json.one_line: This lets you ask for one piece of information — a time, a place, a reason, a person or an amount.
article_json.short_answer: Put the question word first, then build a yes/no question behind it: *Where did the survey take place?*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I ask a question that needs a real answer, not yes or no?

body.text: What this kind of question asks for
A yes/no question offers two answers. This one leaves a hole in the sentence and asks the other person to fill it, so the answer can be anything.
The hole is marked by one word at the front, and that word says what kind of thing is missing: a time, a place, a person, a reason.

body.gloss: *who*, *what*, *which*, *where*, *when*, *why*, *how*

show_first.text: Where is the second entrance?
Why did the line close early?
How many people applied this year?

body.name_line: The word at the front is called the **question word**.
body.anchor_line: Each one names the shape of the missing piece. Answer with the wrong shape and the other person will ask again.

body.text: What each question word asks for

body.caption: Pick the word by the shape of the answer you want back.
rows: a person, in a formal letter
To whom should the form be sent?
Whose signature is on the last page?
a thing, from an open set
Which of the two routes is shorter?
How did they measure the drift?
How long has the ferry been running?
How often is the bridge inspected?
How far is the depot from the port?
What is the coast road like in winter?

body.text: Why the question sounds unfinished without it
Many verbs carry a small placing word with them. You *wait for* a bus, *apply for* a job, *write to* somebody, *depend on* somebody. The verb is not finished without it.
When you turn one of those into a question, the small word has nowhere to go, so English leaves it standing at the end. That is not sloppy. It is the normal shape.

body.text: Why English does not repeat the whole sentence
Somebody asks *Have you sent the form?* Everything in that question is already shared, so repeating it back adds nothing. English keeps one word from it and leaves the rest out.
The word it keeps is the helping verb. That single word is enough to point back at the whole question, and the listener fills in the rest without noticing.

body.right: Have you finished the form? — Yes, I have.
body.why_it_happens: The run-together form is what you hear all day, so it comes out here as well. A short answer ends on the helping verb, and a run-together form cannot be a last word.
body.smallest_fix: Write the helping verb out in full: *Yes, I have.* The negative ones do run together: *No, I haven't.*

body.wrong: Do you work at the clinic? — Yes, I work.
body.right: Do you work at the clinic? — Yes, I do.
body.why_it_happens: Repeating the main verb feels like a fuller, more helpful answer. English brings back the helping verb instead, and the main verb is the word it leaves out.
body.smallest_fix: Use the word that started the question: *do*, *does* or *did*.

body.wrong: Have you sent the application form? — Yes, I have sent the application form.
body.right: Have you sent the application form? — Yes, I have. I sent it on Monday.
body.why_it_happens: Repeating every word looks careful and complete on paper. In speech it sounds like a translation exercise, because everything after the helping verb is already known.
body.smallest_fix: Stop after the helping verb, then add something the other person does not know yet.

body.heard: Answering with only *yes* or *no* is rude in English.
also_known_as: you must always answer in a full sentence
body.truth: A bare *yes* is not rude. It is short. The problem is different: in a conversation where somebody is listening to your English, one word gives them nothing to work with. *Yes, I do.* costs two more words and sounds like speech.
body.what_to_do: Use the short answer, then add one reason or one example. That turns a dead end into an answer without making you talk for a minute.

title: *…, isn't it?*

article_json.also_called: Question tags, all patterns, and what the rise or fall means
article_json.one_line: This lets you turn a statement into something that invites the other person to agree with you or to confirm it.
article_json.short_answer: Take the helping verb, flip positive to negative, and use a short subject word: *The lift works, doesn't it?*

article_json.risk_note: Four things must be right in a tag: the helping verb, the flip, the short subject word and the tune. In writing, use none of them.

body.text: Four steps, and the same four every time
A tag is a two-word question stuck on the end of a statement. It does not ask for new information. It asks the other person to come in and agree.

body.gloss: the short question added to the end: *…, isn't it?*

show_first.text: The ferry runs on Sundays, doesn't it?
You've seen the new timetable, haven't you?
The gates weren't locked, were they?

body.name_line: That two-word ending is called a **question tag**.
body.anchor_line: It belongs to speech. Many languages have one fixed ending that does this job. English rebuilds it for every sentence.

body.text: Take the helping verb out of the statement. Flip it — positive becomes negative, negative becomes positive. Put a short subject word after it. Run the negative together: *isn't it*, never *is not it*.

body.caption: The tag flips whatever the statement had. Nothing else changes.
body.form_line: the helping verb (with or without *not*) + a short subject word

notes: A tag belongs to speech. It has no place in an essay.
The tag always uses a short subject word, never the full name of the thing.
*Aren't I?* is standard in speech. *Am I not?* is the formal version.
Same-shape tags exist — *So you've finished, have you?* — and carry surprise or interest.

body.text: The tune decides what the tag means
Two speakers can say the same tag and mean opposite things. The words are identical. What separates them is whether the voice goes down at the end or up.

body.caption: Down means agree with me. Up means I do not know.

title: The other shapes a question comes in

article_json.also_called: Negative, alternative, echo, reply, declarative and reduced questions

article_json.question_in_learner_words: What does a question like *Didn't you?* or *Has it?* actually ask?

body.text: Not every question is asking for a fact
A plain question leaves a hole and waits. The shapes on this page do something else. They check something you already believe, or they show that you are listening, or they save words.
Five of the six belong to speech, so they are worth recognising more than producing. The first one is different, because it turns up in reading and in letters as well.
Six shapes, and what each one does

body.caption: Only the first shape is safe in an essay. The rest are speech.
rows: Do you want the report or the summary?
the question word in that word's place
a statement, with your voice rising
ask in as few words as you can

footnotes: The two-choice question is answered with one of the two, never with *yes* or *no*.

body.text: The two-choice question is the one learners most often answer wrongly. *Do you want the report or the summary?* is not asking whether you want something. It is asking which.

body.lead_in: Four negative questions. Each one shows what the speaker already thinks.

items.text: Haven't they finished the survey yet?
items.gloss: You expected it to be done by now and it is not.

items.text: Isn't the coast road quicker at this hour?
items.gloss: You think it is quicker and you want the driver to agree.

items.text: Didn't the council promise a decision in June?
items.gloss: You remember a promise and it has not been kept.

items.text: Did the council not consider the second site?
items.gloss: You are surprised that a whole site was left out.

body.so_what: None of them is a blank request for information. Each one carries what the speaker was expecting.

body.text: A negative question is not a neutral request for a fact. It asks the other person to agree, or it shows that you are surprised.

body.lead_in: Three replies that keep a conversation moving. Each one repeats one word from what was said.

items.text: The ferry has been cancelled again. — Has it?
items.gloss: You did not know, and you want to hear more.

items.text: They finished the resurfacing last night. — Did they?
items.gloss: You are surprised it went so fast.

items.text: I've been on the waiting list since May. — Have you?
items.gloss: You are showing that you heard and that it matters.

body.so_what: The reply borrows the helping verb from what the other person said, exactly as a short answer does.

body.text: A plain question, or one that already has an answer in mind?

body.question: Would the answer *no* surprise me?

options.label: the plain question
options.use_it_when: You do not know, and any answer would do. This is the one that belongs in writing.
options.example: Is the second route quicker at this hour?

options.label: the negative question
options.use_it_when: You already think you know, and you want that confirmed — or something has surprised you.
options.example: Isn't the second route quicker at this hour?

a.text: Is the second route quicker?
a.means: You have no idea which one is faster.

b.text: Isn't the second route quicker?
b.means: You believe it is faster and you want that confirmed.

a.text: Did they finish the survey?
a.means: You do not know whether the work is done.

b.text: Didn't they finish the survey?
b.means: You thought it was done, and something suggests it is not.

a.text: Have the results come out?
a.means: You are asking for news you do not have.

b.text: Haven't the results come out?
b.means: You expected them by now, and you are surprised.

a.text: Would you like tea?
a.means: One drink is on offer, and yes or no settles it.

b.text: Would you like tea or coffee?
b.means: Two drinks are on offer, and the answer names one of them.

body.deciding_factor: If the answer *no* would surprise you, use the negative question. If any answer would do, use the plain one.
body.trap: A negative question looks like a plain question with *not* added, so it goes into an essay, where it reads as though you are pushing the reader to agree with you.
body.register_note: The plain question belongs everywhere. The negative one is natural in speech and in an informal letter, and it is out of place in Task 2.

body.lead_in: Three short questions, all of them normal in speech and none of them in an essay.

items.text: Any idea when the results come out?
items.gloss: You are asking whether the other person knows the date.

items.text: Coming to the site visit tomorrow?
items.gloss: You are asking whether they will be there.

items.text: You're taking the early train, then?
items.gloss: You worked it out from something they said and you are checking.

body.so_what: Each one drops words the listener can fill in, which is why a reader with no context cannot.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: Any idea when the results come out?
body.right: Could you tell me when the results come out?
body.why_it_happens: The short shape is what you hear all day, and it feels friendly rather than lazy. On the page there is no voice and no shared context, so the missing words are missing for the reader too.
body.smallest_fix: Put the dropped words back and wrap the question: *Could you tell me…*

body.wrong: Did not the council approve the plan?
body.right: Didn't the council approve the plan?
body.why_it_happens: The full form is learned first and feels safer than the run-together one, so it goes everywhere. When *not* is written out it goes after the subject, and the shape it makes is formal.
body.smallest_fix: Run *not* together with the helping verb, or move it behind the subject: *Did the council not approve it?*

body.heard: *Isn't it…?* is the negative of *Is it…?*, so it means the same thing with *not* added.
also_known_as: a negative question is just a question about a negative
body.truth: The two ask for different things. *Is the coast road open?* is a request for a fact. *Isn't the coast road open?* says you believed it was, and you are checking or you are surprised. The *not* changes what the question expects.
body.what_to_do: Use the negative question when you already have an answer in mind. Use the plain one in writing, where a reader cannot hear your surprise.
